title: Physical Atari: A Robust and Accessible Platform for Real-time Reinforcement Learning on Robots
summary: We built a robot called the Robotroller that actuates an Atari CX40+ controller and a device called the Atari Devbox that renders the game frame and the reward signal from the Arcade Learning Environment on a screen. The Robotroller and the Atari Devbox, together with an off-the-shelf camera and a desktop computer, constitute a system that can be used to study reinforcement learning algorithms in the physical world. We call the full system Physical Atari. In this paper, we detail the key decisions that make Physical Atari a robust and accessible platform. To make the system robust, we designed the Robotroller so that all movement is done through bearings, which reduces wear. Additionally, we wrote software that monitors the state of the servos at a high frequency and intervenes to limit stress. To make the system accessible, we used affordable off-the-shelf components and parts that can be manufactured using consumer 3D printers. Physical Atari can be built for under $1,000 and has been used for weeks of non-stop reinforcement learning experiments without any mechanical failures. We used it to validate that reinforcement learning algorithms can learn directly on robots and show that even small distribution shifts between learning and deployment can significantly degrade the performance of policies. Our results underscore the importance of on-device adaptation for strong performance on robots.

AI.tldr: Physical Atari is an open-source, robust, and affordable hardware platform ($<1,000) built from a Robotroller (actuating an Atari controller), Atari Devbox (rendering ALE game frames), a camera, and a desktop computer. It enables weeks-long, non-stop reinforcement learning experiments directly on physical robots, demonstrating that on-device adaptation is critical to overcome performance degradation from distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: To create a robust, accessible, and low-cost physical platform for studying reinforcement learning algorithms directly on real robots, addressing the gap between simulated and physical-world RL experimentation.
AI.method: The system comprises: (1) Robotroller — actuates an Atari CX40+ controller with bearing-based movement for reduced wear; (2) Atari Devbox — renders game frames and reward signals from the Arcade Learning Environment on a screen; (3) an off-the-shelf camera captures screen output; (4) a desktop computer runs RL algorithms. High-frequency servo monitoring software limits stress. Components use consumer 3D-printed parts and affordable off-the-shelf items.
AI.result: Physical Atari was built for under $1,000, operated for weeks of non-stop RL experiments without mechanical failures. Experiments validated that RL algorithms can learn directly on robots, and revealed that even small distribution shifts between learning and deployment significantly degrade policy performance.
AI.conclusion: On-device adaptation is essential for achieving strong performance on robots; the Physical Atari platform provides a robust, accessible means to study this critical challenge.

title: WorkBenchMark: A LEGO-Based Assembly Benchmark with an Assembly-by-Disassembly Baseline for the Smart Manufacturing League
summary: We introduceWorkBenchMark, a LEGO Duplo-based robotic assembly benchmark motivated by the RoboCup Smart Manufacturing League. Robotic assembly couples low-level manipulation with task-level symbolic reasoning under physical constraints, a combination that current end-to-end learning methods do not yet solve reliably. The benchmark provides 400 tasks across four complexity tiers. We provide an open-vocabulary perception, Assembly-by-Disassembly baseline solution. Our planning-based pipeline outperforms a modern vision-language-action approach across all tiers. The benchmark, simulation environment, and baseline implementation will be released openly to support the broader robotic assembly community.

AI.tldr: WorkBenchMark is a LEGO Duplo-based robotic assembly benchmark with 400 tasks across 4 complexity tiers, where a planning-based pipeline using Assembly-by-Disassembly outperforms vision-language-action approaches.
AI.motivation: Robotic assembly combines low-level manipulation with task-level symbolic reasoning under physical constraints, which current end-to-end learning methods cannot reliably solve.
AI.method: The benchmark provides 400 tasks across four complexity tiers with an open-vocabulary perception, Assembly-by-Disassembly baseline solution.
AI.result: The planning-based pipeline outperforms a modern vision-language-action approach across all tiers.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark, simulation environment, and baseline implementation will be released openly to support the broader robotic assembly community.

title: 3D Scene Graphs: Open Challenges and Future Directions
comment: Invited article for the Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems Volume 10
summary: 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs) have emerged as a powerful representation for spatial AI by combining geometric grounding with semantic and relational abstractions of the environment. Their expressiveness has made them relevant to a broad range of problems in robotics and computer vision, including manipulation, navigation, task planning, scene understanding, and many others. However, the field remains fragmented: different communities adopt distinct formulations, construction pipelines, and evaluation protocols, making it difficult to compare methods, identify common assumptions, and assess remaining challenges for robust real-world deployment. This survey provides a unified and critical review of 3DSGs, with particular emphasis on open challenges and future directions. We first formalize 3DSGs under a common definition and analyze the principal modeling choices that characterize existing formulations, including node and edge attributes, hierarchical structure, dynamic scene representations, and affordance-aware extensions. We then review how 3DSGs are built from raw sensory observations, discussing the most common terminologies, conventions, and techniques. Finally, we examine downstream applications and evaluation strategies, from intrinsic graph quality to task-level performance. To support the community, we also provide a dedicated website that organizes and extends the surveyed content, accessible at https://3dscenegraphs.com/.

AI.tldr: This survey provides a unified and critical review of 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs), formalizing definitions, analyzing modeling choices, reviewing construction pipelines from raw sensory data, and examining downstream applications and evaluation strategies, while highlighting open challenges and future directions for the field.
AI.motivation: 3DSGs have become a powerful representation for spatial AI combining geometric grounding with semantic and relational scene abstractions, applicable to robotics and computer vision problems. However, the field is fragmented across different communities with distinct formulations, pipelines, and evaluation protocols, making comparisons difficult and hindering robust real-world deployment.
AI.method: The paper first formalizes 3DSGs under a common definition and analyzes modeling choices (node/edge attributes, hierarchical structure, dynamic representations, affordance-aware extensions). It then reviews construction pipelines from raw sensory observations, discussing terminologies, conventions, and techniques. Finally, it examines downstream applications and evaluation strategies from intrinsic graph quality to task-level performance.
AI.result: A unified and critical survey that identifies common assumptions, compares existing formulations, and assesses remaining challenges for robust real-world deployment of 3DSGs across manipulation, navigation, task planning, and scene understanding domains.
AI.conclusion: The survey highlights the fragmented nature of 3DSG research and provides a structured framework to unify the field, while identifying open challenges and future research directions for advancing 3DSG-based spatial AI systems.

title: DiffusionVS: A Generative Framework for Robust Visual Servoing Based on Diffusion Policy
summary:
Visual servoing is a fundamental technique in robotic manipulation and navigation. Regression-based visual servoing frequently experiences trajectory jitter as a result of noise-sensitive single-step mappings and the accumulation of errors during distribution shifts. In contrast, Diffusion Policy maintains temporal consistency by predicting action sequences and improves robustness through implicit data augmentation.
  This paper presents a novel diffusion-based servoing method. Based on Diffusion Policy, the proposed approach uses normalized image coordinates of observed tag corners as input and generates camera velocity through conditional denoising. To overcome the generalization limitations of models trained on static datasets, an online training paradigm is adopted, continuously expanding the diversity of training data through interactive experience collection. This strategy substantially enhances both the performance and generalization capability of the model. Comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving success rates of nearly 100\% in simulation and 93\% in physical experiments. Beyond the specific pipeline, we further validate the generality of the diffusion mechanism. Experiments show that existing visual servoing networks consistently achieve improved performance when integrated with our diffusion-based module. These results indicate that the proposed strategy possesses broad applicability and can enhance various visual servoing systems beyond the specific architecture presented here.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based visual servoing method that uses normalized image coordinates of tag corners as input and generates camera velocity via conditional denoising, with an online training paradigm for improved generalization, achieving ~100% simulation and 93% real-world success rates.
AI.motivation: Regression-based visual servoing suffers from trajectory jitter due to noise-sensitive single-step mappings and accumulation of errors during distribution shifts. Diffusion Policy mitigates these with temporal consistency and implicit data augmentation.
AI.method: The method builds on Diffusion Policy, taking normalized image coordinates of observed tag corners as input and generating camera velocity through conditional denoising. An online training paradigm continuously expands training data diversity via interactive experience collection.
AI.result: Nearly 100% success rate in simulation and 93% in physical experiments. The diffusion-based module also improves performance of existing visual servoing networks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed diffusion-based strategy possesses broad applicability and can enhance various visual servoing systems beyond the specific architecture presented.

title: Deontic Policies for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. To be published in the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Agentic Services which is part of the IEEE Conference on Web Services
summary: Autonomous agentic AI systems driven by Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new class of security, privacy, and compliance challenges: an agent that can invoke tools, manipulate data, install software, and coordinate with peer agents across organizational boundaries must be constrained not just by authentication and access control, but by the full structure of enterprise governance. This includes specifying what agents are permitted and prohibited from doing, what they areobliged to do after certain actions (e.g., notify the CISO), under what conditions a standing obligation may be waived, and which rules take precedence when policies conflict. This governance problem exceeds what current policy engines provide. Systems such as XACML, Rego, and Cedar address only the permit/prohibit subset of this governance structure. They do not provide obligation lifecycle management, meta-policy conflict resolution, dispensations that waive obligations in specific circumstances, and ontological reasoning over domain class hierarchies commonly found in applications such as healthcare, cybersecurity, or data privacy. We propose AgenticRei, which realizes key governance requirements such as obligations, dispensations, policy conflict resolutions, and reasoning over policies, as well as the basic permit/prohibit constraints. We use a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework, expressed as OWL (Web Ontology Language) and evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations by the agent and agent-to-agent messages. We show through examples that deontic policies capture governance constraints around security and privacy that mostly cannot be expressed in current production engines. Our approach composes naturally with industry-standard frameworks like A2AS.

AI.tldr: AgenticRei extends LLM-based autonomous agents with deontic governance (obligations, dispensations, conflict resolution, ontological reasoning) beyond traditional permit/prohibit policy engines like XACML, Rego, and Cedar, using OWL-based policies evaluated by an external logic engine at runtime.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven autonomous agents introduce complex governance needs (obligations, waivers, conflict resolution, domain reasoning) that exceed the capabilities of current policy engines like XACML, Rego, and Cedar, which only handle permit/prohibit constraints.
AI.method: AgenticRei implements deontic policies using the Rei framework expressed in OWL, evaluated at runtime by a high-performance external logic engine (outside the LLM), governing both tool invocations and agent-to-agent messages, composable with A2AS standards.
AI.result: Deontic policies capture governance constraints around security and privacy that mostly cannot be expressed in current production policy engines.
AI.conclusion: AgenticRei demonstrates that deontic policy frameworks are necessary and feasible for governing autonomous agentic AI systems, addressing obligations, dispensations, conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning beyond traditional access control models.

title: Playful Agentic Robot Learning
summary: Current agentic robot systems can write executable Code-as-Policy programs, observe feedback, and revise behavior across multiple attempts, but they remain largely task-driven: reusable skills are acquired only after explicit instructions. We study Playful Agentic Robot Learning, where an embodied coding agent uses self-directed play as a continual skill-learning stage before downstream tasks arrive. We introduce RATs, Robotics Agent Teams designed for play-time skill acquisition. During play, RATs proposes novel yet learnable exploratory tasks, plans and executes robot-code policies, verifies intermediate progress, diagnoses failures, retries with dense, step-level feedback, and distills successful executions into a persistent code skill library. At test time, the agent reuses relevant skills from this frozen library to help solve new tasks. Experiments in LIBERO-PRO and MolmoSpaces show that play-learned skills improve held-out downstream tasks over no-play and random-play baselines, with 20.6 and 17.0 percentage-point gains over CaP-Agent0 on LIBERO-PRO and MolmoSpaces, respectively. Moreover, the learned skills can be plugged into other inference-time Code-as-Policy agents by simply retrieving them into the context, improving RoboSuite and real-world transfer by 8.9 and 8.8 points, respectively, without finetuning the underlying model.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RATs (Robotics Agent Teams), a framework for Playful Agentic Robot Learning where an embodied coding agent engages in self-directed play to acquire reusable code skills before downstream tasks. RATs proposes exploratory tasks, executes robot-code policies, verifies progress, diagnoses failures, and distills successful executions into a persistent skill library. Experiments show 20.6% and 17.0% gains over baselines on LIBERO-PRO and MolmoSpaces, and learned skills transfer to other agents without finetuning.
AI.motivation: Current agentic robot systems are largely task-driven and only acquire reusable skills after explicit instructions. The authors aim to enable self-directed play as a continual skill-learning stage before downstream tasks arrive, allowing robots to proactively explore and build skill libraries without task-specific supervision.
AI.method: RATs (Robotics Agent Teams) is introduced as a multi-agent framework for play-time skill acquisition. During play, RATs proposes novel yet learnable exploratory tasks, plans and executes robot-code (Code-as-Policy) programs, verifies intermediate progress, diagnoses failures, retries with dense step-level feedback, and distills successful executions into a persistent code skill library. At test time, the agent retrieves and reuses relevant skills from this frozen library to help solve new tasks.
AI.result: On LIBERO-PRO and MolmoSpaces, RATs achieves 20.6 and 17.0 percentage-point gains over CaP-Agent0. The learned skills also transfer to other Code-as-Policy agents at inference time by retrieval into context, improving RoboSuite and real-world transfer by 8.9 and 8.8 points respectively without finetuning the underlying model.
AI.conclusion: Playful agentic robot learning with RATs effectively enables self-directed skill acquisition that generalizes to downstream tasks and transfers across different Code-as-Policy agents without finetuning, demonstrating the value of play as a continual learning stage in robotics.

title: Measuring Curriculum Alignment across Topical Coverage, Competency, and Cognitive Depth: A Longitudinal Framework Applied to CS2013 and CS2023
summary: Undergraduate computer science is governed by international curricular guidelines revised about once a decade, yet programs lack a reliable, reproducible way to measure how completely they cover the current guidelines and how that coverage shifts when the guidelines are restructured. We address this with a human-in-the-loop pipeline that measures a program's coverage of an external body of knowledge, applied longitudinally to one accredited BSc in Computer Science against Computer Science Curricula 2013 (CS2013) and 2023 (CS2023). The pipeline represents the program and each guideline as structured corpora, generates candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches by semantic retrieval, and confirms them through human judgment under an explicit coverage definition. Of seven benchmarked retrievers, a reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble was strongest, and a reputed long-context model underperformed a small sentence model, so retriever choice must be measured. Both maps were validated by an independent second rater (Cohen's kappa 0.64 for CS2023, 0.69 for CS2013). The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units, near-constant across a decade. Extending the same retrieve-then-confirm design to competency articulation and cognitive depth shows that the program articulates the competency for ~88% of covered units under each guideline, yet delivers it at the recommended depth for 76% of present units under CS2023 against 95% under CS2013, a gap reflecting the newer guideline's raised expectations, not the program. The longitudinal comparison separates persistent structural gaps (parallel and distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, systems fundamentals), uncovered against both guidelines and ABET, from differences that reflect the standard's evolution. The instrument is reusable and available from the authors on request.

AI.tldr: A reusable human-in-the-loop pipeline measures a CS program's coverage of curricular guidelines (CS2013 vs CS2023), finding ~50% knowledge unit coverage across both, stable competency articulation (~88%), but a drop in cognitive depth delivery (95%→76%) due to CS2023's raised expectations rather than program changes.
AI.motivation: Computer science programs lack a reliable, reproducible method to measure how completely they cover international curricular guidelines (revised ~decadally) and how coverage shifts when guidelines are restructured.
AI.method: A human-in-the-loop pipeline that (1) represents the program and guidelines as structured corpora, (2) generates candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches via semantic retrieval (with seven benchmarked retrievers, best being reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble), and (3) confirms matches through human judgment under an explicit coverage definition, validated by independent second rater (Cohen's kappa 0.64–0.69).
AI.result: The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units. Competency articulation is ~88% for covered units under both guidelines, but cognitive depth delivery drops from 95% (CS2013) to 76% (CS2023) due to guideline changes. Persistent structural gaps include parallel/distributed computing, programming languages foundations, and systems fundamentals.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline separates persistent structural gaps from differences caused by guideline evolution; the instrument is reusable and available upon request.

title: Simulating Robotic Locomotion in Sand: Resistive Force Theory in an Open-Source Physics Engine
summary: Recent advancements in Resistive Force Theory (RFT) enable approximation of ground reaction forces for locomotion in sand without the computational expense of modeling interactions with individual grains. However, these tools have been absent in 3D physics engines commonly used for robot simulation. We explore if resistive force approximations are sufficient, when integrated with standard dynamics calculations, to provide a stable substrate for a freely walking robot. To determine this, we implement 3D Granular Resistive Force Theory (3D RFT) in a physics simulation engine, MuJoCo. We verify simulations in multiple scenarios to demonstrate that key trends due to end effector shape, speed, and loading are preserved. Our implementation predicts walking distance and foot sinkage of a 12-Degree of Freedom hexapod robot within 20\% of experiments in sand. While RFT has inherent approximations, the open source tool described here has potential to help develop new and improved robot designs to traverse granular media substrates.

AI.tldr: The paper implements 3D Granular Resistive Force Theory (3D RFT) in the MuJoCo physics engine to simulate robot locomotion on sand, achieving predictions of walking distance and foot sinkage within 20% of experimental results for a 12-DOF hexapod robot.
AI.motivation: Resistive Force Theory (RFT) allows approximating ground reaction forces for sand locomotion without modeling individual grain interactions, but has been absent in 3D physics engines commonly used for robot simulation. The authors want to determine if these approximations are sufficient for stable robot simulation.
AI.method: The authors implement 3D Granular Resistive Force Theory (3D RFT) in the MuJoCo physics simulation engine and verify simulations across multiple scenarios, examining effects of end effector shape, speed, and loading.
AI.result: The implementation predicts walking distance and foot sinkage of a 12-DOF hexapod robot within 20% of experimental sand measurements. Key trends due to end effector shape, speed, and loading are preserved in simulations.
AI.conclusion: Despite inherent approximations in RFT, the open-source tool has potential to help develop new and improved robot designs for traversing granular media substrates.

title: Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized language modeling through autoregressive generation, enabling strong performance across a wide range of tasks. Recently, Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as an alternative paradigm that generates text through iterative denoising rather than next-token prediction, allowing parallel refinement of entire sequences. While numerous diffusion-based architectures have been proposed, differences in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and generation hyperparameters make it difficult to compare their capabilities and understand the trade-offs they offer. In this work, we present a systematic experimental analysis of modern DLMs. Specifically, we evaluate eight state-of-the-art DLMs across eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, and structured problem solving, while explicitly considering both generation quality and computational efficiency. Beyond downstream evaluation, we analyze the impact of key inference-time factors, including denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies, and complement large-scale experiments with controlled comparisons of smaller models trained under identical conditions. Our analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of diffusion-based language modeling across different tasks, architectures, and inference budgets. We show that the behavior of DLMs is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, leading to distinct trade-offs between performance and computational efficiency. Overall, our study provides practical insights into the capabilities and deployment characteristics of contemporary DLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a systematic experimental analysis comparing eight state-of-the-art Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) across eight benchmarks, examining generation quality vs. computational efficiency trade-offs, and analyzing how inference-time factors like denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies impact performance.
AI.motivation: Differences in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and generation hyperparameters across numerous proposed diffusion-based architectures make it difficult to compare DLMs and understand their trade-offs.
AI.method: Evaluated eight state-of-the-art DLMs across eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, and structured problem solving; analyzed key inference-time factors (denoising steps, context length, block size, parallel unmasking); complemented large-scale experiments with controlled comparisons of smaller models trained under identical conditions.
AI.result: DLM behavior is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, leading to distinct trade-offs between performance and computational efficiency. The analysis highlights strengths and limitations of diffusion-based language modeling across tasks, architectures, and inference budgets.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical insights into the capabilities and deployment characteristics of contemporary DLMs, showing that generation-time design choices critically shape performance-efficiency trade-offs.

title: Proprioceptive Invariant State Estimation for Humanoid Robots on Non-Inertial Ground
summary: This paper presents an invariant extended Kalman filtering (InEKF) approach for real-time state estimation of humanoid robots operating on non-inertial ground using only onboard proprioceptive sensing. The proposed approach estimates the robot's base position and velocity relative to the moving ground frame without requiring direct measurements of ground motion or externally mounted sensors. By exploiting kinematic constraints at the stance foot through foot-mounted IMUs, the filter accounts for ground-induced nonlinearities in the process and measurement models while remaining fully proprioceptive. The estimator is formulated to admit a right-invariant measurement model, enabling favorable error dynamics under large initial uncertainties. Observability analysis establishes conditions under which the robot's relative base position and velocity are observable with respect to the non-inertial ground frame. Experiments with the Digit humanoid robot standing and squatting atop a swaying and pitching ground showcase a 96% speedup in convergence rate and an 80% reduction in position estimate errors over existing InEKFs. Walking experiments on a uni-axially rotating ground achieve an average estimation error of less than 9 cm for an initial error of up to 1 m.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an invariant extended Kalman filtering (InEKF) approach for humanoid robot state estimation on moving (non-inertial) ground using only onboard proprioceptive sensors. The method exploits foot-mounted IMUs and kinematic constraints to estimate base position/velocity relative to the moving ground. Experiments on the Digit robot demonstrate 96% faster convergence and 80% lower position errors versus standard InEKFs, with walking errors under 9 cm even with 1 m initial error.
AI.motivation: Existing state estimators for humanoid robots assume an inertial (stationary) ground frame. However, real-world scenarios like ships, vehicles, or earthquake zones involve non-inertial ground motion, which degrades estimator performance. The goal is to enable accurate proprioceptive state estimation on moving ground without external sensors or ground motion measurements.
AI.method: An invariant extended Kalman filter (InEKF) is formulated with a right-invariant measurement model using foot-mounted IMUs. Kinematic constraints at the stance foot are exploited to handle ground-induced nonlinearities. Observability analysis determines conditions for base position/velocity observability relative to the non-inertial ground frame.
AI.result: On the Digit robot: 96% faster convergence rate and 80% reduction in position estimate errors over existing InEKFs during standing/squatting on swaying/pitching ground. Walking on rotating ground achieved under 9 cm average estimation error with up to 1 m initial error.
AI.conclusion: The proposed InEKF effectively enables humanoid robots to estimate their state relative to moving ground using only proprioceptive sensing, with significantly improved convergence and accuracy over conventional methods.

title: Hidden Anchors in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation
summary: Multi-agent LLM deliberation, where agents exchange and revise answers over several rounds, is increasingly used to improve reasoning and accuracy, yet how and why it works is rarely modelled. Such deliberation mirrors how humans reach decisions. As social animals we are pulled both by the group, the herd effect that classical opinion-dynamics models such as DeGroot and Friedkin--Johnsen capture, and by our own internal belief, which they do not. We model multi-agent deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system in which each agent carries a hidden internal belief, its anchor, that continually pulls its opinion regardless of its neighbours. We show this anchor can be recovered from the deliberation alone, and that it explains a behaviour classical consensus rules forbid: an agent's confidence in the correct answer can climb past where any agent started, escaping the space (convexhull) formed by the initial beliefs. Checking whether the recovered anchor also predicts held-out runs (generalizes) gives a simple test for when a model is truly driven bysuch an anchor. Across three open-weight model families this is a spectrum, not all-or-nothing. All anchors' influence are about equally strongly, but they differ in where the anchor sits, and only when it sits far from the initial opinions does deliberation escape the hull and need the full closed-loop model.

AI.tldr: The paper models multi-agent LLM deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent has a hidden internal belief (anchor) that pulls its opinion away from pure consensus, enabling confidence to exceed initial extremes. Using DeGroot/Friedkin-Johnsen opinion dynamics, they show anchors can be recovered from deliberation data and predict held-out runs, revealing a spectrum of anchor-driven behavior across open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM deliberation is widely used but lacks formal models explaining how and why it improves reasoning. Classical opinion-dynamics models capture group influence but ignore internal belief persistence. This work aims to model the tension between social conformity and internal conviction.
AI.method: The authors model deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent has a hidden anchor (internal belief) that continually pulls its opinion. They extend DeGroot/Friedkin-Johnsen models to include anchors, show anchors can be recovered from deliberation traces, and test whether recovered anchors predict held-out deliberation runs across three open-weight model families.
AI.result: Anchors can be recovered from deliberation alone and explain why confidence can climb past initial beliefs (escaping the convex hull). Anchor influence is equally strong across models, but anchor location varies; only when anchors are far from initial opinions does escape from the convex hull occur. The anchor recovery generalizes to held-out runs, providing a test for anchor-driven deliberation.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent LLM deliberation is driven by hidden internal anchors on a spectrum rather than an all-or-nothing basis, and the closed-loop model is necessary only when anchors sit far from initial opinions. The framework provides both explanatory power and a predictive test for when anchor dynamics are at play.

title: A Categorial and Sheaf-Theoretic Semantics for Autonomic Component Ensembles
summary: The proliferation of large-scale, decentralized systems of autonomous agents, such as swarms of robots and networked cyber-physical systems, presents a formidable challenge to traditional formal methods. The Software Component Ensemble Language (SCEL) offers a formal model for such systems, but its operational semantics is not ideal for reasoning about global, structural, and emergent properties. This report proposes a new, multi-layered mathematical model for SCEL using category theory and sheaf theory. We argue that a society of robots described in SCEL can be formally modeled as a sheaf on a topological space, where components are points, ensembles are open sets, and distributed knowledge forms the sheaf's data. In this framework, computational processes like information sharing become equivalent to the sheaf-theoretic operation of "gluing" local data. System failures can then be understood and quantified as topological obstructions, measurable by sheaf cohomology. This approach transforms the verification of a complex distributed system into the analysis of the geometry of a mathematical object, providing deep, structural insights for the design of robust autonomic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a category/sheaf-theoretic model for SCEL (Software Component Ensemble Language) to formalize large-scale decentralized multi-agent systems, where computational processes become gluing operations and system failures are quantified via sheaf cohomology.
AI.motivation: Traditional formal methods struggle to reason about global, structural, and emergent properties of large-scale decentralized autonomous systems (e.g., robot swarms, cyber-physical systems). SCEL's operational semantics is insufficient for such reasoning, motivating the need for a richer mathematical framework.
AI.method: The authors construct a multi-layered mathematical model using category theory and sheaf theory: components are points in a topological space, ensembles are open sets, and distributed knowledge forms sheaf data. Information sharing is modeled as the sheaf-theoretic gluing of local data, and system failures are interpreted as topological obstructions measurable by sheaf cohomology.
AI.result: The framework transforms verification of distributed systems into analysis of the geometry of a mathematical object, enabling quantification of failures via cohomological invariants and providing structural insights into system robustness.
AI.conclusion: The sheaf-theoretic approach offers deep structural insights for designing robust autonomic systems by reifying computational properties as geometric/topological features, potentially opening new avenues for formal verification of emergent behaviors.

title: DeXposure-Claw: An Agentic System for DeFi Risk Supervision
summary: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks. General-purpose LLM agents fit this setting poorly: they over-read weak evidence and recommend high-stakes interventions, while existing evaluations offer no regulator-aligned way to measure the resulting false alarms. We introduce DeXposure-Claw, a forecast-grounded agentic supervision system that routes LLM decisions through structured evidence: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model, forecasts future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios then turn those forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; and (3) data-health and confidence gates constrain escalation before DeXposure-Claw emits auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. We further develop DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis evaluation harness, whose decision axis scores tickets against a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate. Experiments on five years of weekly real data fully support our system. Code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-Claw.

AI.tldr: DeXposure-Claw is a forecast-grounded agentic supervision system that uses a graph time-series foundation model (DeXposure-FM), deterministic monitors, and confidence gates to generate auditable supervisory tickets for decentralized finance risks, evaluated via a six-axis benchmark (DeXposure-Bench) that measures false-intervention rates against regulator-aligned ground truth.
AI.motivation: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks that general-purpose LLM agents handle poorly—they over-read weak evidence and recommend high-stakes interventions, while existing evaluations lack regulator-aligned metrics for false alarms.
AI.method: The system (DeXposure-Claw) routes LLM decisions through structured evidence: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model forecasting future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios turning forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; (3) data-health and confidence gates constraining escalation before emitting auditable supervisory tickets. Evaluation uses DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis harness with a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and explicit false-intervention rate.
AI.result: Experiments on five years of weekly real data fully support the system's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed structured evidence routing approach with confidence gating and regulator-aligned evaluation can mitigate LLM over-intervention in decentralized finance supervision.

title: SCAN-Planner: Spatial Collision-Aware Local Planning for Route-Guided Long-Range Quadruped Navigation
summary: Quadruped robots are increasingly expected to navigate through narrow passages, cluttered indoor scenes, and large-scale 3D unstructured environments. Existing local planners commonly approximate the robot using isotropic geometric inflation or rely on planar and elevation-map representations, leading to conservative motion in tight spaces and limited reasoning about overhanging structures. This letter presents SCAN-Planner, a spatial collision-aware local planning framework for long-range quadruped navigation. A yaw-aware twin-cylinder footprint is used to model the elongated robot body, enabling whole-body collision evaluation through sparse queries in an inflated 3D occupancy map. We further introduce a projected A* search that generates collision-free guidance on an interpolated ground-following surface, with z-gradient suppression to avoid obstacles horizontally while maintaining vertical stability. For large-scale deployment, a robot-centric sliding map with boundary fallback provides high-resolution local collision checking and recovery from local dead ends. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that SCAN-Planner generates safe, smooth, and efficient trajectories in dense clutter, 3D unstructured scenes, stair traversal, and long-range navigation tasks.

AI.tldr: SCAN-Planner is a spatial collision-aware local planning framework for quadruped robots using a yaw-aware twin-cylinder footprint model and projected A* search on a ground-following surface, enabling safe and efficient navigation through narrow passages, dense clutter, 3D unstructured environments, and over long ranges.
AI.motivation: Existing local planners for quadruped robots use oversimplified isotropic models or planar/elevation-map representations, leading to conservative motion in tight spaces and limited ability to reason about overhanging structures, which hinders navigation through narrow passages and complex 3D environments.
AI.method: SCAN-Planner uses (1) a yaw-aware twin-cylinder footprint to model the elongated robot body for whole-body collision evaluation via sparse queries in an inflated 3D occupancy map; (2) a projected A* search generating collision-free guidance on an interpolated ground-following surface with z-gradient suppression; and (3) a robot-centric sliding map with boundary fallback for high-resolution local collision checking and dead-end recovery.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that SCAN-Planner generates safe, smooth, and efficient trajectories in dense clutter, 3D unstructured scenes, stair traversal, and long-range navigation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed spatial collision-aware framework with anisotropic footprint modeling and projected A* search significantly improves quadruped navigation performance in challenging environments compared to conventional local planners.

title: LLM Doesn't Know What It Doesn't Know: Detecting Epistemic Blind Spots via Cross-Model Attribution Divergence on Clinical Tabular Data
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to structured clinical data, yet whether they can recognize the limits of their own knowledge on such tasks remains unexplored. We study this question through the lens of cross-model attribution divergence with the goal of reducing epistemic uncertainty for structured tasks, comparing Qwen 2.5 7B and XGBoost on a prediction task via attribution divergence analysis. We report four findings. First, LLM verbalized confidence is epistemically vacuous, it outputs a near-constant (0.856-0.937) regardless of whether accuracy is 49% or 75.3%, tracking prompt format rather than prediction quality. Second, the LLM exhibits an inverse difficulty effect: accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct, but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) when it is moderately uncertain. Third, few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence are orthogonal, super-additive interventions: they reduce the Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) from 1.54 to 0.38 and improve accuracy from 49% to 75.3% without training. Fourth, a cross-model calibrator that determined LLM reliability using attribution divergence signals reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080, replacing uninformative verbalized confidence with patient-specific reliability estimates, without accessing model internals or requiring repeated inference. We frame these findings as a cold start problem for LLMs on structured data and outline a path toward genuine epistemic self-awareness.

AI.tldr: LLMs lack epistemic self-awareness on structured clinical tasks: their verbalized confidence is uninformative (0.856-0.937 across 49%-75.3% accuracy), they exhibit an inverse difficulty effect (accuracy drops when XGBoost is certain), but combining few-shot examples with SHAP-derived evidence reduces attribution disagreement (ADS 1.54→0.38) and boosts accuracy (49%→75.3%), and a cross-model calibrator using attribution divergence signals reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080 without model internals.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs can recognize the limits of their own knowledge when applied to structured clinical data, specifically through cross-model attribution divergence analysis.
AI.method: Compared Qwen 2.5 7B and XGBoost on a structured prediction task; analyzed attribution divergence using Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS); evaluated LLM verbalized confidence; tested few-shot + SHAP feature interventions; developed a cross-model calibrator using attribution divergence signals.
AI.result: (1) LLM verbalized confidence is nearly constant (0.856-0.937) regardless of accuracy, tracking prompt format; (2) LLM accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct but matches at moderate uncertainty (73.8% vs 73.1%); (3) few-shot + SHAP super-additively reduces ADS from 1.54 to 0.38 and raises accuracy 49%→75.3%; (4) cross-model calibrator reduces ECE from 0.254 to 0.080.
AI.conclusion: LLMs exhibit a cold start problem on structured data: they lack genuine epistemic self-awareness, but attribution divergence signals from a simpler model can calibrate LLM reliability without internal access or repeated inference, pointing toward epistemic self-awareness.

title: pdSTL: Probabilistic Differentiable Signal Temporal Logic for Stochastic Systems
summary: Autonomous robots operating in uncertain environments must satisfy complex temporal and safety specifications despite stochastic dynamics and sensing noise. While Signal Temporal Logic (STL) offers robustness measures for gradient-based optimization, existing extensions either lack differentiability or ignore belief-space uncertainty. We introduce pdSTL (probabilistic differentiable Signal Temporal Logic), a framework that unifies probabilistic semantics with differentiable robustness over belief trajectories. pdSTL employs interval-valued probabilistic semantics to compute conservative satisfaction bounds, propagated compositionally through the STL syntax tree. We formulate the temporal robustness evaluation as a recurrent, LSTM-style unfolding of STL operators, enabling linear-time, differentiable monitoring suitable for end-to-end trajectory optimization. We validate pdSTL on simulated obstacle avoidance, lane-change maneuvers, and real-world Crazyflie quadcopter flight experiments under aerodynamic disturbances. Results demonstrate that pdSTL achieves efficient optimization with formal probabilistic guarantees, significantly outperforming deterministic differentiable STL in maintaining safety margins under real-world uncertainty.

AI.tldr: pdSTL introduces a differentiable Signal Temporal Logic framework with probabilistic semantics for belief-space trajectory optimization under uncertainty, validated on real-world quadcopter flight.
AI.motivation: Existing STL extensions either lack differentiability (needed for gradient-based optimization) or ignore belief-space uncertainty (critical for robots operating under stochastic dynamics and sensing noise).
AI.method: pdSTL uses interval-valued probabilistic semantics to compute conservative satisfaction bounds propagated compositionally through the STL syntax tree, and formulates temporal robustness evaluation as a recurrent, LSTM-style unfolding of STL operators for linear-time differentiable monitoring.
AI.result: pdSTL achieves efficient optimization with formal probabilistic guarantees and significantly outperforms deterministic differentiable STL in maintaining safety margins under real-world uncertainty on simulated obstacle avoidance, lane-change maneuvers, and real Crazyflie quadcopter experiments.
AI.conclusion: pdSTL unifies probabilistic semantics with differentiable robustness over belief trajectories, enabling end-to-end trajectory optimization for autonomous robots operating under uncertainty while providing formal safety guarantees.

title: REVEAL++: Differentiable Phenotypic Grouping for Vision-Language Retinal Modeling of Alzheimer's Disease Risk
summary: The retina offers a noninvasive window into neurodegenerative disease, capturing subtle structural patterns associated with a risk of future cognitive decline. Vision-language alignment frameworks such as REVEAL have shown that pairing retinal fundus images with structured clinical risk narratives improves early prediction of Alzheimer's disease (AD). A key design choice in these approaches is the use of phenotypic grouping, where individuals with similar risk profiles are treated as multi-positive pairs during contrastive learning. However, existing methods operationalize phenotypic similarity as a discrete construct, relying on hard group assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. We propose a continuous formulation of phenotypic structure within contrastive learning. Rather than assigning samples to fixed clusters, we model inter-subject similarity as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and risk profiles. These weights define soft multi-positive relationships through a continuous aggregation operator, enabling graded supervision that reflects the spectrum nature of disease risk. We further introduce a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure in an end-to-end manner. Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines. By treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule, our approach provides a principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

AI.tldr: Proposes a continuous phenotypic similarity formulation for contrastive learning in vision-language alignment of retinal images and clinical risk profiles, replacing discrete group assignments with differentiable weighting functions to improve Alzheimer's disease prediction from UK Biobank data.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language alignment methods like REVEAL use hard phenotypic group assignments (discrete clusters) for multi-positive contrastive learning, which imposes rigid supervision and decouples group formation from representation learning, failing to capture the continuous spectrum nature of disease risk.
AI.method: Models inter-subject similarity as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and risk profiles. These weights define soft multi-positive relationships via a continuous aggregation operator, with a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure end-to-end.
AI.result: Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging for incident AD prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines.
AI.conclusion: Treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule provides a principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

title: One Demo is Worth a Thousand Trajectories: Action-View Augmentation for Visuomotor Policies
summary: Visuomotor policies for manipulation have demonstrated remarkable potential in modeling complex robotic behaviors, yet minor alterations in the robot's initial configuration and unseen obstacles easily lead to out-of-distribution observations. Without extensive data collection effort, these result in catastrophic execution failures. In this work, we introduce an effective data augmentation framework that generates visually realistic fisheye image sequences and corresponding physically feasible action trajectories from real-world eye-in-hand demonstrations, captured with a portable parallel gripper with a single fisheye camera. We introduce a novel Gaussian Splatting formulation, adapted to wide FoV fisheye cameras, to reconstruct and edit the 3D scene with unseen objects. We utilize trajectory optimization to generate smooth, collision-free, view-rendering-friendly action trajectories and render visual observations from corresponding novel views. Comprehensive experiments in simulation and the real world show that our augmentation framework improves the success rate for various manipulation tasks in both the same scene and the augmented scene with obstacles requiring collision avoidance.

AI.tldr: A data augmentation framework using fisheye Gaussian Splatting and trajectory optimization generates realistic visual sequences and feasible action trajectories from real-world demonstrations, improving visuomotor policy robustness against out-of-distribution observations and unseen obstacles.
AI.motivation: Visuomotor policies fail catastrophically due to minor changes in robot configuration or unseen obstacles causing out-of-distribution observations, and existing data collection is insufficient to cover all variations.
AI.method: Novel Gaussian Splatting formulation adapted to wide FoV fisheye cameras for 3D scene reconstruction and editing with unseen objects; trajectory optimization for smooth, collision-free, view-rendering-friendly action trajectories; rendering visual observations from novel views.
AI.result: The augmentation framework improves success rates for manipulation tasks in both the same scene and augmented scenes with obstacles requiring collision avoidance.
AI.conclusion: Fisheye-based Gaussian Splatting with trajectory optimization is an effective data augmentation strategy for enhancing visuomotor policy generalization and robustness.

title: Emergent Alignment
summary: Can Large Language Models (LLMs) discern when their own outputs are misaligned with human ethics? And can they self-correct? We endow an LLM with a conscience step that reviews its own reasoning and outputs, and we extend the training loss with an alignment component using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to steer the model away from non-ethical outputs. The result is an online technique to align models in a wide range of applications: training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot learning. It does not require a weaker or stronger judge, relying instead on a frozen copy of itself. In previous work, the Emergent Misalignment scenario showed a range of emergent unethical behaviors from fine-tuning the model to hack code. Instead, we empirically show how to achieve Emergent Alignment: a single high-level introspective question steers training toward an ethical model under the same code hacking scenario.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method where LLMs self-review their outputs for ethical alignment using a conscience step and DPO-based training loss, enabling emergent alignment without external judges. It demonstrates effectiveness in a code hacking scenario where previous work showed emergent misalignment.
AI.motivation: To enable LLMs to autonomously detect and correct ethical misalignment in their own outputs without relying on external weaker or stronger judge models.
AI.method: The approach adds a conscience step where the LLM reviews its own reasoning and outputs, extends the training loss with an alignment component via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and uses a frozen copy of the model itself. A single high-level introspective question guides training toward ethical behavior.
AI.result: Empirically demonstrates Emergent Alignment: in a code hacking scenario previously shown to cause emergent unethical behaviors, the proposed method steers training toward an ethical model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed online alignment technique works across training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot learning without external judges, successfully achieving emergent ethical alignment where prior work showed emergent misalignment.

title: Safe, Real-Time Active Model Discrimination and Fault Diagnosis for Nonlinear Systems via Differentiable Reachability
summary: We present a safe, real-time algorithm for active fault diagnosis and model discrimination for uncertain continuous-time nonlinear systems with process and measurement disturbances. Given a finite set of candidate models representing nominal and faulty modes, including actuator and sensor faults, we formulate an output-feedback, time-varying policy optimization problem that (i) robustly enforces state-input safety constraints over a finite horizon and (ii) drives the system to produce sampled measurements consistent with at most one model, enabling deterministic diagnosis. To solve this problem in real time, we develop a tractable approximation using interval over-approximations of reachable state and output sets, and encode diagnosability via a differentiable objective that penalizes overlap between the reachable output sets of possible models. The resulting optimization is solved efficiently online with gradient-based methods using JAX and differentiable reachability primitives. We evaluate our method on sensor and actuator fault diagnosis (up to 11 fault modes) in several high-dimensional nonlinear robotic systems, including a simulated quadrotor and fighter-jet model, a hardware differential-drive robot, and quadrupedal navigation. Across these case studies, our approach achieves reliable model discrimination in under 50 ms, outperforming baselines in discrimination success rate and speed while providing formal safety guarantees.

AI.tldr: A real-time, safe active fault diagnosis algorithm for nonlinear systems using interval over-approximations and differentiable reachability to robustly discriminate among fault models while enforcing safety constraints.
AI.motivation: To enable real-time active fault diagnosis for uncertain nonlinear systems where process and measurement disturbances exist, while simultaneously ensuring safety and computational tractability for high-dimensional robotic systems.
AI.method: Formulates an output-feedback time-varying policy optimization that robustly enforces safety constraints and drives measurements consistent with at most one candidate model. Uses interval over-approximations of reachable sets and a differentiable objective penalizing output set overlap, solved via gradient-based methods with JAX and differentiable reachability primitives.
AI.result: Achieves reliable model discrimination in under 50 ms across simulated quadrotor, fighter-jet, hardware differential-drive robot, and quadrupedal navigation, outperforming baselines in success rate and speed with formal safety guarantees.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method enables safe, real-time active fault diagnosis for nonlinear systems with up to 11 fault modes, demonstrating practical applicability on both simulated and real robotic hardware.

title: ITNet: A Learnable Integral Transform That Subsumes Convolution, Attention, and Recurrence
summary: Convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers each encode different inductive biases -- locality, sequential memory, and content-dependent pairwise interaction -- and have remained mathematically distinct since their inception. We show that this fragmentation reflects not a fundamental diversity in how signals should be processed, but rather incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object: a learnable integral transform. We introduce the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified architecture built around a learnable kernel that depends jointly on positions and features. This kernel is implemented as a small neural network, specifically an MLP, that models pairwise interactions, enabling the model to adapt its behavior from data. We show that convolution, self-attention (including multi-head), and autoregressive recurrence (including LSTM, GRU, S4, and Mamba) arise as special cases under appropriate parameterizations, and that ITNet is a universal approximator of continuous operators. To make this practical, we develop tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization, enabling efficient and scalable computation. A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K , GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA\,v2 and NLVR2. The results demonstrate that a single learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of all three architectural families from data.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers are all special cases of a single unified architecture called the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), which uses a learnable kernel implemented as an MLP to model pairwise interactions. ITNet matches or exceeds specialized baselines across diverse tasks including image classification, NLP, 3D point cloud, and VQA.
AI.motivation: To unify the mathematically distinct architectures (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) under a single framework, demonstrating that their apparent diversity reflects incomplete views of a common underlying object: a learnable integral transform.
AI.method: The paper introduces ITNet, built around a learnable kernel (implemented as an MLP) that depends jointly on positions and features. To make computation practical, they develop tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization.
AI.result: Convolution, self-attention (including multi-head), and autoregressive recurrence (LSTM, GRU, S4, Mamba) arise as special cases. ITNet matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K, GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA v2, and NLVR2 with a single shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders.
AI.conclusion: A single learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of all three major architectural families from data, suggesting the fragmentation of architectures is unnecessary.

title: Fail-RAG : A Retrieval Augmented Generation Informed Framework for Robot Failure Identification
summary: Industry automation is witnessing an evolution in robotics driven by both technological breakthroughs and societal changes: progress towards generalist robots, embodied and physical artificial intelligence (AI), and increasing labor shortage in manufacturing.An intelligent autonomous robot needs to not only act according to planned motions but also react to any unexpected events. In this study, we focus on such unexpected events in warehouses where robots are used for material handling. Specifically, we refer to any unexpected events as failures and develop methods to detect robot operations related failures. Rule-based detection methods may break since the form of failures could change due to the dynamic nature of both environments and tasks. We propose 'Fail-RAG', a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)-based failure detection framework where failure images and context information are embedded and queried against a failure database by calculating their similarities. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are further used to analyze failures and provide details by following our instruction template. We evaluated the performance of Fail-RAG by conducting both simulation and physical experiments using fixed robot arms and a mobile manipulator for multiple tasks that are common in warehouse automation. Fail-RAG achieved 25 percentage point higher failure detection accuracy on average across five types of robot operations compared to using off-the-shelf VLMs, indicating its effectiveness for real-world failure detection.

AI.tldr: Fail-RAG is a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)-based framework that uses Vision-Language Models and a failure database to detect robot operation failures in warehouse automation, achieving 25 percentage point higher detection accuracy than off-the-shelf VLMs across five operation types.
AI.motivation: Robots in warehouses need to react to unexpected events (failures) during material handling, but rule-based detection methods are insufficient due to the dynamic nature of environments and tasks.
AI.method: Fail-RAG embeds failure images and context information, queries against a failure database via similarity calculation, and uses Vision-Language Models with an instruction template to analyze and detail failures.
AI.result: Fail-RAG achieved 25 percentage point higher failure detection accuracy on average across five types of robot operations compared to off-the-shelf VLMs, validated through both simulation and physical experiments with fixed robot arms and a mobile manipulator.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RAG-based approach is effective for real-world failure detection in warehouse automation, outperforming standard VLM baselines.

title: Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents
summary: Recent position papers argue that the classical aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty framework is insufficient for interactive large language model (LLM) agents and call for underspecification-aware, decomposed, and communicable uncertainty representations that can unlock new agent capabilities such as proactive clarification seeking and shared mental-model building. Practical deployment constraints -- black-box APIs, interactive latency budgets, and the absence of labeled trajectories -- rule out logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods, leaving prompt-based estimation as the most viable family for surfacing such signals at deployment time. We answer this call with a simple prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u), enabling the agent to ask for clarification when the task specification is ambiguous. To evaluate it, we introduce two clarification-augmented benchmarks (WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification) in which 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified, and systematically compare the proposed decomposition against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B) on these variants together with the standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL benchmarks for fault detection. Averaged across the five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and by 36% over UAM, and leads clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, indicating that the gains generalize beyond a single LLM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a prompt-based decomposition separating action confidence from request uncertainty (u) to enable LLM agents to ask for clarification under underspecified task specifications, showing significant F1 improvements on two new clarification-augmented benchmarks across five LLM backbones.
AI.motivation: The classical aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty framework is insufficient for interactive LLM agents; existing methods (logprob-based, multi-sampling, training-based) are ruled out by black-box APIs, latency budgets, and lack of labeled trajectories. There is a need for underspecification-aware, decomposed, communicable uncertainty representations to enable proactive clarification seeking.
AI.method: A simple prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u), allowing the agent to ask for clarification when task specification is ambiguous. Two new benchmarks (WebShop-Clarification, ALFWorld-Clarification) were introduced with 50% tasks deliberately underspecified.
AI.result: Across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B): On ALFWorld-Clarification, clarification F1 improved by 73% over ReAct+UE and 36% over UAM. The method led clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on 4/5 backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, demonstrating generalization beyond a single LLM.
AI.conclusion: The proposed prompt-based uncertainty decomposition is a viable, generalizable approach for surfacing underspecification signals in interactive LLM agents under practical deployment constraints, enabling proactive clarification seeking capabilities.

title: Formal Verification of Learned Multi-Agent Communication Policies via Decision Tree Distillation
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026), Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA, September 27-October 1, 2026
summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables agents to develop coordination strategies through emergent communication, but neural policies lack the formal safety guarantees required for safety-critical robotic deployment in drone swarms and autonomous vehicle fleets. We present the first end-to-end framework for safety verification of learned multi-agent communication policies through policy abstraction: neural policies are distilled into interpretable decision trees, then formally verified, with empirical validation confirming that verified safety properties transfer to original networks. Our four-stage pipeline consists of domain-specific feature extraction from agent observations, decision tree distillation achieving 97.9% +/- 1.2% fidelity to neural policies, automated translation to PRISM probabilistic model checker specifications with complete feature-to-state-variable correspondence, and compositional verification of Probabilistic Computation Tree Logic (PCTL) properties via pairwise decomposition with union-bound aggregation and empirical neighbor modeling. Evaluating Vector-Quantized Variational Information Bottleneck (VQ-VIB) policies for multi-drone coordination with 5-7 agents, we verify 18 temporal logic properties across safety, liveness, and cooperation, achieving 88.9% property satisfaction with all five safety thresholds satisfied (0.3% collision probability vs. 1% threshold). Monte Carlo validation of original neural policies confirms that verified safety properties transfer with <=0.6 percentage-point deviation (95% CI). Discrete VQ-VIB messages provide +11.6 to +13.6 percentage-point fidelity advantages over continuous methods, enabling 3-4x faster verification. Our framework provides empirically validated safety verification for distilled policy abstractions, serving as a practical bridge between deep MARL and formal safety workflows for multi-robot deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first end-to-end framework for safety verification of learned multi-agent communication policies by distilling neural policies into interpretable decision trees, formally verifying them with PRISM model checker, and confirming that verified safety properties transfer back to original neural networks with ≤0.6 percentage-point deviation.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables coordination through emergent communication, but neural policies lack formal safety guarantees required for safety-critical robotic deployment in domains like drone swarms and autonomous vehicle fleets.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline: (1) domain-specific feature extraction from agent observations; (2) decision tree distillation achieving 97.9% ± 1.2% fidelity; (3) automated translation to PRISM probabilistic model checker specifications with complete feature-to-state-variable correspondence; (4) compositional verification of PCTL properties via pairwise decomposition with union-bound aggregation and empirical neighbor modeling.
AI.result: Evaluated on VQ-VIB policies for multi-drone coordination (5-7 agents), verified 18 temporal logic properties achieving 88.9% satisfaction; all five safety thresholds satisfied (0.3% collision probability vs. 1% threshold); Monte Carlo validation confirmed ≤0.6 percentage-point deviation (95% CI); discrete VQ-VIB messages provided +11.6 to +13.6 percentage-point fidelity advantages over continuous methods with 3-4x faster verification.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides empirically validated safety verification for distilled policy abstractions, serving as a practical bridge between deep MARL and formal safety workflows for multi-robot deployment.

title: Analyzing the Narration Gap in LLM-Solver Loops
summary: Formal tools such as SAT and SMT solvers are increasingly embedded in language model reasoning pipelines when a safety or security critical question can be formulated in logic. Unlike chain of thought whose steps are sampled from the model distribution without formal guarantee, a solver produces a sound and independently verifiable answer. However, the soundness guarantee can be lost in the interaction between the solver and the model. The hybrid pipeline has three components: formalizing the question, deciding it, and narrating the result. Prior work has studied the formalization and decision, but not narration, which is the step that turns a formal tool's output into the user answer. To fill the narration gap, we first model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure. We further evaluate five open-sourced models under prompt injection, and we find certificate gating makes the solver verdict sound, while an adversary can invert a verified conclusion across phrasings and channels. We study the mitigation through hardened prompt that reduces injection significantly but cannot eliminate it and still suffers under adaptive attack. Combining the formal analysis and empirical studies, we show in the LLM-solver loop, robustness does not reach to the answer that the user finally reads.

AI.tldr: LLM-solver pipelines lose soundness guarantees at the narration stage (converting solver output to user answer), where prompt injection can invert verified conclusions; certificate gating helps but hardened prompts remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks.
AI.motivation: To fill the "narration gap" in LLM-solver hybrid pipelines — prior work studied formalization and decision steps but neglected how solver outputs are narrated to users, which can break soundness guarantees.
AI.method: Modeled the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure; empirically evaluated five open-source LLMs under prompt injection at the narration stage; tested certificate gating and hardened prompts as mitigations against adaptive attacks.
AI.result: Certificate gating preserves solver verdict soundness; prompt injection can invert verified conclusions across different phrasings and channels; hardened prompts reduce injection significantly but cannot fully eliminate it and fail under adaptive attacks.
AI.conclusion: In the LLM-solver loop, robustness does not extend to the final user-facing answer; the narration step remains a vulnerability point that current mitigations cannot fully address.

title: CTS-MoE: Implicit Terrain Adaptation via Mixture-of-Experts for Perceptive Locomotion
summary: Perceptive legged locomotion over discontinuous terrain (e.g., stairs, gaps, and obstacles) requires adaptive behavior, as a single conservative gait cannot produce the anticipatory maneuvers needed for abrupt topology changes. Cast as multi-task reinforcement learning, this problem introduces a tension between sharing and separation. Tasks use a common locomotion base but have conflicting rewards, so a policy must share behavior while avoiding value interference. Prior work addresses only one side, with monolithic policies sacrificing specialization and hierarchical sub-policies sacrificing generalization across transitions and unseen terrain. We propose CTS-MoE, which combines a dense mixture-of-experts actor with perception-based gating to compose shared behaviors and a multi-critic with task-specific value heads to prevent interference. The model is trained end-to-end in a single-stage concurrent teacher-student setup that handles partial observability and avoids sequential distillation, with task labels used only during training. At deployment, routing depends solely on perception, allowing terrain adaptation without a high-level selector or terrain classifier. Experiments on a Unitree Go1 in simulation and on hardware across seen and unseen terrains show task-aware specialization, with lower tracking error and higher success rates than monolithic baselines. Project Website: https://cts-moe.github.io/ .

AI.tldr: CTS-MoE combines a dense mixture-of-experts actor with perception-based gating and a multi-critic with task-specific value heads for perceptive legged locomotion over discontinuous terrain, achieving better specialization and generalization than monolithic and hierarchical baselines in simulation and on hardware.
AI.motivation: Legged locomotion over discontinuous terrain (stairs, gaps, obstacles) requires adaptive anticipatory maneuvers that a single conservative gait cannot produce. The multi-task RL formulation introduces tension between sharing (common locomotion base) and separation (conflicting task rewards), which prior monolithic policies (sacrificing specialization) and hierarchical sub-policies (sacrificing generalization) fail to resolve.
AI.method: CTS-MoE uses a dense mixture-of-experts actor with perception-based gating to compose shared behaviors, paired with a multi-critic employing task-specific value heads to prevent interference. Training is end-to-end in a single-stage concurrent teacher-student setup that handles partial observability without sequential distillation; task labels are used only during training, while deployment routing depends solely on perception.
AI.result: Experiments on a Unitree Go1 in simulation and on hardware across seen and unseen terrains demonstrate task-aware specialization, lower tracking error, and higher success rates compared to monolithic baselines.
AI.conclusion: CTS-MoE effectively balances sharing and separation in multi-task legged locomotion, enabling terrain adaptation without a high-level selector or terrain classifier at deployment.

title: Configurable Clinical Information Extraction with Agentic RAG: What Works, What Breaks, and Why
summary: Patient contexts span hundreds of heterogeneous documents and thousands of structured data points, yet the document-level metadata that AI systems need for retrieval and triage is absent or incomplete. Standard retrieval-augmented generation fails on this data, mishandling temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and missing metadata. We deploy ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction) at University Medicine Essen: an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline that reasons over complete patient contexts and grounds every answer in source passages for clinician verification. We quantify the metadata gap, trace the architectural decisions it shaped, and evaluate extraction alongside an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study, in which nuclear-medicine physicians verify every extracted value against its cited sources. Across 7,326 judgments, clinicians accepted 96.5\% of extractions, with per-type acceptance ranging from 80\% to 99\%.

AI.tldr: ACIE is an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline deployed at University Medicine Essen that extracts clinical metadata from heterogeneous patient documents, achieving 96.5% clinician acceptance across 7,326 judgments.
AI.motivation: Patient contexts contain heterogeneous documents with missing document-level metadata, causing standard RAG systems to fail at temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and metadata extraction.
