AI.method: ACIE is an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline that reasons over complete patient contexts, grounds answers in source passages, and was evaluated by nuclear-medicine physicians against an independent lymphoma registry study.
AI.result: Clinicians accepted 96.5% of extractions across 7,326 judgments, with per-type acceptance ranging from 80% to 99%.
AI.conclusion: Agentic RAG pipelines like ACIE can effectively bridge the metadata gap in clinical contexts, achieving high clinician acceptance through source-grounded extraction.

title: Scaling Self-Play for End-to-End Driving
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving models are typically trained on offline human-demonstration datasets that provide limited state coverage and often no closed-loop feedback, making them prone to compounding errors when deployed in closed-loop and brittle to long-tail agent interactions. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative strategy for training end-to-end driving models: large-scale self-play directly from pixels in simulation. While prior self-play approaches have shown promising transfer to real-world driving, they typically assume vectorized Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) observations that are incompatible with end-to-end policies operating directly on sensor observations. To this end, we introduce Gigapixel, a high-throughput batched driving simulator with perspective rendering, enabling scalable self-play directly from pixel observations. Rather than targeting compute-costly photorealistic sensor simulation, Gigapixel renders a simplified bounding-box world that preserves essential scene structure while achieving throughput at 50k agent steps per second. Since direct pixel-space self-play RL is prohibitively sample-inefficient at end-to-end model scale, we propose self-play DAgger training: we train pixel-based policies in self-play via on-policy distillation from a privileged RL teacher. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we subsequently transfer the self-play trained policies to real-world sensor data through lightweight perception adaptation. Policies trained in Gigapixel and adapted to real-world sensor data achieve competitive performance on the HUGSIM and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks without human trajectory supervision. Moreover, scaling self-play training yields proportional gains in policy performance, establishing self-play as a practical and scalable strategy for training end-to-end models.

AI.tldr: Gigapixel is a high-throughput batched driving simulator with perspective rendering that enables scalable self-play training of end-to-end pixel-based autonomous driving policies via on-policy distillation from a privileged RL teacher, achieving competitive benchmark performance without human trajectory supervision.
AI.motivation: End-to-end driving models trained on offline human demonstrations suffer from limited state coverage and compounding errors in closed-loop deployment, especially under long-tail agent interactions. Self-play cannot be easily applied to pixel-based end-to-end policies because prior simulators use vectorized BEV observations incompatible with sensor-input policies.
AI.method: Proposes Gigapixel, a high-throughput batched driving simulator that renders simplified bounding-box worlds at 50k agent steps/second. Introduces self-play DAgger training: pixel-based policies are trained via on-policy distillation from a privileged RL teacher in self-play. Sim-to-real transfer is achieved through lightweight perception adaptation to real-world sensor data.
AI.result: Policies trained in Gigapixel and adapted to real-world data achieve competitive performance on HUGSIM and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks without human trajectory supervision. Scaling self-play yields proportional gains in policy performance.
AI.conclusion: Self-play is a practical and scalable strategy for training end-to-end pixel-based driving models, overcoming the limitations of offline human-demonstration training.

title: Which Pairs to Compare for LLM Post-Training?
summary: Preference-based post-training has become a central paradigm for aligning language models. A common data-collection strategy is to generate a small set of completions for each prompt and label the resulting comparison pairs. However, human preference labels are often much more expensive than generating additional completions, suggesting a different use of the same labeling budget: generate a larger pool of completions, but label only the most informative comparison pairs. This paper studies which pairs should be compared in preference-based post-training. We formulate comparison curation as a sampling-design problem and evaluate designs by the quality of the final policy under the preference-based post-training objective. We instantiate this framework for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), analyzing how the choice of labeled pairs propagates through DPO training to downstream policy performance. Our main results provide matching upper and lower bounds on the post-training optimality gap of the DPO-trained policy. The bounds show that comparison selection affects downstream performance through a single design-dependent information matrix, which links label allocation to parameter estimation error and policy suboptimality. This yields an explicit optimization criterion for budgeted comparison curation and motivates practical sampling designs for selecting informative pairs from large generated completion pools. Experiments on synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks show that the proposed designs consistently improve sample efficiency over common comparison-selection heuristics.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how to optimally select comparison pairs for preference-based post-training of language models under a fixed labeling budget, proposing a sampling-design framework with matching bounds on policy optimality, and demonstrating improved sample efficiency over common heuristics.
AI.motivation: Human preference labels are much more expensive than generating additional model completions, yet common practice generates few completions and labels all pairs. This motivates exploring a more budget-efficient strategy: generate a larger pool of completions but only label the most informative comparison pairs.
AI.method: Formulates comparison curation as a sampling-design problem; instantiates for DPO with theoretical analysis providing matching upper/lower bounds on the post-training optimality gap; derives an explicit optimization criterion linking label allocation to parameter estimation error via a design-dependent information matrix.
AI.result: Matching upper and lower bounds on the DPO-trained policy's optimality gap are derived; the proposed sampling designs consistently improve sample efficiency over common comparison-selection heuristics in synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Comparison selection affects downstream performance through a design-dependent information matrix; budgeted comparison curation can be explicitly optimized, and practical sampling designs from this framework outperform heuristic selection methods.

title: DF-ExpEnse: Diffusion Filtered Exploration for Sample Efficient Finetuning
summary: A natural recipe for intelligent robotic decision-making is initializing from pretrained generative control policies, which have summarized offline experience, and adapting them to self-collected online experience. We present DF-ExpEnse, an exploration technique that improves the quality of online experience collection, thus increasing finetuning sample-efficiency. DF-ExpEnse leverages the multimodal modeling capabilities of the generative control policy to create an expressive and tractably evaluatable candidate set. It then utilizes an ensemble of critics to identify the action that best balances quality with high exploration interest. In fleet settings, DF-ExpEnse further enables cross-agent communication to facilitate collaborative exploration as a group. DF-ExpEnse can be seamlessly integrated with existing strategies that finetune pretrained generative control policies via reinforcement learning. We experimentally validate consistent sample-efficiency benefits through DF-ExpEnse across a variety of manipulation and locomotion tasks, compared to default finetuning and alternative action selection schemes. Project can be found at https://df-expense.github.io.

AI.tldr: DF-ExpEnse is an exploration technique that improves sample-efficiency when finetuning pretrained generative control policies by creating an expressive candidate set from the policy's multimodal outputs and using an ensemble of critics to select actions that balance quality and exploration interest, with additional cross-agent communication capabilities for fleet settings.
AI.motivation: To improve the quality of online experience collection during finetuning of pretrained generative control policies, thereby increasing sample-efficiency in robotic decision-making.
AI.method: DF-ExpEnse leverages the multimodal modeling capabilities of generative control policies to create an expressive, tractably evaluatable candidate set, then uses an ensemble of critics to select actions balancing quality with exploration interest. In fleet settings, it enables cross-agent communication for collaborative exploration.
AI.result: Consistent sample-efficiency benefits across a variety of manipulation and locomotion tasks compared to default finetuning and alternative action selection schemes.
AI.conclusion: DF-ExpEnse is an effective exploration technique that seamlessly integrates with existing finetuning strategies for pretrained generative control policies, improving sample-efficiency in both single-agent and multi-agent fleet settings.

authors: Antonio de Sousa Leitão Filho; Allan Kardec Duailibe Barros Filho; Fabrício Saul Lima; Selby Mykael Lima dos Santos; Rejani Bandeira Vieira Sousa
title: Toten: Knowledge-Based Ontological Tokenization Of Physical Quantities And Technical Notation In Brazilian Portuguese
summary: Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization is statistically efficient for vocabulary compression, but semantically blind to structured technical entities, fragmenting physical quantities, numbers, units, and symbolic expressions into lexically arbitrary subwords. We present TOTEN, a knowledge-based ontological tokenization framework that replaces statistical derivation with declarative classification grounded in a formal ontology of engineering entities (OEE). We formalize TOTEN as the triple <O, classify, {inst_tau}>: the ontology gathers types, structural principles, composition relations, and preservable invariants; the classification function maps raw text into typed regions; and the instantiator family yields a self-descriptive structured representation. Robustness derives from deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional), Unicode Character Database (typographic), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology). Intrinsic evaluation covers four properties verifiable by construction -- ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, and numerical reconstruction -- over an internal, physically validated benchmark (EngQuant, N=800) and four Brazilian Portuguese external corpora (N=1771 eligible cases). We also report detection recall, distinguishing coverage from conditional atomicity. Against eight state-of-the-art baselines, TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts and numerical reconstruction of 0.775-0.904 on external corpora, vs. 0.627-0.703 for the best baseline (Quantulum3); on EngQuant, 0.780 vs. 0.340. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms concurrent validity of the control benchmark. Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with Pint, the oracle from which the system inherits dimensional authority.

AI.tldr: TOTEN replaces BPE's statistical tokenization with an ontology-driven framework for technical text, achieving superior ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, and numerical reconstruction over eight baselines, with statistically significant results across internal and external benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization fragments structured technical entities (physical quantities, units, symbolic expressions) into semantically arbitrary subwords, despite being statistically efficient for vocabulary compression. This semantic blindness motivates a knowledge-based alternative.
AI.method: TOTEN is formalized as a triple <O, classify, {inst_tau}>, where O is a formal ontology of engineering entities (OEE), classify maps raw text into typed regions, and the instantiator family produces self-descriptive structured representations. It deterministically couples with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional analysis), Unicode Character Database (typography), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology).
AI.result: TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity across all contrasts. On external corpora, numerical reconstruction reaches 0.775-0.904 vs. 0.627-0.703 (best baseline Quantulum3); on EngQuant, 0.780 vs. 0.340. All differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation confirms concurrent validity of the control benchmark.
AI.conclusion: TOTEN demonstrates that declarative, ontology-grounded tokenization outperforms statistical subword methods for structured technical entities, with deterministic robustness and verifiable properties by construction.

title: Safe Local Navigation for Ackermann-Steered Robots in Unmapped Environments
comment: Presented at the 23rd Conference on Robots and Vision (CRV 2026)
summary: A control framework is proposed for safe local navigation of mobile robots equipped with Ackermann steering in unmapped environments where a global goal is absent. Based on local obstacle detections, the safest heading angle is determined along the direction of the largest open space ahead of the vehicle. Guided by this direction, bounding lines are constructed on the left and right sides of the vehicle to achieve obstacle separation. These bounding lines are obtained by solving a convex quadratic optimization that maximizes vehicle-to-obstacle clearance. Optionally, conditions are imposed on the bounding lines to preserve parallelism and smooth abrupt changes from prior control steps. A feedback-linearizing controller is then used to regulate the vehicle's distance from one or both bounding lines, effectively enabling tracking of a local reference path that preserves safety through obstacle clearance maximization. Open-source code is included for the application of this control scheme. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method produces safer navigation paths with significantly shorter computation times, compared to some existing exploration-based planners.

AI.tldr: A control framework for safe local navigation of Ackermann-steering mobile robots in unmapped environments without a global goal, using obstacle clearance maximization via convex quadratic optimization and feedback-linearizing control.
AI.motivation: To enable safe local navigation for Ackermann-steering robots in unmapped environments where global goals are absent, addressing the need for computationally efficient obstacle avoidance without relying on exploration-based planners.
AI.method: The safest heading is determined by the largest open space direction. Bounding lines are constructed via convex quadratic optimization to maximize vehicle-to-obstacle clearance, with optional parallelism and smoothness constraints. A feedback-linearizing controller regulates distance to bounding lines for local path tracking.
AI.result: The proposed method produces safer navigation paths with significantly shorter computation times compared to existing exploration-based planners.
AI.conclusion: The control framework offers efficient and safe local navigation for Ackermann-steering robots in unmapped environments, supported by open-source code.

title: AI4SE and SE4AI Exploration: A Decade Looking Back and Forward
summary: The March 2020 INCOSE INSIGHT special issue on AI and Systems Engineering (SE) became the most downloaded issue in the publication's history and launched a research community that now draws over 250 registrants to its annual workshop. In this article, we trace the progress in AI and SE across three phases (labeled here foundational, applied, and LLM inflection) based on the authors' reading of the field's core papers, and describe our opinions of where the community has converged and where critical gaps remain. Separately, a human-AI agreement literature review leveraging both human expertise and six AI models was performed to assess the relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications. The results identify five critical research gaps and offer guidance for practitioners navigating AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation in SE. We share the agreement data and the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application so readers can compare their own relevance judgments with the human and AI raters.

AI.tldr: This article traces progress in AI and Systems Engineering across three phases (foundational, applied, LLM inflection), identifies five critical research gaps via a human-AI agreement literature review of 2,601 articles, and provides an interactive web application for readers to compare relevance judgments.
AI.motivation: To trace the progress of AI and SE integration across three phases, identify where the community has converged, highlight critical research gaps, and provide guidance for practitioners navigating AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation in SE.
AI.method: A literature review combining human expertise with six AI models to assess relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications (total 2,601 articles), followed by analysis of human-AI agreement data to identify research gaps.
AI.result: Five critical research gaps identified; the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application created; agreement data shared publicly for community comparison.
AI.conclusion: The AI-SE community has converged on key areas but five critical research gaps remain; the shared data and web application enable readers to compare their own relevance judgments with human and AI raters.

title: ForEnt: A Multi-Modal Dataset for Characterizing Quadruped Robot Entrapments in Forest Environments
summary: Legged robots are increasingly deployed in forests for ecological surveying and monitoring, yet their autonomy is often interrupted consequent to the challenges posed in traversing forest environments. Forest entrapments, for example, when a robot's legs are ensnared in vines or other vegetation, result in loss of stability and toppling. Such events not only disrupt the mission and require manual intervention, but also risk damage to the robot hardware. To address the absence of a dedicated dataset to investigate these failure modes in forest environments, we present ForEnt, a multi-modal dataset collected with the low-cost Unitree Go2 quadruped across eight forest sites in the Southampton Common Woodlands, UK. For our dataset, over approximately 1.7 km of traversals in 11 sequences were conducted, yielding 69 recorded entrapment events. ForEnt includes time-synchronized RGB-D images, LiDAR scans, proprioceptive data, and third-person video, enabling analysis of terrain factors contributing to entrapment and providing labeled sensor streams for reproducible benchmarking. By supporting the evaluation of entrapment detection strategies, ForEnt lowers the barrier to developing robust quadruped robot deployments in challenging forest environments.

AI.tldr: ForEnt is a multi-modal dataset collected with a Unitree Go2 quadruped across 8 forest sites in the UK, containing 11 traversal sequences (~1.7 km) and 69 recorded entrapment events. It includes synchronized RGB-D, LiDAR, proprioceptive data, and third-person video to support analysis and detection of leg entrapment failures in forest environments.
AI.motivation: Legged robots deployed in forests frequently experience entrapment (e.g., legs ensnared in vines), causing mission failure, damage, and need for manual intervention. No dedicated dataset existed to study these failure modes, hindering the development of robust traversal strategies.
AI.method: The authors collected data using a low-cost Unitree Go2 quadruped across 8 forest sites in Southampton Common Woodlands, UK. Over ~1.7 km of traversals in 11 sequences, they recorded 69 entrapment events. The dataset includes time-synchronized RGB-D images, LiDAR scans, proprioceptive data, and third-person video with labeled sensor streams for reproducible benchmarking.
AI.result: 69 recorded entrapment events across 11 traversal sequences covering ~1.7 km in 8 forest sites, providing a multi-modal, labeled dataset for entrapment detection and analysis.
AI.conclusion: ForEnt lowers the barrier to developing robust quadruped robot deployments in challenging forest environments by supporting evaluation of entrapment detection strategies and providing a reproducible benchmark.

title: BrainG3N: A Dual-Purpose Tokenizer for Controllable 3D Brain MRI Generation
summary: Three-dimensional (3D) brain MRI is central to clinical neurology and neuro-oncology, where generative models could augment under-represented cohorts, simulate disease trajectories, and support privacy-preserving data sharing. Latent diffusion has been the go-to solution for modeling imaging data, but it places two competing demands on the tokenizer: encoder embeddings must retain the clinical information that downstream tasks act on, and the decoder must reconstruct anatomically faithful volumes. Existing reconstruction-driven tokenizers achieve the second at the expense of the first. To address this, we introduce a fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) based tokenizer for 3D brain MRI latent diffusion, decoupling encoder and decoder: a frozen 3D MAE encoder produces clinically informative embeddings, while a dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. We pretrain the encoder on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts spanning four modalities, ten disease categories, and 200+ acquisition sites, and demonstrate its dual utility in two settings. First, on a 23-task linear-probing benchmark, the encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models (i.e., BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, and MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 tasks. Second, a conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) trained on these clinically informative embeddings supports both conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting. Together these results establish a single 3D brain-MRI embedding space capable of both downstream clinical tasks and controllable generation.

AI.tldr: Introduces a 3D brain MRI tokenizer using a frozen MAE encoder for clinical embeddings and a CNN decoder for reconstruction, enabling both strong downstream task performance and controllable latent diffusion generation.
AI.motivation: Existing reconstruction-driven tokenizers for 3D brain MRI latent diffusion prioritize anatomical fidelity at the cost of preserving clinically informative embeddings needed for downstream tasks; the paper aims to decouple these competing demands.
AI.method: A fully volumetric MAE-based tokenizer with a frozen 3D MAE encoder (pretrained on 35,309 volumes from 18 cohorts, 4 modalities, 10 disease categories, 200+ sites) for clinically informative embeddings, paired with a dedicated CNN decoder that reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings.
AI.result: On a 23-task linear-probing benchmark, the encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models on 21 tasks. The learned embedding space also supports conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) training for conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting.
AI.conclusion: A single 3D brain-MRI embedding space can simultaneously support both diverse downstream clinical tasks and controllable generative modeling, resolving the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and clinical informativeness.

title: Route-Constrained Robust Fusion Estimation for MEMS/GNSS Integrated Navigation of Unmanned Ground Vehicles in GNSS Degraded Environments
comment: Accepted workshop paper, 1st Workshop on Robot Meets GNSS and Ranging for Seamless Autonomy, IEEE ICRA 2026
summary: To address cumulative localization drift of unmanned ground vehicles in structured road environments under severe Global Navigation Satellite System signal occlusion, this paper proposes a robust route-constrained state estimation method. During periods without satellite signals, the proposed method establishes the correspondence between the historical dead reckoning trajectory and local segments of the mission route extracted from a high-definition map, and estimates a route-referenced position via a two-dimensional rigid transformation. The estimated position is then formulated as a pseudo-position observation and incorporated into an Extended Kalman Filter update. In this way, route constraints at the road level can be continuously injected into a unified state estimation framework, thereby suppressing position deviation relative to the mission route while indirectly improving azimuth estimation. To enhance practical applicability, engineering strategies, such as trigger control, matching quality validation, route offset compensation, and single update correction limiting, are further introduced. Experiments in three representative scenarios, including a long tunnel, a multi-segment tunnel, and a curved tunnel, show that the proposed method effectively suppresses error accumulation during satellite outages, reduces the risk of large maximum deviation, and improves localization continuity and road-level usability.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a route-constrained state estimation method for UGVs in GNSS-denied environments, using historical dead reckoning and HD map matching to produce pseudo-position observations for an EKF, with engineering strategies to suppress drift and improve localization continuity.
AI.motivation: Cumulative localization drift of UGVs in structured roads under severe GNSS signal occlusion remains a critical problem, as existing methods lack robustness for road-level constraints during prolonged satellite outages.
AI.method: Correspondence between historical dead reckoning trajectory and HD map route segments is established via 2D rigid transformation to produce a route-referenced pseudo-position observation, which is integrated into an EKF update. Engineering strategies (trigger control, matching validation, offset compensation, single-update limiting) are added for robustness.
AI.result: Experiments in long tunnel, multi-segment tunnel, and curved tunnel scenarios show that the method suppresses error accumulation, reduces maximum deviation risk, and improves localization continuity and road-level usability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed route-constrained EKF with HD map matching effectively mitigates drift during GNSS outages, enhancing practical deployment of UGVs in structured road environments.

title: Denoising Implicit Feedback for Cold-start Recommendation
summary: Implicit feedback is widely used in recommender systems due to its accessibility and generality, yet it usually presents noisy samples (e.g., clickbait, position bias). Meanwhile, recommenders inevitably face the item cold-start problem due to the continuous influx of new items. We identify that cold items are more prone to noisy samples due to the aforementioned factors, and researchers often overlook the significance of denoising implicit feedback for cold items. Previous denoising studies usually identify noisy samples based on heuristic patterns, such as higher loss values, and mitigate noise through sample selection or re-weighting. However, these methods have limited adaptability and are ineffective in cold-start scenarios. To achieve denoising implicit feedback for cold-start recommendation, we propose a model-agnostic denoising method called DIF. First, user preferences for content remain stable, which allows us to infer pseudo-labels indicating whether a user is interested in a cold item through content-similar warm items. Furthermore, to improve pseudo-label accuracy, we model the confidence of pseudo-labels based on the content similarity between the cold item and warm items, and then aggregate multiple pseudo-labels for each sample. Finally, we explicitly estimate the uncertainty of the noisy sample label by considering its relative entropy and the cold-start status of the item, which adaptively guides the role of pseudo-labels to correct the noisy labels at the sample level. DIF's superiority is supported by both theoretical justification and extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The method has been deployed on a billion-user scale short video application Kuaishou and has significantly improved various commercial metrics within cold-start scenarios.

AI.tldr: DIF is a model-agnostic denoising method that corrects noisy implicit feedback for cold-start items by leveraging content-similar warm items to generate pseudo-labels, modeling confidence via similarity, and adaptively guiding label correction using relative entropy and cold-start status. It shows strong theoretical and empirical results, including deployment at Kuaishou.
AI.motivation: Cold-start items suffer disproportionately from noisy implicit feedback (e.g., clickbait, position bias), yet existing denoising methods (e.g., loss-based sample selection/re-weighting) lack adaptability and fail in cold-start scenarios.
AI.method: (1) Infer pseudo-labels for cold items from content-similar warm items based on stable user preferences. (2) Model pseudo-label confidence via content similarity between cold and warm items, then aggregate multiple pseudo-labels. (3) Estimate uncertainty of noisy sample labels using relative entropy and item cold-start status to adaptively guide pseudo-label correction at the sample level.
AI.result: Superior performance over baselines on real-world datasets; deployed on Kuaishou (billion-user scale) with significant improvements in commercial cold-start metrics.
AI.conclusion: DIF effectively addresses denoising for cold-start items by leveraging content-based pseudo-labels with uncertainty-guided correction, providing both theoretical and practical benefits for large-scale recommender systems.

title: Comparative Study on Agility, Efficiency, and Impact Absorption of Bipedal Robots with Active Toes
summary: Human legs exhibit high efficiency, agility, and impact absorption, with toes playing a crucial role in these capabilities. While many attempts have been made to implement human-like toes in robots, they have not fully replicated human characteristics nor rigorously validated their benefits. We propose a 14-DOF biped robot emulating human toes' lightweight, high-torque, robust nature. To quantitatively analyze the effectiveness of the active toes in terms of agility, efficiency, and impact absorption, we developed a high-fidelity simulation training environment that reflects actual actuators with coupled transmissions and accurate power consumption. To ensure a fair comparison between configurations with and without active toes, we designed a minimal RL reward function and applied an identical training procedure to both. The simulation results indicate that, at 1.33 m/s walking, the toe-equipped robot reduced CoT by 17.5% and heel-strike GRF by 5.0% compared with the toe-ablation configuration. On the agility test, average and maximum path deviation decreased by 25.0% and 34.0%, respectively.

AI.tldr: A 14-DOF biped robot with human-like active toes was developed, and simulation results show that active toes reduce cost of transport (CoT) by 17.5%, heel-strike ground reaction force by 5.0%, and path deviation by 25-34% compared to without toes.
AI.motivation: Human toes contribute significantly to walking efficiency, agility, and impact absorption, but existing robotic toe implementations fail to replicate human characteristics or rigorously validate their benefits.
AI.method: A 14-DOF biped robot with lightweight, high-torque, robust active toes was built. A high-fidelity simulation environment with coupled transmissions and accurate power consumption was used. A minimal RL reward function and identical training procedure were applied to compare toe-equipped vs toe-ablation configurations.
AI.result: At 1.33 m/s walking: CoT reduced by 17.5%, heel-strike GRF reduced by 5.0%. Agility test: average path deviation reduced by 25.0%, maximum path deviation reduced by 34.0%.
AI.conclusion: Active toes quantitatively improve bipedal robot efficiency, impact absorption, and agility, validating their benefit over toe-less configurations.

title: Exit-and-Join Dynamics for Decentralized Coalition Formation
summary: This paper studies coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical process driven by unilateral exit-and-join decisions. Agents evaluate local moves using the Aumann-Dreze value, so payoffs are computed within the agent's current coalition rather than through a globally negotiated coalition structure. The resulting model links cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative best-response behavior: a terminal partition is precisely a coalition structure with no admissible, individually profitable exit-and-join deviation. We establish equilibrium characterizations, identify conditions under which the dynamics admit scalar Lyapunov or exact-potential representations, and analyze how switching and acceptance costs shape local stability. Numerical experiments test finite-time stabilization, cost sensitivity, and a special convex-game benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper studies coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical process where agents use unilateral exit-and-join decisions based on the Aumann-Dreze value, leading to terminal partitions with no profitable deviations. It establishes equilibrium characterizations, Lyapunov/potential representations, and analyzes switching/acceptance costs through numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: To model coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical process rather than a static, globally negotiated one, linking cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative best-response behavior.
AI.method: Agents evaluate local moves using the Aumann-Dreze value; dynamics are driven by unilateral exit-and-join decisions; terminal partitions correspond to coalition structures with no admissible individually profitable deviations. Lyapunov/potential function analysis and numerical simulations are employed.
AI.result: Equilibrium characterizations are established; conditions for scalar Lyapunov or exact-potential representations are identified; switching and acceptance costs are shown to shape local stability; numerical tests confirm finite-time stabilization and cost sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework bridges cooperative and noncooperative game theory in coalition formation, with stability properties tunable via cost parameters, validated by both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments including a convex-game benchmark.

title: A Differentiable Composite Approximation Framework for Autonomous Underwater Vehicle Maneuvering Modeling from Sea-Trial Data
summary: Field-based modeling from onboard measurements can produce autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) maneuvering models that reflect real operating characteristics. From an approximation perspective, conventional maneuvering models use predefined constraint polynomial bases, whereas data-driven models use data-adaptive bases. Motivated by this basis-function view, this paper presents a differentiable composite-approximation formulation, in which the polynomial-basis component and the data-adaptive basis component are treated as differentiable parts of a single predictor and calibrated jointly. A gradient-based co-calibration method is developed for full-scale AUV maneuvering prediction, where a sensitivity-aware mechanism regulates bounded polynomial updates while the neural residual captures remaining nonlinear discrepancies under a shared prediction objective. To account for ocean-current effects in field data, a turning-motion-based current estimation and compensation procedure is incorporated to construct current-compensated learning targets for training and rollout. The framework is evaluated using sea-trial data collected from a 7-meter AUV under multiple maneuvering conditions. Results show that the proposed method improves recursive trajectory and velocity prediction compared with polynomial-only, neural-only, and frozen-prior hybrid baselines, demonstrating its applicability to field-data-based AUV maneuvering modeling.

AI.tldr: A differentiable composite-approximation framework combining polynomial and neural bases with gradient-based co-calibration and current compensation for AUV maneuvering modeling from field data, outperforming pure polynomial, pure neural, and frozen-prior hybrid methods on real 7-meter AUV sea-trial data.
AI.motivation: Conventional AUV maneuvering models use predefined polynomial bases, while data-driven models use data-adaptive bases. The paper is motivated by unifying both into a single differentiable formulation to leverage their complementary strengths for field-data-based modeling.
AI.method: A differentiable composite-approximation formulation treating polynomial-basis and data-adaptive (neural) basis components as differentiable parts of a single predictor, co-calibrated via gradient descent. A sensitivity-aware mechanism regulates bounded polynomial updates, while a neural residual captures remaining nonlinearities. A turning-motion-based current estimation and compensation procedure constructs current-compensated learning targets.
AI.result: The method improves recursive trajectory and velocity prediction compared to polynomial-only, neural-only, and frozen-prior hybrid baselines using sea-trial data from a 7-meter AUV under multiple maneuvering conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates strong applicability to field-data-based AUV maneuvering modeling by effectively combining polynomial and neural bases with current compensation.

title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Predictive Validity for the Evaluation of LLM Agents
summary: Agent benchmarks are growing fast, but no single benchmark touches more than four or five of the dimensions that deployment exposes. This paper aggregates the largest coordinated deep-dive of one MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark to date: fourteen parallel implementation studies covering new asset classes (including a multi-modal visual extension), alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation-methodology probes. Consolidating those studies with seven prior agent benchmarks, we argue that aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation. Rankings derived from aggregate scores do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings; recent public-to-hidden competition retrospectives provide direct empirical evidence of this rank instability. We propose ranking configurations by predictive validity, the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank, rather than in-sample mean, and report a twelve-tier measurement apparatus that exposes the deployment-relevant dimensions HELM and its agent-era successors collapse. The position is operationalized through three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds; existing evidence partly supports it but is too thin to confirm. We close with a pre-registered pilot design and a field-level vision for what the next generation of agentic benchmarks should report.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a coordinated deep-dive of an MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark across 14 parallel implementation studies, arguing that aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation due to rank instability in out-of-distribution settings. The authors propose ranking by predictive validity and introduce a twelve-tier measurement apparatus, concluding with a pre-registered pilot design and vision for next-generation agentic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks fail to capture the multiple dimensions that real-world deployment exposes, and aggregate-score leaderboards produce rankings that do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings, creating a gap between benchmark performance and practical utility.
AI.method: Fourteen parallel implementation studies covering new asset classes, multi-modal visual extensions, alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation-methodology probes, consolidated with seven prior agent benchmarks; proposes ranking by predictive validity (correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank) and a twelve-tier measurement apparatus with three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria.
AI.result: Aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation; rankings are unstable across distribution shifts; existing evidence partially supports the proposed criteria but is insufficient for confirmation.
AI.conclusion: The field should move beyond aggregate-score leaderboards toward ranking by predictive validity, and adopt the proposed measurement apparatus and falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria for next-generation agentic benchmark reporting.

title: Bidirectional Tutoring for Developmental Motor Learning in Robots: Co-Developed Interaction Dynamics Support Stable Learning
summary: Infants are well known to develop their motor skills through dense interaction with caregivers. Although such social interaction is crucial for human development, motor-skill learning in robots is often treated as a unidirectional process in which robots passively receive demonstrations from tutors. This overlooks a key property of social interaction: it is inherently bidirectional, with tutor and learner dynamically adapting to each other. In such interactions, the robot's past experiences may function as prior constraints that shape the dynamics of their co-developed trajectories. We hypothesize that bidirectional tutoring allows such constraints to guide the formation of consistent behavioral patterns that preserve behavioral coherence and support generalization, whereas unidirectional interaction lacks such constraints and leads to broader, less consistent behavioral patterns. To examine this hypothesis, we conducted two experiments with a physical humanoid robot performing an object manipulation task: one involving human-robot interaction and another employing an AI tutor interacting with the real robot through an adaptive intervention mechanism designed to examine whether similar effects would emerge under more controlled conditions. We implement the developmental learning framework using a free-energy-principle-based neural network extended with generative replay, which supports stable sequence-by-sequence learning from single tutored episodes. Across both settings, bidirectional tutoring fostered consistent behaviors and stage-wise generalization, while the robot gradually required less tutor guidance. These results suggest that bidirectional tutoring, as an embodied and socially grounded approach, provides an effective scaffold for developmental motor learning in robots.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how bidirectional tutoring (robot and tutor dynamically adapting to each other) improves motor-skill learning in a humanoid robot compared to unidirectional passive demonstration, using a free-energy-principle-based neural network with generative replay. Experiments with both human tutors and AI tutors show bidirectional interaction fosters consistent behaviors, stage-wise generalization, and reduced tutor guidance over time.
AI.motivation: Traditional robot motor learning treats social interaction as unidirectional (robot passively receives demonstrations), ignoring the bidirectional, adaptive nature of human caregiver-infant interaction. The authors hypothesize bidirectional tutoring provides prior constraints that guide consistent behavioral patterns and generalization.
AI.method: Two experiments with a physical humanoid robot performing object manipulation: (1) human-robot bidirectional interaction, and (2) AI tutor with adaptive intervention mechanism. A free-energy-principle-based neural network extended with generative replay enables stable sequence-by-sequence learning from single episodes.
AI.result: Bidirectional tutoring produced consistent behaviors and stage-wise generalization across both settings. The robot gradually required less tutor guidance over time, unlike unidirectional interaction which yielded broader, less consistent patterns.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional tutoring, as an embodied and socially grounded approach, serves as an effective scaffold for developmental motor learning in robots, supporting the hypothesis that interactive constraints shape coherent behavioral development.

title: GLARE: A Natural Language Interface for Querying Global Explanations
summary: While global explanations are crucial for understanding vision models across datasets, classes, and decision contexts, their complex and monolithic nature often hinders practical exploration. Because users typically seek targeted answers to specific questions rather than static artifacts, we present an LLM-based interactive interface that provides natural language access to global explanations for black-box image classifiers. The system's core LLM acts as a mediator, translating natural language questions into structured SQL queries over local explanation data. This enables flexible aggregation without exposing users to low-level representations. For each query, the interface outputs statistics-augmented natural language responses, supporting local explanations, and intent-aligned visualizations. We evaluate the system on intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors. Our results demonstrate that LLM-mediated querying substantially improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based interactive interface translates natural language questions into SQL queries over local explanation data, enabling flexible and accessible global explanations for black-box image classifiers.
AI.motivation: Global explanations for vision models are often complex and monolithic, hindering practical exploration. Users need targeted, question-driven access rather than static artifacts.
AI.method: An LLM acts as a mediator, translating natural language questions into structured SQL queries over local explanation data, producing statistics-augmented natural language responses with visualizations.
AI.result: The system performs well on intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries/datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors.
AI.conclusion: LLM-mediated querying substantially improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI.

title: VOiLA: Vectorized Online Planning with Learned Diffusion Model for POMDP Agents
comment: Submitted to the 2026 International Symposium of Robotics Research (ISRR)
summary: Planning under uncertainty is an essential capability for autonomous robots. The Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) provides a powerful framework for such a capability. Although POMDP-based planning has advanced significantly, its application to real-world problems is often limited by the difficulty of obtaining faithful POMDP models. We present Vectorized Online planning wIth Learned diffusion model for POMDP Agents (VOiLA), a framework that learns task-agnostic POMDP models for online planning under uncertainty. VOiLA learns transition and observation samplers using conditional diffusion models and learns observation-likelihood models for particle-based belief updates. To enable efficient online planning, the diffusion samplers are distilled into compact feedforward generators and integrated with Vectorized Online POMDP Planner (VOPP), an online POMDP planner designed to leverage GPU parallelization. Experimental results indicate the distillation strategy reduces sampling cost by up to nearly three orders of magnitude, making learned generative POMDP models practical for online planning. Evaluation of VOiLA on three benchmark problems indicate that VOiLA achieves equal or better performance than Recurrent Soft Actor Critic while using less than 10% training data, and generalizes much better to unseen environment configurations. Physical robot evaluation indicates VOiLA uses the models learned using only simulated data and generates a policy that successfully accomplish the task in 10 of 10 runs.

AI.tldr: VOiLA is a framework that learns task-agnostic POMDP models using conditional diffusion models for online planning under uncertainty. It distills diffusion samplers into compact feedforward generators integrated with a GPU-parallelized planner (VOPP), achieving up to ~1000x sampling cost reduction, outperforming Recurrent Soft Actor Critic with less than 10% of training data, and demonstrating successful real-robot deployment from simulated data alone.
AI.motivation: The difficulty of obtaining faithful POMDP models limits the application of POMDP-based planning to real-world problems. The authors aim to overcome this by learning task-agnostic POMDP models directly from data for online planning under uncertainty.
AI.method: VOiLA (1) learns transition and observation samplers using conditional diffusion models, (2) learns observation-likelihood models for particle-based belief updates, (3) distills diffusion samplers into compact feedforward generators to reduce computational cost, and (4) integrates these with VOPP, a GPU-parallelized online POMDP planner.
AI.result: Distillation reduces sampling cost by up to nearly three orders of magnitude. VOiLA achieves equal or better performance than Recurrent Soft Actor Critic using less than 10% training data and generalizes better to unseen environments. Physical robot evaluation succeeded in 10/10 runs using models learned from simulated data only.
AI.conclusion: Learned generative POMDP models, when efficiently distilled and parallelized, are practical for online planning under uncertainty and can bridge the sim-to-real gap without requiring real-world training data.

title: Interpreting Neural Combinatorial Optimization via Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks
summary: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) achieves strong performance, yet its black-box nature remains a key roadblock to deployment and scientific diagnosis. Standard interpretability tools, such as Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs), are ill-equipped for NCO, whose decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack proper concept vocabulary definition. To close this gap, we introduce Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks (EPB), to our knowledge, the first framework for interpreting NCO policies by distilling black-box NCO models into human-readable program portfolios. EPB employs an LLM to autonomously evolve a bank of programs, where each program's per-step action distribution serves as the bottleneck. EPB works through an iterative framework: Block I fixes program bank capacity and introduces a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent scheme that couples numerical gradients for student router updates and textual gradients for LLM-based program revision; Block II dynamically adapts bank capacity via fault-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate EPB's effectiveness and broad applicability, where the distilled program portfolios largely match original performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as a composition of classic heuristic variants. Our work advances interpretable NCO and establishes EPB as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models.

AI.tldr: EPB (Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks) is a framework that interprets black-box Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) policies by distilling them into human-readable program portfolios using LLM-driven evolution, hybrid gradient descent, and dynamic capacity adaptation.
AI.motivation: NCO models achieve strong performance but suffer from black-box nature, hindering deployment and scientific diagnosis. Standard interpretability tools like Concept Bottleneck Models fail because NCO decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack proper concept vocabulary.
AI.method: EPB uses an LLM to evolve a bank of programs. Block I fixes capacity and uses hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent (numerical gradients for student router, textual gradients for LLM-based program revision). Block II dynamically adapts bank capacity via fault-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning.
AI.result: Distilled program portfolios largely match original NCO performance. EPB reveals NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as a composition of classic heuristic variants.
AI.conclusion: EPB advances interpretable NCO and serves as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models.

title: Temporal Self-Imitation Learning
summary: Long-horizon robot manipulation policies trained with reward shaping can still exploit dense rewards through inefficient interaction, while rare efficient behaviors may be forgotten during training. We argue that temporal efficiency itself provides a powerful and underutilized source of self-supervision for reinforcement learning. We introduce Temporal Self-Imitation Learning (TSIL), a reinforcement learning framework that mines temporally efficient successful trajectories generated during learning and converts them into reusable supervision for future policy improvement. TSIL progressively refines learning using configuration-conditioned adaptive temporal targets derived from fast successful trajectories, while preserving and replaying efficient behaviors through efficiency-weighted self-imitation learning. Across 15 distinct long-horizon manipulation tasks, TSIL consistently improves learning efficiency, task-completion efficiency, revisitation of fast successful behaviors, and robustness to unstable training conditions. More broadly, our results suggest that the temporal structure of successful behavior itself provides a scalable self-supervisory signal for reinforcement learning beyond manually engineered reward shaping alone.

AI.tldr: TSIL mines temporally efficient successful trajectories during RL training and uses them as self-supervision to improve long-horizon robot manipulation, outperforming reward shaping across 15 tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon robot manipulation policies trained with reward shaping can still exploit dense rewards through inefficient interaction, and rare efficient behaviors may be forgotten during training. Temporal efficiency itself provides a powerful but underutilized source of self-supervision.
AI.method: TSIL (Temporal Self-Imitation Learning) mines temporally efficient successful trajectories generated during learning, converts them into reusable supervision via configuration-conditioned adaptive temporal targets, and preserves efficient behaviors through efficiency-weighted self-imitation learning.
AI.result: Across 15 long-horizon manipulation tasks, TSIL consistently improves learning efficiency, task-completion efficiency, revisitation of fast successful behaviors, and robustness to unstable training conditions.
AI.conclusion: The temporal structure of successful behavior provides a scalable self-supervisory signal for RL beyond manually engineered reward shaping alone.

title: A Comparative Study of Pretrained Transformer Models for Quranic ASR: Speech Representations, Label Formats, and Dataset Composition
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables, Submitted to International Journal of Speech Technology
summary: Quran Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) aims to convert Quranic recitation into text, enabling applications such as aided memorisation tools and Quranic search engines. However, existing ASR models often exhibit high Word Error Rates (WER) on user-recited verses and lack full coverage of the Quranic corpus. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of domain-specific fine-tuning of pretrained Transformer-based models for Quranic ASR, using advanced speech feature extraction methods: Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, and XLS-R. These models apply self-supervised learning by masking portions of input audio and using Transformer architectures to learn context-aware speech features. The pretrained models are fine-tuned on a filtered Quranic dataset exceeding 870 hours of professional and user recitations. Through comprehensive ablation studies across feature extractors, output label formats, training strategies, and clip durations, we identify the key factors that affect transcription accuracy in this domain. Our best-performing configuration achieves a WER of 0.08 on the EveryAyah subset and 0.11 on the combined EveryAyah+Tarteel setting, representing roughly a five-percentage-point gain over the Citrinet baseline (WER = 0.163) while reducing combined-model training time from 140 hours to 40 hours. Arabic text without diacritics yields the best fine-tuning results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest overall representation. Future work includes improving dataset quality and developing phoneme-aware models to extract deeper speech feature representations for Tajweed-sensitive applications.

AI.tldr: This study fine-tunes pretrained Transformer-based ASR models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) on a filtered Quranic dataset of 870+ hours, achieving a best WER of 0.08 on EveryAyah and 0.11 on EveryAyah+Tarteel, a ~5 percentage point improvement over the Citrinet baseline with 100 hours less training time. Arabic text without diacritics yields the best results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 is the strongest feature extractor.
AI.motivation: Existing Quranic ASR models suffer from high Word Error Rates on user-recited verses and lack full coverage of the Quranic corpus, motivating a systematic empirical study of domain-specific fine-tuning of pretrained Transformer-based models.
AI.method: Three self-supervised pretrained Transformer models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) are fine-tuned on a filtered Quranic dataset of over 870 hours combining professional and user recitations. Comprehensive ablation studies are conducted across feature extractors, output label formats (with/without diacritics), training strategies, and clip durations.
AI.result: Best configuration achieves WER of 0.08 on EveryAyah and 0.11 on EveryAyah+Tarteel settings, outperforming the Citrinet baseline (WER=0.163) by ~5 percentage points while reducing training time from 140 to 40 hours. Arabic text without diacritics yields optimal fine-tuning, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest speech representation.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning of self-supervised Transformer models significantly improves Quranic ASR. Future work includes improving dataset quality and developing phoneme-aware models for Tajweed-sensitive applications.

title: Data Standards for Humanoid Robotics: The Missing Infrastructure for Physical AI
summary: The scalability of humanoid robots will depend not only on models and hardware, but also on whether physical experience can accumulate across robots, tasks, organizations, and time. Drawing on the authors' work in developing ISO/WD 26264-1, Humanoid robot datasets -- Part 1: General requirements, within ISO/TC 299/WG 16, this article argues that data standards are becoming foundational infrastructure for Physical AI. We develop three insights. First, humanoid robot data is embodied interaction data, not a collection of isolated digital samples; a useful dataset must preserve the relationship among robot body, action, task, scene, execution trace, and outcome. Second, its value depends on physical coherence: multimodal streams are reusable only when timing, coordinate frames, calibration, kinematics, units, and synchronization assumptions remain inspectable. Third, the main bottleneck is not only data scarcity, but non-cumulative data caused by high collection costs, data silos, and inconsistent evaluation. We argue that humanoid robot data standards address these bottlenecks by making embodied experience interpretable, shareable, traceable, and reusable. A general standard should provide horizontal infrastructure for lifecycle management, metadata, provenance, quality, versioning, and traceability, while capability-specific parts should define domain grammar for manipulation, locomotion, human-robot interaction, cognition, and future humanoid capabilities. As AI moves from screens into bodies, data standards must evolve from organizing digital information to structuring physical interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that data standards are foundational infrastructure for Physical AI, particularly for humanoid robots. It presents three insights: humanoid robot data is embodied interaction data requiring relational preservation; its value depends on physical coherence (timing, calibration, kinematics, etc.); the main bottleneck is non-cumulative data due to high costs, silos, and inconsistent evaluation. The authors advocate for standards (based on ISO/WD 26264-1) that provide horizontal infrastructure for lifecycle management, metadata, provenance, quality, versioning, and traceability, plus capability-specific parts for manipulation, locomotion, HRI, cognition, etc.
AI.motivation: The scalability of humanoid robots depends on physical experience accumulating across robots, tasks, organizations, and time. Current data practices lack the infrastructure to enable this accumulation.
AI.method: Drawing on the authors' work developing ISO/WD 26264-1 within ISO/TC 299/WG 16, the paper conceptually analyzes the nature of humanoid robot data and argues for standardization as foundational infrastructure for Physical AI.
AI.result: Three insights: (1) humanoid robot data is embodied interaction data requiring relational preservation of body, action, task, scene, execution trace, and outcome; (2) data value depends on physical coherence (timing, coordinate frames, calibration, kinematics, units, synchronization); (3) the main bottleneck is non-cumulative data from high costs, silos, and inconsistent evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Data standards must evolve from organizing digital information to structuring physical interaction. A general standard should provide horizontal infrastructure (lifecycle management, metadata, provenance, quality, versioning, traceability), while capability-specific parts define domain grammar for manipulation, locomotion, HRI, cognition, and future capabilities.

title: Benchmarking Agentic Review Systems
summary: A new class of agentic review systems are emerging as a remedy to the pressure placed on peer review systems by AI-assisted research, but it is unclear how they should be evaluated. We evaluate two open-source systems (OpenAIReview and coarse), one proprietary system (Reviewer3), and a zero-shot baseline, across six LLMs spanning frontier and efficient models. First, we study whether AI reviews on ICLR/NeurIPS papers track with papers' quality as approximated by external signals such as citations and acceptance decisions. Every system performs above chance in pairwise accuracy, and the best is OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 at 83.0%. Second, to test whether systems can catch errors with known ground truth, we construct a perturbation benchmark that injects four categories of errors into papers across eight arXiv subject classes and measure detection recall. The strongest configuration (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) catches 71.6% of injected errors, leaving substantial room for improvement. The union of detections across six models reaches 83.3% recall, suggesting different models detect different errors and better harness design can potentially increase performance. Beyond these benchmarks, we study a public deployment of OpenAIReview with real users. Votes on its comments skew positive at 1.44 to 1, and the most common complaints are about false positives and minor nitpicks. Together, by evaluating full review systems backed by state-of-the-art models on real research papers, we show that while AI reviews still have room for improvement, they can already track human quality judgments well, catch important errors, and earn positive feedback from real users.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates AI-powered peer review systems (OpenAIReview, coarse, Reviewer3, and a zero-shot baseline) across six LLMs, finding that the best system (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) achieves 83.0% accuracy in tracking paper quality, catches 71.6% of injected errors (83.3% when combining models), and receives positive real-user feedback (1.44:1 vote ratio), though substantial room for improvement remains.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted research is increasingly pressuring traditional peer review systems, and while new agentic review systems are emerging as a potential remedy, there is no established methodology for evaluating how well these systems actually perform.
AI.method: The authors evaluate two open-source systems (OpenAIReview, coarse) and one proprietary system (Reviewer3) plus a zero-shot baseline across six LLMs. They conduct three evaluations: (1) pairwise accuracy against paper quality signals (citations, acceptance decisions) on ICLR/NeurIPS papers; (2) a perturbation benchmark injecting four error categories across eight arXiv classes to measure recall; (3) a public deployment study with real user feedback analysis.
AI.result: OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 achieves 83.0% pairwise accuracy, outperforming all other systems. For error detection, the same configuration catches 71.6% of injected errors, while the union across six models reaches 83.3% recall. Real users voted positively (1.44:1 ratio), with main complaints about false positives and minor nitpicks.
AI.conclusion: AI reviews can track human quality judgments well, catch important errors, and earn positive user feedback, but substantial room for improvement remains—particularly in recall and reducing false positives.

title: Start Right, Arrive Right: Asynchronous Execution via Initial Noise Selection
comment: First version 19 pages, project site: https://paint-action-chunking.github.io
summary: Action chunking enables robot policies to produce temporally coherent behavior, but generating multi-step action sequences with flow-based policies incurs latency that is incompatible with real-time control. Under asynchronous execution, the robot continues executing the current chunk while the next one is generated, causing even minor delays to create inconsistencies at chunk boundaries. Existing methods address this problem by steering generation toward the already executed action prefix. We instead show that prefix consistency can be achieved by selecting an appropriate initial noise before generation begins, allowing the unmodified flow ODE to produce a coherent next chunk. This reframes asynchronous inference as a noise selection problem rather than a trajectory steering problem. We introduce \textbf{PAINT}, a training-free method that finds this noise via backward Euler inversion and constructs the final chunk through a repainting rule. In summary, \texttt{PAINT} requires no gradients, retraining, or policy modification; yet it improves execution consistency and task performance across \textit{12 simulated benchmarks} and \textit{6 real-world manipulation tasks} spanning single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid embodiments. Website: ~\href{https://paint-action-chunking.github.io}{\texttt{https://paint-action-chunking.github.io}}.

AI.tldr: PAINT reframes asynchronous action chunking as a noise selection problem, achieving prefix consistency via backward Euler inversion and repainting—requiring no training, gradients, or policy changes—and improving execution consistency across 12 simulated and 6 real-world robotic manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-step action chunking with flow-based policies incurs latency mismatched with real-time control; asynchronous execution causes inconsistencies at chunk boundaries when the robot continues executing the current chunk while the next one is generated.
AI.method: Instead of steering generation toward an executed action prefix, PAINT selects an appropriate initial noise before generation begins via backward Euler inversion, then constructs the final chunk through a repainting rule—requiring no gradients, retraining, or policy modification.
AI.result: Improves execution consistency and task performance across 12 simulated benchmarks and 6 real-world manipulation tasks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid embodiments.
AI.conclusion: Prefix consistency can be achieved by selecting appropriate initial noise, allowing the unmodified flow ODE to produce a coherent next chunk; this reframes asynchronous inference as a noise selection problem rather than a trajectory steering problem.

title: Grounded Inference: Principles for Deterministically Encapsulated Generative Models
summary: The incorporation of generative models into traditional computational systems presents both enormous opportunity and tremendous peril. Although many early adopters have realized these perils at great expense, the field still requires foundational frameworks to de-risk incorporation of AI into traditional systems. This manuscript establishes this foundation through the definition of four specific primitives of AI blended architecture, designed to enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models. It further establishes two overarching anti-patterns broadly represented across industry to serve as warnings for engineers in this field. This framework was designed to enable successful integration of AI into traditional systems while providing a foundation upon which generative model providers could build the next generation of generative model interfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes foundational architectural primitives and anti-patterns for deterministically encapsulating probabilistic generative models within traditional computing systems, enabling safer AI integration.
AI.motivation: The field lacks foundational frameworks to de-risk incorporation of AI into traditional systems, despite many costly failures by early adopters.
AI.method: The paper defines four specific primitives of AI-blended architecture for deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models, and identifies two overarching anti-patterns observed across industry.
AI.result: A framework of four architectural primitives and two anti-patterns that enable successful AI integration into traditional systems.
AI.conclusion: This framework enables successful AI integration into traditional systems and provides a foundation for generative model providers to build next-generation interfaces.

title: EquiVLA: A General Framework for Rotationally Equivariant Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: Comment: First version 22 pages, project site: https://equivla.github.io/
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for generalist robot manipulation, yet they lack geometric inductive biases: policies trained at specific orientations require substantially more data to generalize across rotational configurations. We present \textsc{EquiVLA}, the first general framework for end-to-end $\mathrm{SO}(2)$-equivariant VLA models, applicable to any architecture coupling a frozen vision-language backbone with a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer action head. \textsc{EquiVLA} introduces \textsc{EquiPerceptor}, which produces approximately $\mathrm{SO}(2)$-equivariant visual representations from frozen ViT features; and \textsc{EquiActor}, an exactly $\mathrm{SO}(2)$-equivariant flow-matching Diffusion Transformer action head. Together, they establish an approximate $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ equivariance chain from camera observations to predicted action sequences. Instantiated on GR00T~N1.5 and evaluated across four LIBERO suites, CALVIN ABCD$\to$D, and five real-robot tasks on Mobile ALOHA, \textsc{EquiVLA} achieves $92.6\%$ average success on LIBERO (vs. $78.1\%$ baseline), an average sequence length of $4.03$ on CALVIN (vs. $3.45$), and improves real-robot success from $54\%$ to $72\%$.

AI.tldr: EquiVLA introduces SO(2)-equivariant inductive biases to VLA models for robot manipulation, achieving substantial improvements across LIBERO (+14.5%), CALVIN, and real-robot (+18%) tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models lack geometric inductive biases, requiring excessive data to generalize across rotational configurations.
AI.method: EquiVLA consists of EquiPerceptor (approximate SO(2)-equivariant visual representations from frozen ViT) and EquiActor (exact SO(2)-equivariant flow-matching Diffusion Transformer action head), forming an approximate equivariance chain from camera to action.
AI.result: LIBERO: 92.6% vs 78.1% baseline; CALVIN: 4.03 avg sequence length vs 3.45; Real-robot: 72% vs 54% success rate.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating SO(2) equivariance as an inductive bias significantly improves sample efficiency and generalization of VLA models for robot manipulation.

title: Optimal Scheduling in a Question-Answering Forum of Knowledge Workers
summary: As individuals turn to the Internet to find answers to questions they may have, several Question Answering (QA) forums have evolved, where users knowledgeable in certain topics can contribute their expertise to answering these requests for information. While these are currently volunteer based, we consider a future version employing knowledge workers who are experts in certain topics. In such a system, the request-answer processes forming the queuing system may utilize schedulers that assign requests in different topics to the experts in the forum, who may be able to answer them according to their expertise levels in different topics. With this model, we calculate the capacity of the system for handling the requests while keeping the system stable, and design schedulers that achieve capacity. We also investigate how collaboration between experts in answering requests can potentially increase capacity.

AI.tldr: This paper models QA forums with expert knowledge workers as a queuing system, calculates system capacity for stable request handling, designs schedulers that achieve capacity, and shows how expert collaboration can increase capacity.
AI.motivation: To formally model and analyze the scalability of QA forums where expert knowledge workers answer topic-specific requests, moving beyond volunteer-based systems to a queuing-theoretic framework.
AI.method: Models the request-answer process as a queuing system with topic-specific schedulers assigning requests to experts based on their expertise levels; uses capacity calculation and scheduler design to achieve system stability.
AI.result: Computes the capacity of the system for handling requests under stability constraints; designs schedulers that achieve this capacity; demonstrates that collaboration between experts can increase overall system capacity.
AI.conclusion: Formal queuing models can guide the design of stable, scalable expert-based QA forums, and expert collaboration enhances throughput capacity.

title: TIDY: Thermal Infrared Image Denoising via Wavelet Domain Entropy and Directional Stripe Index
summary: Thermal infrared (TIR) imaging has been a popular choice for field robotics due to its robust perception capability under low light visual degradation, but it suffers from severe stochastic and fixed-pattern noise that breaks downstream estimation. This noise is intensified indoors due to low thermal contrast and uniform temperature distributions, contributing to the relative lack of indoor TIR deployments. Existing TIR denoising methods exhibit a poor accuracy-efficiency tradeoff, either too slow for online deployment required in robotics or insufficiently robust to severe degradation, while typically being trained on synthetic noise. Addressing these problems, we propose TIDY, a lightweight wavelet-domain denoiser trained on real clean-noisy TIR data. By reformulating TIR denoising in the wavelet domain, TIDY explicitly disentangles noise from structural content, enabling targeted suppression with reduced spatial complexity, significantly improving inference speed over prior methods (~34Hz). TIDY introduces two new metrics, Wavelet Entropy and Wavelet Directional Stripe Index, as complementary loss terms to explicitly suppress stochastic noise and stripe artifacts. Across severe indoor corruption and zero-shot settings, TIDY improves robustness and yields consistent gains in downstream robotics tasks including thermal inertial odometry and monocular depth estimation. Code and dataset is available at: https://github.com/williamrheeth/TIDY

AI.tldr: TIDY is a lightweight wavelet-domain TIR denoiser trained on real clean-noisy data that achieves ~34Hz inference speed, using Wavelet Entropy and Wavelet Directional Stripe Index as loss terms to suppress stochastic noise and stripe artifacts, improving downstream robotics tasks like thermal inertial odometry and monocular depth estimation under severe indoor corruption and zero-shot settings.
AI.motivation: TIR imaging suffers from severe stochastic and fixed-pattern noise, intensified indoors due to low thermal contrast and uniform temperature distributions. Existing TIR denoising methods have poor accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs—too slow for online robotics deployment or insufficiently robust—and are typically trained on synthetic noise.
AI.method: TIDY is a lightweight wavelet-domain denoiser trained on real clean-noisy TIR data. It reformulates denoising in the wavelet domain to explicitly disentangle noise from structural content, reducing spatial complexity. It introduces two novel loss terms: Wavelet Entropy and Wavelet Directional Stripe Index, to suppress stochastic noise and stripe artifacts respectively.
AI.result: TIDY achieves ~34Hz inference speed, significantly faster than prior methods. It demonstrates improved robustness under severe indoor corruption and zero-shot settings, yielding consistent gains in downstream robotics tasks including thermal inertial odometry and monocular depth estimation.
AI.conclusion: The wavelet-domain approach with real training data and specialized loss terms effectively addresses the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in TIR denoising, enabling practical online deployment in field robotics.

title: Beyond Entropy: Learning from Token-Level Distributional Deviations for LLM Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning; however, it faces a fundamental optimization instability: uniform token updates precipitate entropy collapse, leading to premature convergence to suboptimal strategies, whereas excessive Shannon Entropy maximization can cause entropy explosion, driving blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning chains.
