A heterogeneous LLM Validation Agent verifies completeness, parameter accuracy, and execution order, and triggers a self-correction loop with structured feedback when errors are detected. A sweep involving 7 Parsers and 3 Validators on randomly selected ELISA protocols evaluates how model scale and Validator type affect translation accuracy and pass rates under cross-model verification. The accuracy-latency trade-off is further verified by comparing the rule-based mapping of the proposed framework with LLM end-to-end direct mapping. Finally, Bradford assay-based protein quantification using a microplate was demonstrated on a robotic laboratory platform, validating end-to-end autonomous execution from natural-language protocols to real-world experiments. The proposed framework provides a flexible approach to narrowing the semantic gap between natural-language protocols and microplate-based self-driving laboratories.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an agent-based framework that converts natural-language microplate-based biological experiment protocols into executable robotic control commands using a Parser Agent, rule-based mapping engine, and LLM Validation Agent with self-correction, validated through ELISA protocol sweeps and Bradford assay demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Natural-language biological protocols cannot be directly executed by automation systems due to a semantic gap; microplate-based experiments add complexity from well mapping, sample-reagent combinations, replicate placement, and parallel dispensing, necessitating a translation framework.
AI.method: A Parser Agent formalizes natural-language protocols into structured representations; a rule-based mapping engine applies platform constraints to generate device-level commands; a heterogeneous LLM Validation Agent verifies correctness and triggers self-correction via structured feedback. Sweeps across 7 Parsers and 3 Validators on ELISA protocols evaluate translation accuracy and pass rates.
AI.result: Cross-model evaluation on ELISA protocols showed dependency of translation accuracy and pass rates on model scale and Validator type; rule-based mapping outperformed LLM end-to-end direct mapping in accuracy-latency trade-off; Bradford assay protein quantification validated end-to-end autonomous execution on a robotic platform.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively narrows the semantic gap between natural-language protocols and microplate-based self-driving laboratories, enabling autonomous execution of biological experiments from text to real-world robotic operation.

title: ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World
summary: Achieving dexterous robotic manipulation in the real world heavily relies on human supervision and algorithm engineering, which becomes a central bottleneck in the pursuit of general physical intelligence. Although emerging coding agents can generate code to automate algorithm search, their successes remain largely confined in digital environments. We conjecture that the missing abstraction to automate robotics research is a repeatable feedback loop for real-world policy improvement: reset the scene, execute a policy, verify the outcome, and refine the next iteration. To bridge this gap, we introduce ENPIRE, a harness framework for coding agents that instantiates this physical feedback routine with four core modules: an Environment module (EN) for automatic reset and verification, a Policy Improvement module (PI) that launches policy refinement, a Rollout module (R) to evaluate policies with one or multiple physical robots operating in parallel, and an Evolution module (E) in which coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, improve training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. This closed-loop system transforms real-world manipulation learning into a controllable optimization procedure, minimizing human effort while allowing fair ablations across training recipe and agent variants. Powered by ENPIRE, frontier coding agents can autonomously train a policy to achieve a 99% success rate on challenging, dexterous manipulation tasks, such as organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, and tool use, a process that further accelerates when we dispatch an agent team on a robot fleet. Our results suggest a practical and scalable path toward deploying coding agents to autonomously advancing robotics in the physical world.

AI.tldr: ENPIRE is a harness framework enabling coding agents to autonomously improve real-world robotic manipulation policies through a closed-loop feedback system (Environment → Policy Improvement → Rollout → Evolution), achieving 99% success on dexterous tasks like pin organizing, zip-tying, and tool use without human intervention.
AI.motivation: Dexterous real-world robotic manipulation suffers from reliance on human supervision and manual algorithm engineering, which is a major bottleneck for general physical intelligence. Existing coding agents succeed in digital environments but lack a repeatable feedback loop for physical policy improvement.
AI.method: ENPIRE framework with four modules: (1) Environment module (EN) for automatic scene reset and verification; (2) Policy Improvement module (PI) for launching policy refinement; (3) Rollout module (R) for parallel policy evaluation on physical robots; (4) Evolution module (E) where coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, and improve training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes.
AI.result: Frontier coding agents powered by ENPIRE achieve 99% success rates on challenging dexterous manipulation tasks (pin box organizing, zip tie fastening, tool use). Performance further accelerates when an agent team is dispatched on a robot fleet. The system enables fair ablations across training recipes and agent variants.
AI.conclusion: ENPIRE provides a practical and scalable path toward deploying coding agents to autonomously advance robotics research in the physical world by transforming real-world manipulation learning into a controllable optimization procedure with minimal human effort.

title: Frequency-Aware Flow Matching for Continuous and Consistent Robotic Action Generation
summary: Flow matching has emerged as a standard paradigm for robotic manipulation owing to its strong expressive power for modelling complex, multimodal action distributions, alongside similar approaches like diffusion policy. However, existing methods rely on discretized action chunks, making them brittle to demonstrations collected at heterogeneous control frequencies and prone to temporally inconsistent actions that degrade control stability. In this paper, we propose Frequency-Aware Flow Matching (FAFM), which outputs continuous, temporally consistent actions. To handle heterogeneous frequency input, we transform discrete action sequences into the frequency domain with the discrete cosine transform (DCT), perform flow matching over the resulting coefficients, and reconstruct continuous actions via cosine basis expansion. To generate temporally consistent actions, we regularize the first-order temporal derivative to promote smooth actions. This corresponds to a Sobolev-type constraint that suppresses high-frequency errors and discourages abrupt action changes. Our FAFM is simple, introduces no additional network parameters and applies to standalone flow-matching policies and vision-language action models. Across synthetic toy benchmark, obstacle avoidance, LapGym, and LIBERO, FAFM improves success rates, multimodal expressivity, motion smoothness, convergence speed, robustness to mechanical bias and mixed-frequency input. These gains are consistent when deployed on a real-world Franka robot. Code available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FAFM.

AI.tldr: FAFM uses frequency-domain flow matching (via DCT) with Sobolev regularization to generate smooth, temporally consistent continuous actions from heterogeneous-frequency demonstrations for robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing flow matching / diffusion policies rely on discretized action chunks, which are brittle to heterogeneous control frequencies and produce temporally inconsistent actions that degrade control stability.
AI.method: (1) Transform discrete action sequences to frequency domain via DCT; (2) perform flow matching over DCT coefficients; (3) reconstruct continuous actions via cosine basis expansion. Temporal consistency is enforced via first-order derivative regularization (Sobolev-type constraint) that suppresses high-frequency errors.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines on synthetic toy benchmark, obstacle avoidance, LapGym, and LIBERO; improves success rates, multimodal expressivity, motion smoothness, convergence speed, robustness to mechanical bias and mixed-frequency input. Validated on real-world Franka robot.
AI.conclusion: FAFM is a simple, parameter-free enhancement to flow matching that yields temporally consistent, smooth continuous actions, effective for both standalone policies and vision-language action models across diverse robotic tasks.

title: Reward as An Agent for Embodied World Models
summary: While RL has become a promising tool for refining world models, existing methods largely rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, limiting exploration, behavioral diversity, and richer dynamic discovery. In this work, we challenge this conservative paradigm. We argue that the core limitation is not exploration itself, but the lack of reliable verification strategies to support broader exploration. Without reliable verification, expanded exploration becomes highly susceptible to reward hacking, where policies exploit imperfect rewards without achieving genuine improvement. To evaluate this motivation, we instantiate our method in embodied world models, where physical plausibility, and task completion provide a rigorous testbed for scalable RL under complex dynamics. On the verification side, we introduce Reward as an Agent, an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals and mitigate reward hacking under distribution shifts. On the exploration side, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification through DynDiff-GRPO, which explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors beyond conservative rollout regimes. By unifying Reward as an Agent with DynDiff-GRPO, we enable RL on a more reliable reward foundation with substantially diversified sampling, effectively mitigating reward hacking while yielding significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models, thereby demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework combining an agentic reward system (Reward as an Agent) with diversified exploration (DynDiff-GRPO) to enable broader, scalable RL for world models without reward hacking, achieving significant accuracy gains across multiple embodied world models.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-based world model refinement relies on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, which limits exploration, behavioral diversity, and dynamic discovery. The authors argue the core issue is not a lack of exploration but the absence of reliable verification strategies to support broader exploration without reward hacking.
AI.method: The paper proposes: (1) Reward as an Agent — an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals and mitigate reward hacking under distribution shifts; (2) DynDiff-GRPO — Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification that explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories and broaden state-action coverage. These two components are unified into a single RL framework.
AI.result: The unified framework mitigates reward hacking and yields significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source embodied world models, demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification.
AI.conclusion: Broader exploration in RL for world models is viable when paired with reliable verification. The proposed framework enables scalable RL with diversified sampling and robust reward signals, challenging the conservative rollout paradigm.

title: Robust Assembly State Reasoning from Action Recognition for Human-Robot Collaboration
comment: Preprint accepted to the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026). 8 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables
summary: Human Action Recognition (HAR) is frequently investigated in Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) research to understand what actions have been performed and hence the state of a collaborative task. Accurately tracking an assembly state from HAR is however not fully investigated, and in realistic scenarios is not a trivial task. This research systematically investigates and compares methods for tracking assembly state using action recognition inputs. Investigations using two diverse datasets and five state tracking approaches, including logic-based, Hidden Markov Model (HMM), and neural network (NN) methods, show that optimal approaches are not uniform across different tasks and that different methods fail under different circumstances. Testing is performed using both simulated inputs with varying noise levels and realistic inputs from a HAR model. Results show NN and HMM methods can perform well in tasks with limited variability, but for other scenarios logic-based approaches can be more robust. Methods which model expected action duration are also important for tasks with repeated actions where no additional sensing is provided.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates and compares methods (logic-based, HMM, neural network) for tracking assembly state from human action recognition inputs in Human-Robot Collaboration, finding optimal approaches vary by task—NN and HMM work well for limited variability tasks, while logic-based methods are more robust in other scenarios.
AI.motivation: Accurately tracking assembly state from HAR inputs is not fully investigated and is non-trivial in realistic scenarios; this research aims to systematically compare methods to address this gap.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of five state tracking approaches (logic-based, Hidden Markov Model, neural network) using two diverse datasets, tested with both simulated inputs at varying noise levels and realistic HAR model inputs.
AI.result: Optimal approaches are not uniform across tasks; NN and HMM perform well in tasks with limited variability, logic-based approaches are more robust in other scenarios; methods modeling expected action duration are important for tasks with repeated actions and no additional sensing.
AI.conclusion: Different state tracking methods fail under different circumstances, and no single approach is universally optimal—choice depends on task characteristics such as variability and action repetition.

title: Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale
summary: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates multi-agent orchestration architectures (DAG Plan and Execute vs. ReAct) across 208 enterprise scenarios at Persona, Department, and Enterprise scales, finding that scale—not task complexity—is the dominant performance bottleneck, and introduces a Task Manager that reduces high-priority latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by 20+ percentage points at enterprise scale.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI requires continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, but existing multi-agent systems assume discrete request-response workflows and are underexplored at enterprise scale.
AI.method: Evaluated DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct on 208 production-derived scenarios at three scales (Persona <10 agents, Department 20–80, Enterprise 200 agents); introduced a Task Manager for continuous operation using priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption.
AI.result: Scale dominates orchestration performance: both architectures degrade at enterprise scale due to agent discovery noise, with simple tasks degrading more sharply. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and parallelization at small scales but suffers higher overhead at scale; ReAct is more robust via incremental failure handling. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by >20 percentage points at enterprise scale.
AI.conclusion: Scale is the primary bottleneck in multi-agent enterprise orchestration rather than task complexity; the proposed Task Manager effectively mitigates scale-induced performance degradation.

title: Belt-Finger: An Affordable Soft Belt-Driven Gripper for Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
summary: Parallel-jaw grippers are the default manipulator choice in robotics because they are simple, robust, and inexpensive. Their limited in-hand mobility, however, often forces large arm motions and restricts dexterous manipulation in confined workspaces. We present a parallel-gripper upgrade: a double-soft-belt-based finger module that preserves standard opening/closing while adding three in-hand degrees of freedom (DoF): translation, pitch, and roll. The mechanism is deliberately kept simple and engineered for inexpensive manufacturing and straightforward integration, preserving the reliability and precise control of traditional parallel grippers while greatly broadening the range of manipulation capabilities. To demonstrate the utility of the added DoFs, we integrate the gripper in two control pipelines. First, we adapt a model predictive controller for in-hand manipulation of known objects. Second, we introduce a lightweight teleoperation interface that enables simultaneous control of the robot arm and gripper (10 DoFs total) with minimal hardware. Across a suite of challenging manipulation tasks executed via teleoperation, MPC, and trained policies, the proposed gripper consistently improves dexterity and task feasibility compared to a conventional parallel gripper

AI.tldr: The paper presents a parallel-jaw gripper upgrade using double-soft-belt finger modules that adds three in-hand degrees of freedom (translation, pitch, roll) while preserving standard gripping, enabling improved dexterity via MPC, teleoperation, and learned policies.
AI.motivation: Parallel-jaw grippers are simple and robust but lack in-hand mobility, requiring large arm motions and limiting dexterous manipulation in confined spaces. This work aims to enhance their manipulation capabilities while preserving their reliability and low cost.
AI.method: A double-soft-belt-based finger module is designed to add three in-hand DoFs (translation, pitch, roll) to a standard parallel gripper. The gripper is integrated into two control pipelines: (1) a model predictive controller for in-hand manipulation of known objects, and (2) a lightweight teleoperation interface for simultaneous 10-DoF control of arm and gripper.
AI.result: Across teleoperation, MPC, and trained policy tasks, the proposed gripper consistently improves dexterity and task feasibility compared to a conventional parallel gripper.
AI.conclusion: The double-soft-belt gripper upgrade broadens manipulation capabilities of parallel grippers while maintaining their simplicity, robustness, and precise control, making it suitable for inexpensive manufacturing and integration.

title: Process-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Theorem Proving via Lean
summary: While reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically has relied on a single binary verification signal, symbolic proof assistants in formal reasoning offer rich, fine-grained structured feedback. This gap between structured processes and unstructured rewards highlights the importance of feedback that is both dense and sound. In this work, we demonstrate that the Lean proof assistant itself can serve as a symbolic process oracle, supplying both outcome-level and fine-grained tactic-level verified feedback during training. Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences, and Lean's elaboration marks both locally sound steps and the earliest failing step, yielding dense, verifier-grounded credit signals rooted in type theory. We incorporate these structured rewards into a GRPO-style reinforcement learning objective with first-error propagation and first-token credit methods that balances outcome- and process-level advantages. Experiments with STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 show that tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, delivering improvements on benchmarks such as MiniF2F and ProofNet. Beyond empirical gains, our study highlights a broader perspective: symbolic proof assistants are not only verifiers at evaluation time, but can also act as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward reinforcement learning frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper leverages the Lean proof assistant as a symbolic process oracle to provide both outcome-level and fine-grained tactic-level feedback during reinforcement learning training, surpassing outcome-only baselines on formal reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RLVR relies on a single binary verification signal, which lacks the dense, structured feedback needed for formal reasoning. Symbolic proof assistants like Lean can offer richer feedback, but this potential remains underexplored during training.
AI.method: Parse proof attempts into tactic sequences, use Lean's elaboration to mark locally sound steps and the earliest failing step for dense, verifier-grounded credit signals. Incorporate these structured rewards into a GRPO-style RL objective with first-error propagation and first-token credit methods.
AI.result: Tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, with improvements on MiniF2F and ProofNet benchmarks using STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic proof assistants can serve as process-level reward oracles during training, not just as evaluators at test time, enabling RL frameworks that combine language model scalability with symbolic verification reliability.

title: Stable Transformer-Actor-Critic Model Predictive Control: A Contraction Analysis Approach
summary: Actor-Critic Model Predictive Control (MPC) effectively addresses complex, non-convex control problems, but guaranteeing the closed-loop stability of sequence-based learning models within these pipelines remains challenging. This paper introduces a novel Transformer-Actor-Critic MPC architecture with formal robustness guarantees. First, we prove that Transformer networks can satisfy global incremental Input-to-State Stability ($δ$ISS). We then leverage Riemannian contraction theory to analyze the interconnected dynamics between the physical plant and the predictive neural network. Finally, we integrate these theoretical bounds as a training regularizer to yield a certifiably robust policy. The framework is validated on a nonlinear 3D drone model executing target-reaching and obstacle-avoidance maneuvers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Transformer-Actor-Critic MPC architecture that provides formal robustness guarantees for complex control problems, proven via δISS and Riemannian contraction theory, and validated on a 3D drone model.
AI.motivation: Actor-Critic MPC effectively handles complex non-convex control problems, but guaranteeing closed-loop stability of sequence-based learning models within these pipelines remains a challenge.
AI.method: The authors prove that Transformer networks can satisfy global incremental Input-to-State Stability (δISS), leverage Riemannian contraction theory to analyze interconnected dynamics between the physical plant and predictive neural network, and integrate these theoretical bounds as a training regularizer to produce a certifiably robust policy.
AI.result: The framework is validated on a nonlinear 3D drone model executing target-reaching and obstacle-avoidance maneuvers, demonstrating practical effectiveness of the formally robust architecture.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Transformer-Actor-Critic MPC with formal robustness guarantees successfully addresses the stability challenge in sequence-based learning models for complex control problems.

title: Residual-Space Evolutionary Optimization via Flow-based Generative Models
comment: Accepted by ICML 2026 Workshop SPIGM, 5 pages, 3 figures
summary: Data editing with generative methods typically requires differentiable objectives and gradient-based search. However, these assumptions break down in flow-based settings, where edits are performed through forward and backward integration and often involve non-differentiable or black-box objectives. We introduce residual-space evolutionary optimization, a model-agnostic framework that addresses this gap by combining flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms. Building on the observation that conditional flow matching (CFM) can disentangle condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals, our framework directly operates in residual space and separates two complementary search regimes: self-pollination performs local exploitation through feature-preserving residual refinement, and cross-pollination promotes broader exploration by recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples. As a proof of concept, we validate on MorphoMNIST, a benchmark dataset for counterfactual generation, and on crystal data, demonstrating that this exploration--exploitation decomposition provides a useful mechanism for balancing target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity, and extends beyond images to real-world scientific domains.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces residual-space evolutionary optimization, a framework that combines flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms to enable non-differentiable, black-box objectives in conditional flow matching models, validated on MorphoMNIST and crystal data.
AI.motivation: Existing generative editing methods require differentiable objectives and gradient-based search, which fail in flow-based settings where edits involve forward/backward integration and non-differentiable or black-box objectives.
AI.method: A model-agnostic framework that operates in residual space of conditional flow matching (CFM), employing two complementary evolutionary search regimes: self-pollination (local exploitation via feature-preserving residual refinement) and cross-pollination (broader exploration via recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples).
AI.result: Validated on MorphoMNIST (counterfactual generation benchmark) and crystal data, demonstrating that the exploration-exploitation decomposition balances target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework extends beyond images to real-world scientific domains, effectively addressing the gap in flow-based generative editing for non-differentiable objectives.

title: FlowMaps: Modeling Long-Term Multimodal Object Dynamics with Flow Matching
summary: Joint spatial and temporal understanding of 3D scenes is a crucial requirement for robots deployed in everyday household environments. Such agents must not only comprehend and navigate spatial layouts, but also reason about how these spaces evolve over time. In particular, humans interact with objects daily, causing them to change position throughout the environment and making it difficult for robots to reliably associate current observations with previously seen objects. However, these interactions are not random: human habits and routines induce spatio-temporally consistent patterns in object locations, which robotic agents can potentially learn and then exploit for downstream tasks such as navigation. To this end, we introduce FlowMaps, a latent flow matching model for estimating multimodal distributions over the future locations of dynamic objects in a continuous 3D space. By learning the implicit dependencies among objects and their temporal evolution, FlowMaps predicts likely changes in object locations conditioned on past human interactions, while supporting generalization across previously unseen environments that share similar object routines. To demonstrate the utility of this method, we deploy FlowMaps in a downstream dynamic Object Navigation task in both simulated and real-world environments. Across more than 600 episodes, FlowMaps outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, showing that modeling object dynamics through continuous, multimodal spatio-temporal distributions improves robotic search and navigation in changing household environments. Code and additional material is available at https://fra-tsuna.github.io/flowmaps/.

AI.tldr: FlowMaps is a latent flow matching model that predicts multimodal distributions over future locations of dynamic objects in 3D space by learning spatio-temporal patterns from human-object interactions, improving robot navigation in changing household environments across 600+ episodes.
AI.motivation: Robots in household environments need joint spatial and temporal understanding to reliably associate current observations with previously seen objects that change position due to human interactions. These interactions follow habitual patterns that robots can learn.
AI.method: FlowMaps uses a latent flow matching model to estimate multimodal distributions over future locations of dynamic objects in continuous 3D space, learning implicit dependencies among objects and their temporal evolution conditioned on past human interactions.
AI.result: Across 600+ episodes in simulated and real-world environments, FlowMaps outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in dynamic Object Navigation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Modeling object dynamics through continuous, multimodal spatio-temporal distributions improves robotic search and navigation in changing household environments, and FlowMaps generalizes across previously unseen environments sharing similar object routines.

title: Multi-Head Attention-Based Feature Extractor Integration with Soft Actor-Critic for Porosity Prediction and Process Parameter Optimization in Additive Manufacturing
summary: Additive manufacturing process optimization requires precise parameter control to minimize defects such as porosity. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) approaches using discrete action spaces suffer from slow convergence and susceptibility to local optima, limiting their effectiveness for high-precision manufacturing tasks. This study addresses these limitations by employing a continuous action space combined with a novel architecture that integrates a multi-head attention mechanism with the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm. The attention-based feature extractor enhances the agent's ability to capture subtle variations in low-dimensional input features, enabling more effective exploration-exploitation balance for navigating value spaces with local minima. We validate our approach on porosity prediction and process parameter optimization in laser powder bed fusion, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final reward values compared to standard RL methods including DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC. The proposed methodology achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, outperforming existing approaches while maintaining stability throughout training.

AI.tldr: Proposes a continuous-action SAC algorithm with multi-head attention for additive manufacturing process optimization, achieving faster convergence (322.79 reward in 14 episodes) and outperforming DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC on laser powder bed fusion porosity optimization.
AI.motivation: Traditional RL with discrete action spaces suffers from slow convergence and local optima when optimizing additive manufacturing parameters for defect minimization (e.g., porosity).
AI.method: Integrates a multi-head attention mechanism with the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm in a continuous action space; attention-based feature extractor captures subtle variations in low-dimensional inputs to improve exploration-exploitation trade-off.
AI.result: Achieves convergence reward of 322.79 within 14 episodes; outperforms DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC in convergence speed, final reward, and training stability on laser powder bed fusion porosity prediction and parameter optimization.
AI.conclusion: Continuous-action SAC with multi-head attention effectively addresses RL limitations for high-precision manufacturing optimization, offering faster convergence and robust performance.

title: Mobile Target Search with Imperfect Perception: A Partially Observable Stochastic Game Theoretical Approach
summary: This paper investigates mobile target search under imperfect perceptions caused by sensor limitations, malicious jamming, or communication noise. Searchers and targets operate in a grid-shaped area with bounded mobility, leading to a dynamic interplay between search and evasion. To capture this adversarial interaction under imperfect perceptions, we adopt the partially observable stochastic game (POSG) approach, which generalizes partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) by incorporating target intelligence. To handle false alarms and missed detections caused by perceptual uncertainties, we propose a novel detectability concept to determine whether a search strategy guarantees eventual detection, and provide sufficient detectability criteria based on stochastic recurrence analysis. We further develop a server-assisted distributed algorithm that utilizes the aggregative potential game structure for searchers and a KL-divergence-based reduction for target prediction. Numerical simulations validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm and support the detectability analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper studies mobile target search with imperfect perceptions (false alarms, missed detections) using a POSG framework, proposes a detectability concept with stochastic recurrence criteria, and develops a server-assisted distributed algorithm based on potential games and KL-divergence for target prediction.
AI.motivation: To address mobile target search under imperfect perceptions caused by sensor limitations, jamming, or communication noise, where traditional POMDP approaches fail to account for target intelligence and adversarial evasion.
AI.method: POSG framework; detectability concept via stochastic recurrence analysis; server-assisted distributed algorithm using aggregative potential game structure for searchers; KL-divergence-based reduction for target prediction.
AI.result: Numerical simulations validate the effectiveness of the proposed distributed algorithm and support the detectability analysis.
AI.conclusion: The POSG-based approach with detectability criteria and distributed algorithm effectively handles mobile target search under perceptual uncertainties, providing sufficient conditions for guaranteed detection.

title: ScaffoldAgent: Utility-Guided Dynamic Outline Optimization for Open-Ended Deep Research
summary: Open-ended deep research (OEDR) requires systems to acquire knowledge through multi-round retrieval and generate coherent long-form reports. The outline plays a central role as a structural scaffold that coordinates retrieval, evidence organization, and generation. However, existing methods either fix the outline before writing or refine it with local heuristics, leading to scaffold drift under continuous information accumulation and delayed feedback for evaluating outline modifications. We propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for OEDR. ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision, enabling controlled updates to the report scaffold. It further introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates the downstream value of each outline operation from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. The resulting utility signal guides node selection, operation scheduling, and termination during inference. Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves long-form report generation and factual grounding over existing deep research agents.

AI.tldr: ScaffoldAgent is a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for open-ended deep research that models outline evolution as structured operations (Expansion, Contraction, Revision) and uses utility signals to guide retrieval, organization, and generation, outperforming existing methods on benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing OEDR methods suffer from scaffold drift due to fixing outlines prematurely or using local heuristics for refinement, lacking global evaluation of outline modifications under continuous information accumulation.
AI.method: ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations (Expansion, Contraction, Revision) and introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates downstream value of each operation based on retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality to guide node selection, operation scheduling, and termination.
AI.result: Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show consistent improvements in long-form report generation and factual grounding over existing deep research agents.
AI.conclusion: Utility-guided dynamic outline optimization effectively addresses scaffold drift in OEDR, enabling more coherent and factually grounded long-form report generation.

title: Finetuning Vision-Language-Action Models Requires Fewer Layers Than You Think
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models pre-trained on massive video-robot datasets have revolutionized robotic manipulation, yet their multi-billion parameter architectures impose prohibitive computational burdens during downstream fine-tuning and real-time inference. In this work, we reveal a highly non-trivial architectural characteristic of these continuous control foundation policies (e.g., pi_0, GR00T-N1.5): despite being trained on diverse physical trajectories, they exhibit severe layer-wise representational redundancy. To exploit this, we introduce a structural compression pipeline that is entirely training-free, bypassing the need of existing methods to load full-scale models to learn optimized token reductions or dynamic layer selectors. Instead, using only a single forward pass via Centered Kernel Alignment to identify redundant layer features, we remove twin layers to permanently compress the model depth by up to 50% across both the VLM backbone and the continuous control policy head. Downstream fine-tuning of this streamlined architecture yields a dual acceleration benefit: a 40-50% reduction in training time and up to 30% faster real-time inference, while matching or exceeding full-scale base model performance. We comprehensively validate our method across three simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboCasa, SimplerEnv) and 10 diverse real-world manipulation tasks across 4 unique robotic embodiments. These results prove that advanced VLAs require significantly fewer layers than previously assumed, offering a highly compute-efficient paradigm for scalable robot learning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a training-free structural compression pipeline for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that identifies and removes redundant layers in both the VLM backbone and control policy head, achieving up to 50% depth reduction, 40-50% faster training, and 30% faster inference while matching full-scale model performance across simulation and real-world robotic tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-billion parameter VLA models impose prohibitive computational burdens during downstream fine-tuning and real-time inference, limiting their practical deployment in robotic manipulation.
AI.method: A training-free structural compression pipeline that uses a single forward pass with Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to identify redundant layer features, then removes twin layers to permanently compress model depth by up to 50% across both VLM backbone and continuous control policy head.
AI.result: 40-50% reduction in training time, up to 30% faster real-time inference, while matching or exceeding full-scale base model performance. Validated on LIBERO, RoboCasa, SimplerEnv, and 10 real-world tasks across 4 robotic embodiments.
AI.conclusion: Advanced VLAs require significantly fewer layers than previously assumed, offering a compute-efficient paradigm for scalable robot learning.

title: Learning to Prompt: Improving Student Engagement with Adaptive LLM-based High-School Tutoring
summary: LLMs can personalize education, although current static-prompt tutoring systems struggle to adapt to diverse academic disciplines. We develop and test a system with subject-aware prompting, based on 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) extracted from raw transcripts. We first train a prompt routing model in a simulation environment, and then deploy it for online adaptation with actual high-school students. The simulation benchmark shows the router outperforming two static baselines ($0.694$ vs. $0.647$ and $0.64$, $p<0.001$). A/B testing ($N=656$ conversations from 359 students) shows sim-to-real transfer where the model switches from analytical to scaffolding learning strategies. Our adaptive prompt selection mechanism improves instructional efficiency, maintains pedagogical quality and reduces interactions by around 3 turns ($p=0.007$). While a greedy router achieves a comparable exercise conversion rate with the baseline ($19.1\%$ vs. $19.6\%$), a stochastic router that samples strategies leads to a higher conversion rate ($28.1\%$).

AI.tldr: The paper develops a subject-aware adaptive prompt routing system for LLM-based tutoring that uses 14 pedagogical features to select tutoring strategies, demonstrating improved efficiency and conversion rates in both simulation and real-world high-school settings.
AI.motivation: Current static-prompt LLM tutoring systems struggle to adapt across diverse academic disciplines, necessitating an adaptive mechanism for personalized education.
AI.method: Extracted 14 pedagogical features from raw transcripts (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding), trained a prompt routing model in simulation, and deployed it for online adaptation with real high-school students; compared greedy and stochastic routing strategies.
AI.result: Router outperformed static baselines in simulation (0.694 vs. 0.647/0.64, p<0.001). A/B testing (656 conversations, 359 students) showed sim-to-real transfer, reduced interactions by ~3 turns (p=0.007), and stochastic router achieved higher conversion rate (28.1%) vs. greedy (19.1%) and baseline (19.6%).
AI.conclusion: Adaptive prompt selection improves instructional efficiency and maintains pedagogical quality; stochastic strategy sampling yields better engagement outcomes than greedy selection.

title: Efficiently Linking Real Scenes with Synthetic Data Generation for AI-based Cognitive Robotics and Computer Vision Applications
comment: Accepted and best paper award at MHI-Kolloquium 2024
summary: AI vision models are a driving factor for the potential use case scenarios of cognitive robotics within in the industry and household applications. A large array of methods from semantic environment analysis towards 6D and grasping pose estimation have been proposed based on the latest AI achievements. However, such advancements require further strong and efficient methods w.r.t. training data and AI-architectures, which are capable in synergy to tackle current challenges, precision limits, and scalability beyond domain gaps. In this paper, we discuss these current limits and trends in the related state-of-the-art which are challenging those. Further we discuss our current work in progress on bridging the domain gap between simulations and real world applications by linking those in the training data generation.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses current limits and trends in AI vision models for cognitive robotics, particularly focusing on challenges related to training data, precision, scalability, and domain gaps between simulations and real-world applications.
AI.motivation: AI vision models are crucial for cognitive robotics in industrial and household applications, but current methods face challenges in training efficiency, precision, scalability, and bridging the domain gap between simulated and real-world environments.
AI.method: The paper presents a discussion on state-of-the-art limitations and trends in AI vision for robotics, along with ongoing work on linking simulation and real-world training data to bridge the domain gap.
AI.result: Identification of current limits in semantic environment analysis, 6D pose estimation, and grasping pose estimation, with a focus on domain gap challenges.
AI.conclusion: Future advancements require stronger and more efficient methods in training data and AI architectures to overcome domain gaps and scalability issues in cognitive robotics.

title: RACL: Reasoning-Agent Control Layers for Continuous Metaheuristic Learning
summary: This paper introduces RACL, a Reasoning-Agent Control Layer for metaheuristics. RACL places a reasoning agent above an existing optimizer. The agent does not replace the optimizer and does not modify business constraints. Instead, it controls the optimizer's internal search behavior by observing operational memory, reasoning over past behavior, formulating bounded hypotheses, testing interventions, evaluating outcomes, applying guardrails, consolidating useful policies and explaining its decisions. The experiment uses vehicle routing as a testbed, but the contribution is not a new routing solver, a particular ALNS configuration or a specific set of routing rules. The contribution is the RACL method: a way for a reasoning agent to discover, validate, consolidate and explain algorithmic control rules for a metaheuristic. In the current experimental setting, RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21 of 21 feasible cases and improves or ties a non-reasoning Stagnation-Triggered Policy in 18 of 21 feasible cases, with an average RACL vs STP cost delta of -0.641%. In the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% versus Fixed and -1.605% versus STP without showing material computational overhead. During the proof-of-concept, Codex was used as an in-the-loop reasoning agent observing executions, interpreting logs and proposing live bounded interventions. The policy proxy was later used only to make quantitative evaluation reproducible.

AI.tldr: RACL is a Reasoning-Agent Control Layer that sits above an existing metaheuristic optimizer, controlling its internal search behavior by observing, reasoning, hypothesizing, testing, and consolidating control rules. It improves or ties baselines in 21/21 and 18/21 feasible cases with negligible overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing metaheuristic optimizers lack adaptive, explainable control over their internal search behavior. The goal is to introduce a reasoning layer that can discover, validate, consolidate, and explain algorithmic control rules without replacing the optimizer or modifying business constraints.
AI.method: RACL places a reasoning agent above an existing optimizer. The agent observes operational memory, reasons over past behavior, formulates bounded hypotheses, tests interventions, evaluates outcomes, applies guardrails, consolidates useful policies, and explains decisions. Codex was used as the in-the-loop reasoning agent during proof-of-concept; a policy proxy later enabled reproducible quantitative evaluation.
AI.result: RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21/21 feasible cases and improves or ties a Stagnation-Triggered Policy in 18/21 feasible cases, with an average cost delta of -0.641% vs STP. In the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL achieves -8.337% vs Fixed and -1.605% vs STP without material computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: RACL is an effective method for reasoning-driven control of metaheuristics, demonstrating consistent improvements over baseline policies in vehicle routing without significant overhead, while also providing explainability through consolidated policies.

title: Co-VLA: Coordination-Aware Structured Action Modeling for Dual-Arm Vision-Language-Action Systems
summary:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong capabilities in single and dual-arm robotic manipulation. Prior works show coordinated bimanual behaviors can emerge from end-to-end learning, leveraging large vision-language backbones with continuous action prediction. However, as bimanual tasks become tightly coupled and execution constraints become critical, implicit coordination alone is insufficient to ensure reliable, interpretable, and stable behavior.
  In this work, we propose Co-VLA, a coordination-aware bimanual manipulation framework introducing explicit structural priors into VLA models. We instantiate our method on a state-of-the-art vision-language backbone by replacing its monolithic action head with a Structured Action Expert (SAE) designed for bimanual coordination. Specifically, we introduce explicit structure at the action generation level with a modular coordination-aware loss that shapes shared and residual latents according to task-specific structures. The shared latent encodes task-level coordination intent, while residual latents capture execution adjustments for each arm.
  At deployment, a Latent-Aware Controller (LAC) interprets the learned representations to modulate synchronization strength, execution asymmetry, smoothness, and safety constraints in real time. LAC operates at the joint-command level and remains compatible with standard control pipelines without requiring force or impedance control. Experiments across simulation and real-world benchmarks show Co-VLA significantly outperforms monolithic baselines, achieving a 27% success rate gain in tight-coordination tasks, more than doubling performance in OOD real-world scenarios (from 13% to 27%), and reducing task completion time by up to 25%.

AI.tldr: Co-VLA introduces explicit coordination-aware structural priors into VLA models for bimanual manipulation by replacing monolithic action heads with a Structured Action Expert (SAE) and a Latent-Aware Controller (LAC), achieving 27% success rate gains in tight-coordination tasks and reducing completion time by up to 25%.
AI.motivation: Implicit coordination learned via end-to-end VLA models is insufficient for tightly coupled bimanual tasks where reliable, interpretable, and stable behavior under execution constraints is critical.
AI.method: Co-VLA replaces the monolithic action head of a vision-language backbone with a Structured Action Expert (SAE) that uses a modular coordination-aware loss to produce shared (task-level coordination intent) and residual (per-arm execution adjustments) latents, plus a Latent-Aware Controller (LAC) that interprets these representations to modulate synchronization, asymmetry, smoothness, and safety constraints at the joint-command level in real time.
AI.result: 27% success rate gain in tight-coordination tasks, more than double the OOD real-world performance (13% to 27%), and up to 25% reduction in task completion time compared to monolithic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicit structural priors for coordination significantly improve VLA models' performance, reliability, and interpretability in bimanual manipulation, and the framework integrates seamlessly with standard control pipelines.

title: BIM-Edit: Benchmarking Large Language Models for IFC-Based Building Information Modeling
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to computer-aided design (CAD) to generate design artifacts from textual instructions. In engineering practice, this requires more than creating new geometry, models must also understand existing scenes, edit them correctly, and preserve semantics and relations. However, many CAD benchmarks focus on creating new models rather than editing existing ones, and mostly evaluate geometric correctness. We introduce BIM-Edit, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on natural-language editing of Building Information Models (BIM) represented in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) format. BIM provides a challenging testbed because building models encode geometry together with semantic and relational structure. BIM-Edit contains 324 editing tasks spanning 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes. Tasks are expressed using three instruction categories - direct, spatial, and topological - covering both explicit and scene-grounded edits. We evaluate outputs along three dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency. Across evaluated LLMs, the best-performing model achieves only 49.5% average score across the three metrics, and no model fully solves more than 3.4% of tasks. These results demonstrate a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the requirements of structured engineering design workflows.

AI.tldr: BIM-Edit is a new benchmark evaluating LLMs on natural-language editing of Building Information Models (IFC format), testing geometric, semantic, and topological understanding. The best LLM achieves only 49.5% average score and solves less than 3.4% of tasks fully, revealing a major gap in current LLM capabilities for structured engineering design.
AI.motivation: Existing CAD benchmarks focus on creating new models from text and mostly evaluate geometric correctness. However, real engineering practice requires editing existing models while preserving semantics, relations, and scene context—capabilities that are currently underexplored and unbenchmarked for LLMs.
AI.method: The authors construct BIM-Edit with 324 editing tasks across 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes, using three instruction categories (direct, spatial, topological). LLM outputs are evaluated along three dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency.
AI.result: The best-performing LLM achieves only 49.5% average score across the three metrics. No model fully solves more than 3.4% of tasks, indicating substantial deficiency in handling structured engineering editing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs fall far short of the requirements for structured engineering design workflows, particularly in tasks requiring joint geometric, semantic, and topological reasoning during editing of existing models.

title: Towards 3D karst underwater scene reconstruction from rotating sonar data
comment: 1st Workshop on Long-term Deployments in the Wild (LoWi)
summary: Karst aquifers provide critical freshwater resources but pose significant hazards due to their complex and poorly understood subsurface geometry. Mapping these environments is challenging because sonar data from underwater exploration is sparse and noisy, while navigation estimates suffer from drift limiting standard 3D reconstruction methods. We present a pipeline for reconstructing underwater karst conduits from a sonar profiler. We combine a continuous-time SLAM approach to correct trajectory drift with a novel two-stage deep learning method for surface reconstruction, producing an immersive and navigable 3D mesh for hydrogeological analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a pipeline combining continuous-time SLAM for trajectory correction and a two-stage deep learning method for surface reconstruction to create 3D meshes of underwater karst conduits from sparse, noisy sonar data.
AI.motivation: Karst aquifers are critical freshwater sources but are hazardous due to complex subsurface geometry. Mapping them is difficult because sonar data is sparse/noisy and navigation drift limits standard 3D reconstruction.
AI.method: The pipeline combines (1) continuous-time SLAM to correct trajectory drift, and (2) a novel two-stage deep learning method for surface reconstruction, producing an immersive 3D mesh.
AI.result: The approach produces an immersive and navigable 3D mesh suitable for hydrogeological analysis.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline effectively addresses the challenges of sparse/noisy sonar data and navigation drift, enabling accurate 3D reconstruction of underwater karst conduits for hydrogeological analysis.

title: Modularity-Free Conflict-Averse Training for Generalized PINNs
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have become a powerful framework for solving PDEs by embedding physical laws into differentiable objectives. Despite their advances, training PINNs remains fragile: recent conflict-averse optimization schemes alleviate gradient interference between residual and boundary losses, but we show that their effectiveness deteriorates as model capacity increases. In this paper, we identify a capacity-induced failure mode, where overparameterized networks undergo functional modularity, self-partitioning into task-exclusive modules that suppress cross-objective interaction and hinder convergence toward Pareto-stationary points. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework, Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), which integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways. Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks demonstrate that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Codes are available at \url{https://github.com/heejokong/ModSync}.

AI.tldr: PINNs suffer from a capacity-induced failure mode where overparameterized networks develop task-exclusive modules that hinder multi-objective training. The proposed ModSync framework penalizes these task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing conflict-averse optimization schemes for PINNs degrade as model capacity increases due to functional modularity—networks self-partition into task-exclusive modules that suppress cross-objective interaction and block convergence to Pareto-stationary points.
AI.method: Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync) integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways, addressing the capacity-induced failure mode in overparameterized PINNs.
AI.result: ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across diverse PDE benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Structural regularization of network modularity (via ModSync) is an effective remedy for capacity-induced performance degradation in PINN training, enabling robust multi-objective optimization.

title: Autonomous Driving with Priority-Ordered STL Specifications Under Multimodal Uncertainty
summary: Autonomous vehicles must plan trajectories that satisfy a multitude of requirements on safety, passenger comfort, and compliance with traffic rules. However, in safety-critical scenarios, it is not always possible to satisfy all requirements simultaneously, necessitating their prioritization based on importance. At the same time, in these safety-critical scenarios, the uncertainty in trajectory predictions of the surrounding traffic, such as other vehicles and pedestrians, should be explicitly accounted for. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware trajectory planning framework that incorporates a predefined lexicographic ordering over Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications that stays valid under uncertainty. We implement this formulation with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on simulation scenarios, showing that our framework efficiently handles conflicting objectives under realistic multi-modal uncertainty.

AI.tldr: An uncertainty-aware trajectory planning framework for autonomous vehicles that uses lexicographic ordering over STL specifications within MPPI control to handle conflicting objectives under multi-modal uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Autonomous vehicles must satisfy multiple requirements (safety, comfort, traffic rules) that cannot always be met simultaneously in safety-critical scenarios, requiring prioritization. Additionally, uncertainty in trajectory predictions of surrounding traffic must be explicitly accounted for.
AI.method: The framework incorporates a predefined lexicographic ordering over Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications that remains valid under uncertainty, implemented using Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control.
AI.result: Demonstrated on simulation scenarios, showing efficient handling of conflicting objectives under realistic multi-modal uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The proposed uncertainty-aware trajectory planning framework effectively addresses the challenge of conflicting objectives with prioritized STL specifications under uncertainty using MPPI control.

title: Implicit Semantic-Aware Communication Based on Hypergraph Reasoning
comment: This work is accepted at IEEE Transactions on Communications
summary: Semantic-aware communication has emerged as a transformative paradigm for next-generation communication systems, shifting the fundamental goal from transmitting bit-level symbols to reliably recovering and understanding the semantic meaning of information. Previous studies have demonstrated that representing the semantic content of source messages as graph-based structures can significantly improve communication efficiency and the accuracy of semantic inference at the receiver. However, existing solutions typically employ graphs that capture only pairwise relationships, thereby neglecting higher-order implicit correlations commonly observed in real-world scenarios, such as group interactions, multi-entity associations, and complex relational contexts. This limitation reduces semantic expressiveness and makes semantic inference susceptible to ambiguity and performance degradation, particularly under noisy or corrupted channel conditions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework, HISR, which leverages hypergraphs to represent complex multi-entity relationships among semantic knowledge entities. In HISR, entities and their associated higher-order relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts. This design not only disentangles diverse semantic interactions to mitigate the over-smoothing effects commonly found in traditional graph embedding methods but also enables robust semantic inference even when partial information loss occurs during transmission. Numerical results show that the proposed HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over the state-of-the-art benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HISR, a hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework that captures higher-order entity relationships to improve semantic communication robustness and accuracy, achieving up to 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based semantic communication solutions only capture pairwise relationships, neglecting higher-order implicit correlations (e.g., group interactions, multi-entity associations), which limits semantic expressiveness and causes performance degradation under noisy channel conditions.
AI.method: HISR uses hypergraphs to represent complex multi-entity relationships among semantic knowledge entities, mapping entities and their higher-order relations into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts to disentangle diverse semantic interactions and mitigate over-smoothing effects.
AI.result: HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over state-of-the-art benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Hypergraph-based semantic representation enables robust semantic inference even under partial information loss during transmission, effectively addressing the limitations of pairwise graph-based approaches in semantic-aware communication systems.

title: An Infrastructure-less, Control-Independent Solution to Relative Localisation of a Team of Mobile Robots using Ranging Measurements
summary: The ability to localise teams of robots is essential for applications ranging from robotic fleets in unstructured environments to cooperative control and navigation tasks. In such contexts, fixed infrastructure is often unavailable, deployments must be fast and flexible, and system requirements must be minimal. We present a decentralised cooperative localisation algorithm that addresses all these challenges at once. The method is anchor-less, fully decentralised, and, unlike most existing approaches, does not require controlling the robots motion to ensure team observability. It relies only on local odometry, sparse inter-agent ranging measurements, and short-range communication, all of which are widely available in practice. The algorithm adopts a multi-hypothesis Bayesian framework that maintains the entire set of feasible solutions, ensuring robustness under transient unobservable conditions. Moreover, through information sharing, each agent benefits from the estimates of the entire group, even in partially connected conditions.

AI.tldr: A decentralised, anchor-less cooperative localisation algorithm for robot teams that uses only odometry, sparse ranging, and short-range communication without requiring controlled motion for observability, maintaining multiple hypotheses for robustness under unobservable conditions.
AI.motivation: Robot teams need localisation in unstructured environments where fixed infrastructure is unavailable, deployments must be fast and flexible, and system requirements minimal. Existing approaches often require controlled robot motion for observability, which is impractical.
AI.method: A fully decentralised, anchor-less cooperative localisation algorithm using a multi-hypothesis Bayesian framework. It relies only on local odometry, sparse inter-agent ranging, and short-range communication. It maintains the entire set of feasible solutions and enables information sharing across partially connected networks.
AI.result: The algorithm ensures robustness under transient unobservable conditions and enables each agent to benefit from group-wide estimates even with partial connectivity, without requiring controlled motion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach addresses key practical challenges in decentralised robot team localisation by removing the need for anchors, motion control constraints, and full connectivity, using only widely available sensors and communication.

title: Apparent Psychological Profiles of Large Language Models are Largely a Measurement Artifact
summary: Psychological instruments designed for humans are increasingly used to assign large language models (LLMs) stable psychological profiles that affect their usability, safety assessment, and use as proxies for human participants in research. Using a formal psychometric framework, we show that these profiles are largely a measurement artifact. Administering a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments spanning self-reports and behavioral tasks to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples, we report four findings. First, differences between models are driven not by the traits an instrument targets but by a directional response bias, a tendency to respond toward one end of the scale, or one labeled option, regardless of item content; a variance decomposition attributes 81-90% of between-model variation to this bias, against 9-16% in humans. Second, the bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated by it. Third, because bias rather than trait drives responding, an instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by its response orthogonality, a term we coin for the proportion of items for which trait and bias point in opposite directions. Fourth, the profile a model appears to have shifts with the items used and can be manufactured through item selection. These results demonstrate that the apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of the instrument used to measure them, not properties of the models themselves. As instruments borrowed from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal and may inherently lack validity for LLMs, we call for dedicated assessments centered on response orthogonality.

AI.tldr: Psychological profiles of LLMs are measurement artifacts driven by directional response bias (81-90% of between-model variance), not genuine traits; profiles shift with item selection and can be manufactured.
AI.motivation: Psychological instruments designed for humans are increasingly used to assign stable psychological profiles to LLMs, affecting their usability, safety assessment, and use as human proxies in research. The paper aims to test whether these profiles are valid or artifacts.
AI.method: Administered a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments (self-reports and behavioral tasks) to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples, using formal psychometric framework with variance decomposition and a newly coined concept of response orthogonality.
AI.result: (1) 81-90% of between-model variance is directional response bias vs 9-16% in humans; (2) bias declines with capability but persists; (3) instrument reliability is predicted by response orthogonality; (4) LLM profiles shift with items and can be manufactured via item selection.
AI.conclusion: Apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of measurement instruments, not model properties; call for dedicated assessments centered on response orthogonality.

title: CoLI: A Reproducible Platform for Continuum Robot Learning via Monolithic 3D Printing and Isomorphic Teleoperation
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 1 table, accepted by IROS2026
summary: Continuum robots offer strong potential for manipulation tasks due to their high degrees of freedom, compliant structures, and operational safety. However, their adoption in both research and practical applications has been hindered by reproducibility issues arising from complex fabrication and assembly processes, challenging kinematic modeling, and a lack of intuitive control interfaces. To address these challenges, we present a novel open-source continuum robot design. The platform features a simplified fabrication pipeline enabled by multi-material 3D printing, allowing the arm to be fabricated as a monolithic compliant structure with minimal assembly. Control is achieved through an isomorphic teleoperation interface that establishes a direct actuator-level mapping, eliminating the need for explicit kinematic modeling and providing a singularity-free mapping. Building on this hardware design, the platform further supports imitation-learning-based autonomous control. The proposed system is evaluated through hardware characterization and a set of manipulation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that the platform provides a reproducible, learning-ready continuum robot system, accelerating algorithmic development and systematic benchmarking for the continuum robotics community.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an open-source continuum robot platform featuring multi-material 3D printing for simplified fabrication, an isomorphic teleoperation interface that bypasses kinematic modeling, and support for imitation-learning-based autonomous control, validated through hardware characterization and manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Continuum robots face reproducibility issues due to complex fabrication, challenging kinematic modeling, and lack of intuitive control interfaces, hindering adoption in research and practice.
AI.method: The platform uses multi-material 3D printing for a monolithic compliant structure with minimal assembly, an isomorphic teleoperation interface for direct actuator-level mapping (eliminating kinematic modeling and singularities), and support for imitation-learning-based autonomous control.
AI.result: Hardware characterization and manipulation task experiments show the platform is reproducible, learning-ready, and can accelerate algorithmic development and systematic benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: The proposed open-source continuum robot system addresses key barriers (fabrication, modeling, control) and provides a reproducible, learning-ready platform to advance continuum robotics research.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models
summary: Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a new metric that quantifies how well predictive models respect logical rules, complementing traditional accuracy-based evaluation. RVS handles hard and soft rules separately, works across models and datasets, and is computed via automatically generated SQL queries for Horn rules. Experiments on link prediction and relational regression show models with similar predictive accuracy can differ significantly in logical compliance.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation metrics (ranking quality, prediction error, classification accuracy) measure predictive performance but fail to assess whether model outputs respect logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications like healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency is as critical as accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension.
AI.method: The paper proposes the Rule Violation Score (RVS), which: (1) treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, (2) operates on any dataset and predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, (3) is computed using SQL queries automatically generated for Horn rules, and (4) can also evaluate logical consistency of training datasets and identify poorly defined rules.
AI.result: Evaluated on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic models. Results show two models with comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing behavioral differences that standard metrics fail to capture.
AI.conclusion: RVS provides a complementary evaluation dimension beyond predictive accuracy, enabling practitioners to detect models that violate logical constraints even when achieving strong predictive performance. The metric is widely applicable and can be automated via SQL for Horn rules.

title: Agentic AutoResearch forSpace Autonomy: An Auditable, LLM-Driven Research Agent for Aerospace Control Problems
summary: Spacecraft guidance, navigation, and control functions are increasingly realized as learned policies distilled from expert solvers. Developing such a policy is itself a research process: an investigator selects an architecture and hyperparameters, runs experiments, and must determine whether an apparent improvement is genuine or merely seed noise. This paper presents AutoResearch, a framework in which a large language model autonomously drives that loop for aerospace control problems, coupled with a credibility layer, built into the loop, that certifies each reported result against the problem's own measured seed noise. The language model serves only as the offline research agent that develops the control policy; the trained policy it produces is then deployed onboard the spacecraft, while the model itself never operates the vehicle. At each iteration the agent reads a plain-language problem description and the run history, proposes a single edit to the training script, executes it, and logs the outcome. No reported result is credited until it passes the same three checks: measured per-problem seed noise, reseeded verification of the best configuration, and leave-one-out pruning of the agent's edits. The same loop is applied, unchanged, to two aerospace control problems: a Clohessy-Wiltshire relative rendezvous and a safety-constrained collision-avoidance docking past a keep-out zone, each calibrated against a known optimal control benchmark. In both, the audited policy clears the measured seed noise by many standard deviations; an undirected search over the same parameters does not.
