On the docking problem the gap becomes categorical: undirected search yields no feasible policy, while the learned policy stays outside the keep-out zone on every seed.

AI.tldr: AutoResearch is an LLM-driven framework that autonomously develops control policies for aerospace problems (rendezvous and docking) by iteratively editing training scripts and certifying results against seed noise. The audited policies significantly outperform undirected search, achieving feasible solutions where random search fails entirely.
AI.motivation: Developing learned control policies for spacecraft GNC involves a tedious research loop (architecture/hyperparameter selection, experimentation, detecting genuine improvements over seed noise). Automating this process reliably requires certification against noise to distinguish real progress from random variation.
AI.method: AutoResearch uses a large language model as an offline research agent that reads problem descriptions and run history, proposes one edit per iteration to the training script, executes it, and logs results. A credibility layer in the loop certifies results via three checks: per-problem seed noise measurement, reseeded verification of best configuration, and leave-one-out pruning of edits.
AI.result: On Clohessy-Wiltshire rendezvous and collision-avoidance docking problems (both benchmarked against optimal control), audited policies clear seed noise by many standard deviations. Undirected search over the same parameters does not. On the docking problem, undirected search yields no feasible policy, while LLM-driven policy stays outside the keep-out zone on every seed.
AI.conclusion: An LLM-driven, credibility-certified research loop can reliably develop high-performing control policies for aerospace problems, surpassing undirected search and achieving feasible solutions where naive search completely fails. The LLM never operates the vehicle; it only produces the deployable policy.

title: Augmenting Game AI with Deep Reinforcement Learning
comment: Vision paper, published in Conference on Games 2026
summary: Immersion in video games depends not only on graphics, audio, and game mechanics, but also on the quality of in-game characters. Producing believable characters, or game AI, remains a significant challenge as behavioral complexity is hard to capture with hand-coded systems. Game AI is a source of immersion and engagement; however, the limitations stemming from the challenges of creating game AI often lead to frustration and the breaking of the illusion of realism within the game. The introduction of machine learning models opens the door to creating more believable, authentic, and relatable characters in games. The promise is that they either learn from interacting with the game, or from player data, to develop true human-like behavior. In this paper, we envision more applications of reinforcement learning for game AI in the future. For this to materialize, current research limitations are prohibitive to broad deployment across game genres. Therefore, we propose a framework for training reinforcement learning models with a set of requirements in mind that are suited towards game AI and game development. We present examples of games with reinforcement learning-augmented game AI and describe the practicalities of deploying player-facing machine learning agents in modern games. Furthermore, we identify bottlenecks and hard problems in these areas, which we believe offer promising research directions to accelerate the adoption of machine learning in game AI for the video game industry.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for training reinforcement learning models for game AI, identifies current limitations preventing broad deployment, and offers promising research directions to accelerate ML adoption in the video game industry.
AI.motivation: Hand-coded game AI systems struggle to capture behavioral complexity, breaking immersion and the illusion of realism. Machine learning, particularly reinforcement learning, offers the promise of more believable, authentic characters by learning from game interaction or player data.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework for training RL models with requirements tailored to game AI and game development. They present examples of RL-augmented game AI and describe practicalities of deploying player-facing ML agents in modern games.
AI.result: Identification of bottlenecks and hard problems that currently limit broad deployment of RL-based game AI across game genres.
AI.conclusion: Current research limitations are prohibitive to broad deployment, but the proposed framework and identified research directions offer promising avenues to accelerate ML adoption in game AI for the video game industry.

title: LIT-GS: LiDAR-Inertial-Thermal Gaussian Splatting for Illumination-Robust Mapping
comment: Accepted to IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Gaussian Splatting has enabled real-time neural rendering, yet existing LiDAR-inertial-visual (LIV) Gaussian mapping pipelines remain fragile under illumination changes and texture-deficient scenes due to their reliance on RGB photometric cues. We present LIT-GS, a LiDAR-inertial-thermal Gaussian Splatting framework that injects LiDAR-derived plane geometry as an explicit constraint in both pose/structure refinement and Gaussian optimization. Specifically, we exploit LIV visual map points as confidence-aware cross-modal anchors to establish reliable thermal-LiDAR associations, and incorporate weighted LiDAR point-to-plane residuals into bundle adjustment to jointly refine camera poses and 3D points under weak thermal supervision. Building on the refined structure, we further introduce a LiDAR-plane-regularized differentiable splatting objective that constrains rendered 3D points to align with locally observed planes, mitigating surface thickening and structural drift in low-contrast thermal imagery. Experiments on proprietary sequences and public datasets demonstrate that LIT-GS consistently improves geometric accuracy and rendering quality over state-of-the-art LIV-based Gaussian Splatting baselines, particularly in challenging lighting conditions.

AI.tldr: LIT-GS is a LiDAR-inertial-thermal Gaussian Splatting framework that uses LiDAR-derived plane geometry constraints to improve geometric accuracy and rendering quality under challenging lighting conditions, outperforming existing LIV-based Gaussian Splatting methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR-inertial-visual (LIV) Gaussian mapping pipelines are fragile under illumination changes and texture-deficient scenes due to reliance on RGB photometric cues.
AI.method: (1) Uses LIV visual map points as confidence-aware cross-modal anchors for reliable thermal-LiDAR associations; (2) Incorporates weighted LiDAR point-to-plane residuals into bundle adjustment for joint pose/structure refinement under weak thermal supervision; (3) Introduces LiDAR-plane-regularized differentiable splatting objective that constrains rendered 3D points to align with locally observed planes.
AI.result: Consistently improves geometric accuracy and rendering quality over state-of-the-art LIV-based Gaussian Splatting baselines, especially in challenging lighting conditions, validated on proprietary sequences and public datasets.
AI.conclusion: Injecting LiDAR-derived plane geometry as explicit constraints in pose/structure refinement and Gaussian optimization enhances robustness of neural rendering under poor illumination and texture-deficient environments.

title: QMFOL: Benchmarking Large Language Model Reasoning via Quantifiable Monadic First-Order Logic Test Case Generation
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant progress in reasoning, particularly in deductive reasoning, which is crucial for high-stakes decision-making. As models improve, evaluation benchmarks should evolve to keep pace. However, existing benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and struggle to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency.
  To address these issues, we propose QMFOL, an automated framework for generating monadic first-order logic reasoning tasks with quantifiable and controllable complexity. It constructs formal logical structures using conjunction and disjunction patterns, enabling precise control over reasoning depth, width, label types, and distractors. These structures are then translated into natural language via LLMs, with logical consistency ensured through round-trip verification using an external prover. Based on our framework, we build QMFOLBench, a benchmark comprising 2880 instances with 960 configurations across diverse logical and semantic dimensions. Evaluations on six large reasoning models (LRMs) and two LLMs show that performance degrades and computational overhead increases with rising logical complexity. Models perform better on True-labeled tasks than on False or Unknown ones, and exhibit sensitivity to semantic variation. Overall, QMFOL offers a scalable and reliable approach for constructing deductive reasoning benchmarks with controllable complexity, enabling more precise evaluation of reasoning capabilities in modern language models.

AI.tldr: QMFOL is an automated framework for generating monadic first-order logic reasoning tasks with controllable complexity, used to build QMFOLBench (2880 instances) for evaluating LLMs' deductive reasoning. Evaluations show performance degrades with increasing logical complexity, models handle True tasks better than False/Unknown, and are sensitive to semantic variation.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and struggle to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency, motivating the need for a more controllable and scalable evaluation framework for deductive reasoning in LLMs.
AI.method: QMFOL constructs formal logical structures using conjunction and disjunction patterns to control reasoning depth, width, label types, and distractors. These structures are translated to natural language via LLMs, with logical consistency ensured through round-trip verification using an external prover. This yields QMFOLBench with 2880 instances across 960 configurations.
AI.result: Evaluations on six LRMs and two LLMs show: (1) performance degrades and computational overhead increases with rising logical complexity; (2) models perform better on True-labeled tasks than False or Unknown; (3) models exhibit sensitivity to semantic variation.
AI.conclusion: QMFOL offers a scalable and reliable approach for constructing deductive reasoning benchmarks with controllable complexity, enabling more precise evaluation of reasoning capabilities in modern language models.

title: TaCauchy: An Extensible FEM Framework for Vision-Based Tactile Simulation
comment: Accepted to IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 2026
summary: Vision-based tactile sensors require high-fidelity simulation for reinforcement learning, yet existing approaches struggle to provide accurate mechanical stress fields within GPU-accelerated robotics platforms. We present TaCauchy, an extensible Finite Element Method (FEM) framework that integrates rigorous physics-based force computation into Isaac Sim. Built on the Unified Incremental Potential Contact (UIPC) solver, TaCauchy directly computes Cauchy stress tensors from hyperelastic constitutive laws and projects them onto contact surfaces to obtain traction forces and pressure distributions, providing mechanical ground truth from first principles rather than empirical estimation. Our framework features automatic mesh generation with geometry-aware adaptive refinement and a modular sensor interface enabling rapid integration of diverse sensors (GelSight Mini, DIGIT, 9DTact) with minimal configuration. Performance benchmarks demonstrate 33.40 FPS for single environments and 555 FPS aggregate throughput across 60 parallel environments, with stress extraction overhead under 1 ms. Physical validation experiments show strong agreement between simulated and real tactile responses across force ranges from 1.2556 N to 4.7332 N, achieving SSIM above 0.93, confirming the framework's capability to provide accurate, physically-grounded force supervision for downstream robotic manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: TaCauchy is an FEM-based tactile sensor simulation framework for Isaac Sim that computes physically accurate stress tensors and traction forces using the UIPC solver, achieving 33-555 FPS performance with SSIM >0.93 agreement with real sensors across 1.26-4.73N force ranges.
AI.motivation: Existing GPU-accelerated robotics simulation platforms lack accurate mechanical stress field computation for vision-based tactile sensors, which is needed for high-fidelity reinforcement learning.
AI.method: Integrates Finite Element Method via the Unified Incremental Potential Contact (UIPC) solver into Isaac Sim; computes Cauchy stress tensors from hyperelastic constitutive laws and projects them onto contact surfaces for traction forces; features automatic mesh generation with adaptive refinement and a modular sensor interface.
AI.result: 33.40 FPS for single environment, 555 FPS aggregate across 60 parallel environments, stress extraction <1 ms overhead; SSIM >0.93 between simulated and real tactile responses across 1.2556 N to 4.7332 N.
AI.conclusion: TaCauchy provides accurate, physically-grounded force supervision from first principles, suitable for downstream robotic manipulation tasks requiring tactile sensing.

title: Thermodynamic Measure of Intelligence
summary: Can intelligence be measured? We propose that intelligence can be defined as the lawful amplification of rare but valid futures: a system increases the probability of outcomes that would be unlikely under passive dynamics but remain admissible under the constraints of the domain. We start with the premise that an intelligent system must model the world and its own place within it. Because the system is part of the world it models, this leads naturally to recursive self-simulation: the system represents futures in which its own actions are part of the trajectory. Our central results give a necessity statement and a conditional near-sufficiency statement connecting this architecture to a precise thermodynamic measure of lawful amplification of rare-valid futures: high rare-valid lift is impossible unless the internal simulation identifies rare-valid futures with high fidelity; conversely, when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, the achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Thus recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible feature of intelligence but, under the stated assumptions, is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence. The resulting framework makes intelligence measurable on a universal scale, from passive matter and feedback controllers, large language models, and humans as text generators to Maxwell-demon-like information engines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that intelligence is the lawful amplification of rare but valid futures, and proves that recursive self-simulation is necessary and nearly sufficient for achieving high thermodynamic intelligence, enabling a universal measure of intelligence.
AI.motivation: To establish a formal, measurable definition of intelligence grounded in thermodynamics and information theory, moving beyond subjective or task-specific measures.
AI.method: The authors define intelligence as the amplification of rare-valid futures (outcomes unlikely under passive dynamics but admissible under domain constraints). They derive a necessity statement (high rare-valid lift requires high-fidelity internal simulation of rare-valid futures) and a conditional near-sufficiency statement (high fidelity + effective policy → lift approaches actuation-limited optimum), connecting recursive self-simulation to thermodynamic efficiency.
AI.result: Recursive self-simulation is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence; the framework yields a universal scale for measuring intelligence across passive matter, controllers, LLMs, humans, and Maxwell-demon engines.
AI.conclusion: Intelligence can be rigorously measured via thermodynamic rare-valid lift, with recursive self-simulation as a core architectural requirement.

title: ARC: Adaptive Robust Joint State and Covariance Estimation
comment: Submitted to information IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), June 2026. 8 pages, 7 figures, 1 table
summary: Sensor measurements are frequently corrupted by outliers and non-Gaussian noise. These imperfections in the sensor data can cause classical state estimators to generate biased and unreliable state and uncertainty estimates. Robust estimators reject or downweight outliers but do not perform measurement covariance estimation, whereas joint state and covariance estimators assume Gaussian residuals and fixed loss shape parameters. Integrating these two capabilities into a single framework is an opportunity to simultaneously estimate both state and covariance in the presence of outliers. This paper proposes a unified Block-Coordinate Descent framework that combines a norm-aware adaptive robust loss, an Iteratively Reweighted Least-Squares state update, and a Minimum Weighted Covariance Determinant covariance estimator, yielding a self-tuning joint state and covariance estimator. The framework is evaluated in a Monte-Carlo simulation and on real-world ultra-wideband localization experiments in cluttered non-line-of-sight environments. Results show that the proposed estimator consistently recovers the true inlier measurement covariance and matches or exceeds the state estimation accuracy of all baselines, without requiring any manual parameter tuning.

AI.tldr: A unified Block-Coordinate Descent framework that combines norm-aware adaptive robust loss, IRLS state update, and Minimum Weighted Covariance Determinant estimator for joint state and covariance estimation in the presence of outliers, achieving self-tuning performance without manual parameter tuning.
AI.motivation: Sensor measurements are frequently corrupted by outliers and non-Gaussian noise, causing classical state estimators to generate biased and unreliable estimates. Existing robust estimators don't perform covariance estimation, while joint estimators assume Gaussian residuals and fixed loss shape parameters.
AI.method: Proposes a unified Block-Coordinate Descent framework combining: (1) a norm-aware adaptive robust loss, (2) an Iteratively Reweighted Least-Squares state update, and (3) a Minimum Weighted Covariance Determinant covariance estimator.
AI.result: The estimator consistently recovers the true inlier measurement covariance and matches or exceeds state estimation accuracy of all baselines in Monte-Carlo simulations and real-world UWB localization experiments in cluttered NLOS environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed self-tuning framework successfully integrates robust state estimation and covariance estimation without requiring manual parameter tuning, outperforming baselines in both simulation and real-world experiments.

title: A Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization
comment: Presented at the 17th Workshop on Optimization and Learning in Multiagent Systems (OptLearnMAS, https://optlearnmas.github.io), co-located with the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2026)
summary: Many decision-making problems in computing and networking systems can be naturally formulated as cost-minimization problems under performance constraints. In dynamic environments, reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to solve such problems at runtime by embedding both costs and constraint violations into a single scalar reward through weighted penalty terms, following a Lagrangian-inspired formulation. However, in this context the behavior of the learned policy critically depends on the choice of these weights, which are typically selected manually. This makes it difficult to identify an appropriate trade-off between optimizing the primary objective and effectively avoiding constraint violations, particularly in non-stationary environments where their relative importance may change. This paper presents MAMO (Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization), an approach to tackle this balancing problem through multi-agent RL. MAMO decouples task execution from objective design by formulating the selection of reward weights as a learning problem, providing a !rst step towards more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization problems in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: MAMO uses multi-agent reinforcement learning to automatically learn reward weights for constrained optimization problems, decoupling task execution from objective design and eliminating manual weight tuning.
AI.motivation: In dynamic environments, RL-based solutions to constrained optimization problems require manual tuning of reward weights (via Lagrangian penalties) to balance cost minimization and constraint satisfaction, which is difficult and fails in non-stationary settings where the optimal trade-off changes.
AI.method: MAMO formulates the selection of reward weights as a learning problem using multi-agent reinforcement learning, decoupling task execution from objective design to autonomously balance primary objectives and constraint violations.
AI.result: Provides a first step toward more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization in dynamic environments, eliminating the need for manual weight selection.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling objective design from task execution via multi-agent RL enables adaptive trade-off optimization between costs and constraint violations in non-stationary environments, improving autonomy and robustness.

title: Slow Brain, Fast Planner: Latency-Resilient VLM-Augmented Urban Navigation
summary: Learning-based planners for sidewalk navigation can generate diverse candidate trajectories in real time, yet their scoring functions often fail to select the best trajectory in challenging situations, outputting trajectories that make the mobile robot drive onto grass, toward pedestrians, or in the wrong direction, even when better candidates exist in the same set. We call this the trajectory scoring gap: in real-world sidewalk navigation, the gap between an anchor-based planner's top choice and the best possible candidate is substantial, likely due to limited high-level scene understanding capability of the planner. Rather than replacing the planner with an end-to-end Vision-Language-Action model, we propose a VLM-Planner interface that uses a VLM to select a candidate index from the planner's proposal set and then fuse it with the planner's initial output. However, VLMs take 1--3s per query and so cannot directly drive a 5--20Hz control loop. We contribute a training-free, latency-resilient trajectory-level fusion layer that turns a stale VLM selection into real-time planner scoring via geometric similarity with exponential decay. On $\sim$2,000 challenging real-world scenarios (e.g., junctions, pedestrian encounters), VLM selection achieves 30% ADE reduction versus the planner's best selection, while the planner remains competitive in routine situations. In simulation, Score Fusion maintains >80% success rate with delays up to 5s. We demonstrate the full system on a mobile robot navigating challenging campus sidewalks with varied network latency.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a "trajectory scoring gap" in learning-based sidewalk navigation planners, where the top choice often underperforms vs. better candidates. To address this without replacing the entire planner, the authors propose a VLM-Planner interface that uses a Vision-Language Model to select the best candidate, combined with a training-free, latency-resilient fusion layer (geometric similarity with exponential decay) to handle VLM's slow inference (1-3s) in a real-time control loop (5-20Hz). Results show 30% ADE reduction in challenging scenarios and >80% success rate under delays up to 5s.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based planners for sidewalk navigation produce diverse trajectory candidates, but their scoring functions often fail to pick the best one in challenging situations (e.g., grass, pedestrians, wrong direction), leading to a "trajectory scoring gap." This gap stems from limited high-level scene understanding, motivating the need for a better selection mechanism without replacing the entire planner.
AI.method: The authors propose a VLM-Planner interface: (1) a VLM selects a candidate index from the planner's proposal set; (2) a training-free, latency-resilient trajectory-level fusion layer combines the VLM selection with the planner's output via geometric similarity with exponential decay, enabling real-time scoring despite VLM's 1-3s latency in a 5-20Hz control loop.
AI.result: On ~2,000 challenging real-world scenarios, VLM selection achieves 30% Average Displacement Error (ADE) reduction vs. the planner's best selection. In simulation, Score Fusion maintains >80% success rate with delays up to 5s. The full system was demonstrated on a mobile robot navigating challenging campus sidewalks under varied network latency.
AI.conclusion: The VLM-Planner interface effectively bridges the trajectory scoring gap in sidewalk navigation without requiring end-to-end model replacement. The latency-resilient fusion layer makes VLM integration practical for real-time control, improving performance in challenging scenarios while maintaining competitiveness in routine situations.

title: Navigating Unreliable Parametric and Contextual Knowledge: Explicit Knowledge Conflict Resolution for LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of language-based tasks by leveraging both extensive parametric knowledge and in-context learning ability, enabling them to incorporate external information provided in the input prompt. However, the integration of external knowledge can introduce conflicts, not only between the model's internal parametric knowledge and the external information, but also among multiple pieces of external contexts. Existing approaches typically assume that either the model or the provided context is reliable, overlooking the possibility that both sources may contain errors, and avoid conflicts by privileging one source over the other, rather than actively resolving inconsistencies. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework MACR for LLM knowledge conflict resolution that moves beyond the conventional binary choice paradigm and incorporates an explicit conflict-resolution mechanism based on a multi-agent reasoning approach. Specifically, we first propose an adaptive knowledge assessment and retrieval approach that employs a modified semantic entropy measure to quantify an LLM's confidence in its answer to a given query. Based on this confidence estimation, MACR either externalizes the model's internal knowledge as textual representations or retrieves relevant external knowledge when internal knowledge is insufficient, generating basic contexts for subsequent reasoning. Then we introduce an inductive multi-agent reasoning framework with three specialized agents that, respectively, induce explicit rules, analyze potential conflicts, and resolve inconsistencies across all available contexts. Empirical results demonstrate that MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks, while also providing interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.

AI.tldr: MACR is a multi-agent reasoning framework for LLM knowledge conflict resolution that moves beyond binary choice paradigms by using adaptive confidence estimation and specialized agents to explicitly detect, analyze, and resolve inconsistencies between parametric and external knowledge.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to handling knowledge conflicts in LLMs either privilege parametric knowledge over external context or vice versa, avoiding conflicts rather than actively resolving them, and overlook the possibility that both sources may contain errors.
AI.method: MACR first uses a modified semantic entropy measure to estimate LLM confidence and either externalizes internal knowledge as text or retrieves external knowledge when needed. Then a multi-agent framework with three specialized agents induces rules, analyzes conflicts, and resolves inconsistencies across all contexts.
AI.result: MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks while providing interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-agent conflict-resolution framework effectively addresses knowledge conflicts beyond the binary choice paradigm, achieving superior performance with interpretable reasoning.

title: GroundControl: Anticipating Navigation Failures in Vision-Language Agents via Trajectory-Consistent Uncertainty Estimates
summary: Vision-language navigation agents achieve competitive average success on benchmark tasks, yet failures often arise through predictable trajectory-level breakdowns such as oscillation, stagnation, or inefficient detours. Reliable deployment, therefore, requires uncertainty signals that anticipate emerging failure dynamics during execution rather than reflect only instantaneous action entropy. We introduce \emph{GroundControl}, a trajectory-consistent uncertainty estimator defined as statistical deviation from nominal goal-directed distance-to-goal dynamics aggregated over an episode. GroundControl models distance evolution using a constant-velocity Kalman filter and combines normalized innovation statistics with complementary trajectory features capturing progress, monotonicity, path efficiency, and oscillatory behavior. The resulting uncertainty score reflects geometric and temporal inconsistency in navigation behavior rather than local prediction dispersion. To evaluate uncertainty quality independently of task success, we formalize \emph{Selective Risk--Coverage Navigation (SRCN)}, a protocol that measures how effectively an uncertainty score ranks episodes by failure or inefficiency using risk--coverage curves and AURC / E-AURC summaries. Across five EB-Navigation splits ($N=300$ episodes), trajectory-consistent uncertainty achieves near-oracle ordering under success-based selective risk, with weighted-average $\mathrm{E\text{-}AURC}_{\mathrm{SR}}=0.0024$ for the GPT-4o model, substantially outperforming entropy-, conformal-, and heuristic baselines. Under SPL-based selective evaluation, GroundControl consistently achieves the lowest AURC and E-AURC across models and navigation splits. These results show that modeling deviation from goal-directed dynamics provides an interpretable and robust signal for anticipating navigation failures in vision-language agents.

AI.tldr: GroundControl introduces a trajectory-consistent uncertainty estimator for vision-language navigation that detects emerging failures (oscillation, stagnation, detours) by modeling deviation from goal-directed distance dynamics via a Kalman filter, outperforming entropy and heuristic baselines on selective risk-coverage evaluation.
AI.motivation: Vision-language navigation agents achieve competitive average success but suffer from predictable trajectory-level failures (oscillation, stagnation, inefficient detours), and existing uncertainty signals (e.g., instantaneous action entropy) fail to anticipate these emerging failure dynamics during execution.
AI.method: GroundControl uses a constant-velocity Kalman filter to model distance-to-goal evolution, computes normalized innovation statistics, and combines them with complementary trajectory features (progress, monotonicity, path efficiency, oscillatory behavior). The framework also introduces Selective Risk–Coverage Navigation (SRCN) with risk-coverage curves and AURC/E-AURC metrics for evaluating uncertainty quality independent of task success.
AI.result: Across five EB-Navigation splits (N=300 episodes), GroundControl achieves near-oracle ordering under success-based selective risk (weighted-average E-AURC_SR = 0.0024 for GPT-4o), substantially outperforming entropy-, conformal-, and heuristic baselines. It consistently achieves the lowest AURC and E-AURC across all models and navigation splits under SPL-based evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Modeling deviation from goal-directed dynamics provides an interpretable and robust signal for anticipating navigation failures in vision-language agents, making GroundControl an effective tool for reliable deployment.

title: Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models
summary: Student-generated drawings are widely used in science education to assess learners' conceptual understanding in modeling-based tasks aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). However, scoring such drawings requires expert human judgment to interpret complex visual representations, making large-scale assessment costly to implement and sustain in classroom settings. In this work, we study automated scoring of student-generated scientific drawings using a vision-based model. We evaluate a Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation and propose a confidence-aware scoring framework that derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions. This confidence signal enables selective automation by scoring high-confidence responses automatically while deferring uncertain cases for human review. Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items show that the proposed approach improves scoring reliability while supporting a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk, highlighting the value of confidence-aware methods for trustworthy educational assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a confidence-aware Vision Transformer (ViT) approach for automated scoring of student-generated scientific drawings aligned with NGSS, enabling selective automation where high-confidence responses are scored automatically and uncertain cases are deferred to human review, achieving improved reliability on six middle school assessment items.
AI.motivation: Scoring student-generated scientific drawings requires expert human judgment, making large-scale assessment costly and difficult to sustain in classroom settings. The goal is to automate this process while maintaining reliability and trustworthiness.
AI.method: The authors use a Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation as the vision-based model. They propose a confidence-aware scoring framework that derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions, enabling selective automation by scoring high-confidence responses automatically and deferring uncertain cases for human review.
AI.result: Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items show that the proposed approach improves scoring reliability while supporting a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-aware methods are valuable for trustworthy educational assessment, as they enable selective automation that balances efficiency with reliability in scoring student-generated scientific drawings.

title: Fast Human Attention Prediction for Fixation-guided Active Perception in Autonomous Navigation
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Human visual attention relies on structured scanpaths to efficiently process scenes, yet instilling this behavior into robot autonomy is in its infancy and hindered by the high,computational costs of existing predictive models. To address this, we introduce GazeLNN, a computationally lightweight,scanpath prediction model that leverages Liquid Neural Networks as its recurrent engine and employs MobileNetV3 for feature extraction. Operating auto-regressively, the architecture predicts sequential fixation heatmaps conditioned on the current visual stimulus and fixation history. Despite requiring only 0.61 GFLOPs, GazeLNN achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MIT Low Resolution dataset achieving 0.47 ScanMatch score. It outperforms existing recurrent baselines across diverse evaluation metrics, while reducing computational costs by 99.40% and accelerating inference by up to six times. To investigate the role of human attention modeling in robot autonomy and demonstrate the practical utility of this highly efficient architecture, we integrate GazeLNN into an active camera-robot control policy trained via Reinforcement Learning. This integration enables human-fixation-guided perception during autonomous navigation, validated through successful real-world deployments on an aerial robot.

AI.tldr: GazeLNN is a lightweight scanpath prediction model using Liquid Neural Networks and MobileNetV3, achieving state-of-the-art performance with 99.40% less computation and 6x faster inference, integrated into a real-world aerial robot for human-fixation-guided autonomous navigation.
AI.motivation: Human visual attention relies on structured scanpaths for efficient scene processing, but instilling this behavior into robot autonomy is hindered by the high computational costs of existing predictive models.
AI.method: GazeLNN uses Liquid Neural Networks as a recurrent engine with MobileNetV3 for feature extraction, operating auto-regressively to predict sequential fixation heatmaps conditioned on visual stimulus and fixation history. It is integrated into an active camera-robot control policy trained via Reinforcement Learning.
AI.result: Achieves 0.47 ScanMatch score on MIT Low Resolution dataset with only 0.61 GFLOPs, reduces computational costs by 99.40%, accelerates inference by up to 6x, and outperforms existing recurrent baselines across diverse metrics. Successfully deployed on a real-world aerial robot.
AI.conclusion: GazeLNN demonstrates that highly efficient, biologically-inspired scanpath prediction can be practically integrated into robot autonomy, enabling human-fixation-guided perception for autonomous navigation.

title: Lagrange: An Open-Vocabulary, Energy-Based Sparse Framework for Generalized End-to-End Driving
summary: Scaling end-to-end autonomous driving to complex, open-world environments requires perceptual models that generalize to anomalous scenarios and planners that produce kinematically valid trajectories. Existing paradigms face a distinct dichotomy between representational efficiency and generalization capacity. Dense models (e.g., occupancy networks), while geometrically robust, incur critical computational bottlenecks and struggle with high-level semantic reasoning. Conversely, sparse, query-based planners are efficient but reliant on closed-set definitions, rendering them vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) events. Although recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer open-vocabulary reasoning, their autoregressive, discrete token generation fundamentally conflicts with the continuous, high-frequency control requirements of vehicle dynamics. To address this, we propose Lagrange, an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse driving framework based on Masked Latent Fields (MLF). Rather than relying on dense volumetric reconstructions or closed-set query mechanisms, Lagrange exploits Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens. We introduce an intent-driven masked cross-attention module that temporally filters irrelevant entities, decoding the attended tokens into an implicit continuous energy field defined over spatial coordinates. By framing decision-making as a Lagrangian action minimization problem spanning this energy field, we enforce strict compliance with vehicle kinematics while executing collision avoidance. Extensive offline evaluations on both standard (nuScenes) and long-tail (CODA) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange establishes a promising framework for robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomy.

AI.tldr: Lagrange proposes a Masked Latent Fields (MLF) framework for open-vocabulary autonomous driving that uses VLMs for class-agnostic proposals, intent-driven masked cross-attention for temporal filtering, and Lagrangian action minimization over implicit energy fields to achieve kinematically feasible, sparse, and robust open-world autonomy.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving paradigms face a dichotomy: dense occupancy networks are geometrically robust but computationally expensive and lack semantic reasoning, while sparse query-based planners are efficient but rely on closed-set definitions and fail under out-of-distribution events. VLA models offer open-vocabulary reasoning but their autoregressive discrete token generation is incompatible with continuous, high-frequency vehicle control.
AI.method: Lagrange encodes class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens via VLMs, applies an intent-driven masked cross-attention module to temporally filter irrelevant entities, decodes attended tokens into an implicit continuous energy field over spatial coordinates, and frames decision-making as a Lagrangian action minimization problem over this energy field to enforce kinematic compliance and collision avoidance.
AI.result: Extensive offline evaluations on nuScenes (standard) and CODA (long-tail) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange enables robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomy.
AI.conclusion: Lagrange establishes a promising framework for open-world autonomous driving that bridges the gap between sparse computational efficiency and open-vocabulary generalization while maintaining kinematic feasibility.

title: Increasing Resilience of Continuum Robots via Motion Planning Algorithms
summary: This paper presents an experimental study of motion planning for resilient continuum robots. In this study we mainly focused on multi-criteria decision-making, its application for path-planning algorithms, impact on the generated path and execution time. To do this, we used two well-known algorithms for path planning, namely Genetic algorithm and A star algorithm, and modified them by adding the Analytical Hierarchy Process algorithm to evaluate the quality of the paths generated. In our experiment the Analytical Hierarchy Process considers four different criteria, i.e. distance, motors damage, mechanical damage of the robot's arm and accuracy, each considered to contribute to the resilience of a continuum robot. The use of different criteria is necessary to increase the time to maintenance operations of the continuum robot. We conducted the experiments using two different simulated environments of the robot. Although we significantly simplified the robot's model and its environment, we still implemented some of the features of the environment based on the real robot prototype. In particular, one of the environments has single- as well as multi-path points, and other consists of the multi-path points only. The results show that, in contrast to A star, the performance time of Genetic algorithm does not depend on the environment's cardinality. It generates more diverse paths, which increases the robot's resilience.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally studies multi-criteria motion planning for resilient continuum robots, modifying Genetic Algorithm and A* with Analytical Hierarchy Process (considering distance, motor damage, mechanical damage, and accuracy) to improve robot resilience and time-to-maintenance. Results show Genetic Algorithm outperforms A* in path diversity and resilience, with performance independent of environment cardinality.
AI.motivation: To improve the resilience of continuum robots by incorporating multi-criteria decision-making into path planning, specifically aiming to increase the time between maintenance operations through consideration of factors like motor damage, mechanical damage, distance, and accuracy.
AI.method: Two well-known path planning algorithms (Genetic Algorithm and A*) were modified by integrating the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) to evaluate path quality across four criteria: distance, motors damage, mechanical damage of the robot's arm, and accuracy. Experiments were conducted in two simulated environments (one with single- and multi-path points, another with multi-path points only), incorporating features based on a real robot prototype.
AI.result: The Genetic Algorithm's performance time is independent of environment cardinality, unlike A*. The Genetic Algorithm generates more diverse paths, which enhances robot resilience.
AI.conclusion: The Genetic Algorithm with AHP-based multi-criteria evaluation is more suitable for resilient path planning of continuum robots than A*, as it produces more diverse paths and maintains consistent performance regardless of environment complexity.

title: Leveraging systems' non-linearity to tackle the scarcity of data in the design of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems
summary: Deep Transfer Learning (DTL) allows for the efficient building of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems (IFDS). On the other hand, DTL methods still heavily rely on large amounts of labelled data. Obtaining such an amount of data can be challenging when dealing with machines or structures faults. This document proposes a novel approach to the design of vibration-based IFDS using DTL in condition of strong data scarcity. A periodic multi-excitation level procedure leveraging intrinsic non-linearities of real-world systems is used to produce images that can be conveniently analysed by pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to diagnose faults. A new data visualization method and its augmentation technique are proposed in this paper to tackle the typical lack of data encountered during the design of IFDS. Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure provides effective support for the proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel deep transfer learning approach for intelligent fault diagnosis under strong data scarcity, using periodic multi-excitation levels and nonlinearities to generate images for pre-trained CNNs, with a new visualization and augmentation method validated on railway pantograph structures.
AI.motivation: DTL methods still require large labeled datasets, which are difficult to obtain for machine/structure fault diagnosis. The paper aims to address this data scarcity challenge.
AI.method: A periodic multi-excitation level procedure exploiting intrinsic nonlinearities of real-world systems to produce images analyzable by pre-trained CNNs, plus a novel data visualization method and augmentation technique.
AI.result: Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure provides effective support for the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables vibration-based IFDS design using DTL under strong data scarcity conditions.

title: Generating Robot Hands from Human Demonstrations
summary: Robot learning has advanced rapidly in learning control, but learning the physical body of a robot remains much more difficult because jointly searching over design and control creates a very large combinatorial problem. Here, we present a data-driven framework for generating robot hands from human demonstrations. Instead of learning a complex controller together with each candidate design, we generate robot hand designs using the same simple control policy used after fabrication: matching fingertip positions through inverse kinematics. Using more than 4 million frames of human fingertip motion from everyday manipulation, our algorithm optimizes tree-structured robot hands to reproduce desired target motions. The framework produced both a 6-degree-of-freedom (DoF) general-purpose hand and lower-DoF task-specific hands with spatial four-bar mimic joints. To accelerate the search over designs, we trained a reinforcement-learning (RL) actor to propose good hand designs and joint angles, reducing search time from hours to minutes. We fabricated the mechanisms directly as one-piece articulated structures with print-in-place joints. In real-world experiments, the 6-DoF hand achieved highly accurate teleoperated fingertip tracking better than available commercial robot hands, whereas the specialized 3-DoF hands reproduced structured human and synthetic trajectories with reduced mechanical complexity. These results showed that large-scale human motion data can be used not only to train robot controllers but also as a reference for optimizing and generating the physical embodiment of robots.

AI.tldr: A data-driven framework generates robot hand designs from 4M+ frames of human fingertip motion data, producing both a 6-DoF general-purpose hand and lower-DoF task-specific hands by optimizing tree-structured designs using inverse kinematics, with an RL actor accelerating design search, and fabricated as one-piece articulated structures that achieve high-accuracy teleoperated tracking.
AI.motivation: Robot body design optimization is challenging due to the combinatorial explosion of jointly searching over design and control spaces; existing methods typically co-optimize design with complex controllers, which is computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: Uses 4M+ frames of human fingertip motion data; optimizes tree-structured robot hands by matching fingertip positions via inverse kinematics (same simple policy used after fabrication); employs an RL actor to accelerate design and joint angle search; fabricates as one-piece articulated structures with print-in-place joints.
AI.result: Produced a 6-DoF general-purpose hand and lower-DoF task-specific hands with spatial four-bar mimic joints; 6-DoF hand achieved highly accurate teleoperated fingertip tracking surpassing commercial robot hands; specialized 3-DoF hands reproduced structured trajectories with reduced complexity; RL actor reduced search time from hours to minutes.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale human motion data can serve as a reference for optimizing robot physical embodiment in addition to training controllers, enabling data-driven design of robot hands without complex co-optimization of controllers.

title: SoftSkill: Behavioral Compression for Contextual Adaptation
summary: Agent skills are commonly deployed as natural-language Markdown files that encode answer policies, evidence-use habits, and task procedures. These files are readable and portable, but they are consumed indirectly: for each task instance, a frozen language model must translate a long textual artifact into generation-time behavior. This paper asks whether a natural-language skill can instead initialize a compact continuous context object, refined by a trainable soft delta while the base model remains frozen. We propose SoftSkill, a frozen-backbone method that tunes such soft skills with next-token prediction and deploys them as latent behavioral priors at inference time. In our main single-round setting, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 points on SearchQA, 42.1 points on LiveMath, and 1.3 points on DocVQA. Relative to SkillOpt, SoftSkill improves accuracy by 5.2 points on SearchQA and 12.5 points on LiveMath, while replacing hundreds to thousands of Markdown skill tokens with a few virtual tokens. We further study agentic execution as a harder boundary case, where sparse trajectory imitation provides useful signal but does not yet robustly compress long-horizon procedural behavior. More broadly, the results suggest that some task skills are better treated not as additional Markdown to be reinterpreted at inference time, but as compact latent controls over how a frozen model enters the task.

AI.tldr: SoftSkill replaces natural-language Markdown skill files with compact, trainable continuous context vectors (soft skills) that are tuned via next-token prediction while keeping the backbone model frozen, improving performance across several benchmarks with far fewer tokens than traditional skill descriptions.
AI.motivation: Natural-language Markdown skill files are readable and portable but must be reinterpreted by a frozen LLM at each inference, making them indirect and potentially inefficient. The paper asks whether such skills can be compressed into compact, learnable latent controls instead.
AI.method: SoftSkill uses a frozen backbone model and tunes a soft delta (continuous context vector) via next-token prediction. At inference, these learned soft skills are deployed as latent behavioral priors (prefix vectors), replacing lengthy Markdown tokens with a small number of virtual tokens (e.g., length-32).
AI.result: On a length-32 SoftSkill prefix with Qwen3.5-4B: +8.3 on SearchQA, +42.1 on LiveMath, +1.3 on DocVQA vs. no-skill prompting. Relative to SkillOpt: +5.2 on SearchQA, +12.5 on LiveMath, replacing hundreds-to-thousands of Markdown tokens with few virtual tokens. Agentic trajectory imitation yields useful but limited signal for long-horizon tasks.
AI.conclusion: Task skills are better treated not as additional Markdown to be reinterpreted at inference time, but as compact latent controls that shape how a frozen model enters a task. SoftSkill demonstrates an effective paradigm for skill compression and behavioral priors.

title: MemoryWAM: Efficient World Action Modeling with Persistent Memory
summary: Robust robotic manipulation in the real world requires not only an understanding of the current observation, but also memory and dynamics modeling. World action models (WAMs) possess these capabilities by jointly modeling visual foresight and actions conditioned on both current and historical observations, making them a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation. However, existing WAMs face a fundamental trade-off: methods with efficient inference typically condition only on a bounded window of recent observations and therefore struggle in non-Markovian environments, whereas methods that preserve long histories incur time and space costs that grow substantially with sequence length. To address this challenge, we introduce MemoryWAM, a world action model with efficient persistent memory. MemoryWAM uses a hybrid memory design that combines recent frames, event-boundary anchor frames, and compact gist tokens that summarize long-range history. A tailored attention mechanism enables retrieval of both detailed short-term context and compressed long-term context, supporting memory-dependent decision-making with reduced inference latency and GPU memory usage. Across long-horizon, memory-dependent manipulation tasks in both simulation and the real world, MemoryWAM outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines while maintaining favorable computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: MemoryWAM introduces a world action model with efficient persistent memory that combines recent frames, event-boundary anchors, and compact gist tokens to address the trade-off between long-term memory and computational efficiency in robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing world action models face a fundamental trade-off: efficient methods rely on bounded windows and fail in non-Markovian environments, while methods preserving long histories incur substantial time and space costs that grow with sequence length.
AI.method: MemoryWAM employs a hybrid memory design combining three components: (1) recent frames, (2) event-boundary anchor frames, and (3) compact gist tokens summarizing long-range history. A tailored attention mechanism retrieves both detailed short-term context and compressed long-term context.
AI.result: Across long-horizon, memory-dependent manipulation tasks in both simulation and real-world settings, MemoryWAM outperforms strong VLA and WAM baselines while maintaining favorable computational efficiency (reduced inference latency and GPU memory usage).
AI.conclusion: MemoryWAM effectively resolves the memory-efficiency trade-off in world action models, enabling robust memory-dependent decision-making for robotic manipulation without prohibitive computational costs.

title: Automating SKILL.md Generation for Computer-Using Agents via Interaction Trajectory Mining
summary: Explicit skill libraries make computer-using agents easier to inspect, but it remains unclear whether such libraries can be mined from interaction data in a way that improves downstream policies. We study this question through a three-stage pipeline that segments GUI trajectories, clusters segments into candidate skills, and trains a skill-aware policy from the resulting annotations. The mined clusters are readable on the source benchmark: five of eight clusters have at least 0.95 purity against InteraSkill Workflows labels. However, readability does not imply transfer. GRPO improves IW skill-step accuracy only from 18.5\% to 20.5\%, leaves BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency priors on key source-domain metrics. We therefore present the method as a diagnostic study: trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether explicit skill libraries mined from GUI interaction data can improve downstream computer-using agents. Using a three-stage pipeline (segmentation, clustering, skill-aware policy training), the authors find that mined clusters are readable (5/8 clusters ≥0.95 purity) but fail to transfer: GRPO improves IW skill-step accuracy only marginally (18.5%→20.5%), leaves BrowseComp+ unchanged, and underperforms frequency priors. The work is presented as a diagnostic study, identifying insufficient boundary detection, orderless segment representation, and offline reward modeling as key limitations for cross-domain policy improvement.
AI.motivation: To determine whether explicit skill libraries mined from interaction data can improve downstream policies for computer-using agents, addressing the gap between inspectability and policy utility.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) segment GUI trajectories using a boundary detector, (2) cluster segments into candidate skills using orderless segment representations, (3) train a skill-aware policy via GRPO using an offline reward model. Evaluated on InteraSkill Workflows and BrowseComp+ benchmarks.
AI.result: Mined clusters are readable (5/8 clusters ≥0.95 purity against IW labels). However, GRPO improves IW skill-step accuracy only from 18.5% to 20.5%, leaves BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency priors on key source-domain metrics.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but current methods—boundary detection, orderless segment representation, and offline reward modeling—are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement.

title: Rethinking Shrinkage Bias in LLM FP4 Pretraining: Geometric Origin, Systemic Impact, and UFP4 Recipe
summary: FP4 training promises substantial reductions in memory and computation cost for LLM pretraining, yet current FP4 hardware paths and recipes, including NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin-class systems and AMD MI350-series GPUs, remain centered on E2M1 data elements. In this study, we identify a fundamental limitation of that choice: non-uniform formats such as E2M1 inherently suffer from Shrinkage Bias, a systematic negative rounding error caused by the geometric asymmetry of their representable bins. We show that this bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform (RHT), providing a unified explanation for the training instability observed in existing E2M1-based FP4 recipes. In contrast, uniform grids (E1M2/INT4) bypass this grid-geometry error and better convert the improved bucket utilization from RHT into higher quantization quality. Based on this finding, we propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit training recipe that applies RHT to all three training GEMMs while restricting stochastic rounding to dY alone. On Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B long-run pretraining, UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation than strong E2M1-based baselines, supported by scaling-law analysis and ablation studies. Our results suggest that future accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1.

AI.tldr: FP4 training using E2M1 suffers from Shrinkage Bias (systematic negative rounding error) due to geometric asymmetry; the proposed UFP4 recipe uses uniform grids (E1M2/INT4) which avoid this bias, and achieves lower loss degradation on LLMs up to 124B parameters.
AI.motivation: Current FP4 hardware paths (NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin, AMD MI350) center on E2M1, but the fundamental limitation of this non-uniform format's geometric asymmetry causing training instability has not been identified.
AI.method: Identified Shrinkage Bias in E2M1; proposed UFP4 using uniform grids (E1M2/INT4) with RHT applied to all three training GEMMs and stochastic rounding restricted to dY only.
AI.result: On Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B pretraining, UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation than E2M1-based baselines, validated with scaling-law analysis and ablation studies.
AI.conclusion: Future accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1.

title: Interpretable Sperm Morphology Classification via Attention-Guided Deep Learning
summary: Male infertility is a major cause of couple infertility, often linked to abnormal sperm morphology. While deep learning models offer automated analysis, most lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. This study proposes an attention-guided deep learning framework for sperm morphology classification. We combine a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to focus on key areas of the sperm head, improving both accuracy and interpretability. Evaluated on the SMIDS and HuSHem public datasets, our model achieves accuracies of 90.2% and 93.9% (macro F1 scores of 0.913 and 0.948), outperforming SimpleCNN and standard EfficientNet-B0. Furthermore, we use Grad-CAM++ visualizations to highlight features influencing the model's decisions. The results demonstrate that this accurate and transparent framework is a practical tool for automated sperm analysis in fertility clinics.

AI.tldr: An attention-guided deep learning framework (EfficientNet-B0 + CBAM) for sperm morphology classification achieves 90.2% and 93.9% accuracy on SMIDS and HuSHem datasets, outperforming baselines while providing interpretability via Grad-CAM++ visualizations.
AI.motivation: Male infertility is often linked to abnormal sperm morphology, yet existing deep learning models for automated sperm analysis lack interpretability, limiting their adoption in clinical settings.
AI.method: The study proposes an attention-guided framework combining a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for sperm morphology classification, and uses Grad-CAM++ for visual explanations of model decisions.
AI.result: The model achieves 90.2% accuracy (macro F1: 0.913) on SMIDS and 93.9% accuracy (macro F1: 0.948) on HuSHem, outperforming SimpleCNN and standard EfficientNet-B0.
AI.conclusion: The proposed accurate and transparent framework is a practical tool for automated sperm analysis in fertility clinics, balancing performance with interpretability.

title: Context-Aware Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling of IVF Laboratory Environmental Conditions
summary: IVF pregnancy rates are routinely modeled using patient-level variables, while high-resolution laboratory environmental data remain underutilized. We show that this is a missed opportunity. Rather than relying on raw sensor averages, we engineer 55 context-aware temporal features, including rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, and post-stress recovery speed, that capture the dynamics of incubator microenvironments. On 61 weeks of data from an Asian IVF clinic, these features reduce cross-validated prediction error to 1.27%, compared to 3-5% for raw averages. We then train a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model that shares environmental effects across an Asian and a Northern European clinic via partial pooling, while preserving site-specific baselines. On held-out data from the Northern European clinic, the model achieves R2 = 0.86 and a 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group over a naive baseline, demonstrating that structured environmental monitoring contains clinically meaningful, transferable signal.

AI.tldr: A study showing that context-aware temporal features from incubator microenvironments can significantly improve IVF pregnancy rate prediction (error reduced to 1.27%) and that a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model can transfer these environmental signals across clinics (R²=0.86, 64% error reduction for age 35-39 group).
AI.motivation: IVF pregnancy rate models typically use patient-level variables but ignore high-resolution laboratory environmental data, which the authors identify as a missed opportunity for improving prediction accuracy.
AI.method: Engineered 55 context-aware temporal features (e.g., rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, post-stress recovery speed) from incubator microenvironment data; trained a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model with partial pooling across an Asian and a Northern European clinic.
AI.result: Cross-validated prediction error reduced to 1.27% (vs. 3-5% for raw averages) on the Asian clinic dataset; on held-out Northern European clinic data, R²=0.86 with 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group.
AI.conclusion: Structured environmental monitoring contains clinically meaningful, transferable signal across clinics, demonstrating that incubator microenvironment dynamics should be incorporated into IVF outcome prediction models.

title: What Do Safety-Aligned LLMs Learn From Mixed Compliance Demonstrations?
summary: Prior work has shown that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak language models, but it remains unclear how models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations. We study this by mixing benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request, helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request, helpful response) and testing three hypotheses about how demonstration composition drives harmful compliance. Across four models, we find that benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demonstrations can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. We further show that preference optimization is the critical training stage that prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance, that demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias, and that models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal. Taken together, this work moves beyond showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing how it works: what models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how language models interpret benign vs. harmful compliance demonstrations in in-context learning, finding that demonstration type, ordering, and training methodology all affect jailbreak success.
AI.motivation: To move beyond simply showing that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak models, and instead characterize the mechanisms by which different types of compliance demonstrations drive harmful behavior.
AI.method: Mixed benign (non-harmful request, helpful response) and harmful (harmful request, helpful response) compliance demonstrations, tested three hypotheses about demonstration composition across four models, and examined effects of preference optimization, recency bias in ordering, and refusal-ICL interaction.
AI.result: Benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable; benign demonstrations can reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. Preference optimization prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance. Strong recency bias in demonstration ordering exists. Models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning (some adopt formatting even when refusing, others override all in-context signals).
AI.conclusion: What models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology.

title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages
summary:
LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.
  We introduce Multi-LCB, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs across twelve programming languages, including Python. Multi-LCB transforms Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks in other languages while preserving LCB's contamination controls and evaluation protocol. Because it is fully compatible with the original LCB format, Multi-LCB will automatically track future LCB updates, enabling systematic assessment of cross-language code generation competence and requiring models to sustain performance well beyond Python.
  We evaluated 24 LLMs for instruction and reasoning on Multi-LCB, uncovering evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial disparities in multilingual performance. Our results establish Multi-LCB as a rigorous new benchmark for multi-programming-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities.

AI.tldr: Multi-LCB extends LiveCodeBench to evaluate LLMs across 12 programming languages, revealing Python overfitting and multilingual performance gaps.
AI.motivation: LCB is widely used but restricted to Python, failing to assess whether LLMs generalize across diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.
AI.method: Transforms Python tasks from LCB into equivalent tasks in 12 languages while preserving LCB's contamination controls and evaluation protocol; fully compatible with original LCB format to auto-track future updates.
AI.result: Evaluated 24 LLMs for instruction and reasoning on Multi-LCB; found evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial multilingual performance disparities.
AI.conclusion: Multi-LCB addresses LCB's primary limitation, establishing a rigorous benchmark for multi-language code evaluation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM cross-language capabilities.

title: FlowEdit: Associative Memory for Lifelong Pronunciation Adaptation in Flow-Matching TTS
summary: Flow-matching text-to-speech systems achieve remarkable zero-shot quality but remain static after deployment: pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns persist unless the model is retrained. We introduce FlowEdit, a life-long adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that learns pronunciation corrections as latent conditioning edits rather than weight updates. When corrective feedback is provided, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space, then stores the correction in a Modern Hopfield Network serving as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching. On our curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns across 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Corrections complete in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: FlowEdit is a life-long adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that learns pronunciation corrections as latent conditioning edits stored in a Modern Hopfield Network, reducing Phoneme Error Rate on multilingual proper nouns by 92.7% without retraining.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching TTS systems achieve strong zero-shot quality but remain static after deployment, making persistent pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns unless the model is retrained.
AI.method: FlowEdit optimizes token-level perturbations in the text embedding space from corrective feedback, stores corrections in a Modern Hopfield Network as content-addressable episodic memory, and retrieves them at inference via soft attention with a similarity gate for fuzzy morphological matching.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns across 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining general-speech quality, with corrections completing in ~15 seconds on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: FlowEdit enables efficient, life-long pronunciation adaptation for frozen flow-matching TTS without weight updates, achieving substantial error reduction on proper nouns while preserving general speech quality.

title: DeepSWIP: Quotient-WMC Counterfactuals for Neural Probabilistic Logic Programs
summary: Neurosymbolic systems such as DeepProbLog combine neural perception with probabilistic logic, but standard inference is associational. Counterfactual reasoning additionally requires a causal semantics for interventions and evidence. We introduce DeepSWIP, a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog programs. Using neural materialization, we reduce fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices, apply Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs), and compute counterfactuals by weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program. Under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions, DeepSWIP is exact relative to the learned materialized FCM. The standard quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals identifies active neural probabilities and explains intervention cleaning, calibration sensitivity, and rare-evidence instability. Experiments on MPI3D confirm the transformation against a DeepTwin construction against 12,000 queries, as predicted and a 2.14$\times$ inference speedup from avoiding the Twin's endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment shows that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands. Code is at https://github.com/saibib/deep_SWIP.

AI.tldr: DeepSWIP introduces a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog that avoids the costly twin-network duplication, achieving exact counterfactual inference via weighted model counting with up to 2.14× speedup, while revealing how neural calibration affects causal estimands.
AI.motivation: Standard inference in neurosymbolic systems like DeepProbLog is associational, lacking a causal semantics needed for counterfactual reasoning. The authors aim to bridge this gap without incurring the computational overhead of twin-network constructions.
AI.method: DeepSWIP reduces fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices via neural materialization, then applies Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs) to compute counterfactuals through weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program, under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions.
AI.result: Experiments on MPI3D validate the transformation against a DeepTwin construction across 12,000 queries, showing a 2.14× inference speedup by avoiding endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment demonstrates that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands.
AI.conclusion: DeepSWIP provides an exact, efficient counterfactual inference framework for DeepProbLog, identifies the role of active neural probabilities in quotient-WMC form, and shows practical benefits in speed and bias correction for causal estimands.

title: LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents
summary: Policy-adherent tool-calling agents in customer-service domains must maintain task states across turns while calling tools and obeying domain policies. Task states consist of relevant facts, identifiers, constraints, and conditions observed through user interaction and tool calls. In standard agents, task states are not represented separately. Observations, tool returns, and policy instructions are placed in the prompt, leaving agents to reconstruct the relevant states from the prompt each time they decide what to do next. This design makes state management implicit, creating two common failure modes. An agent may retrieve the right facts but later ground its decision in stale, missing, or incorrect information; and a syntactically valid tool call may still violate a domain policy that depends on the current task state. We introduce \textsc{LedgerAgent}, an inference-time method for tool-calling agents that maintains observed task states in a separate ledger and renders the states into the prompt. The ledger is also used to check state-dependent policy constraints before environment-changing tool calls are executed, blocking policy violations. Across four customer-service domains and a mixed panel of open- and closed-weight models, \textsc{LedgerAgent} improves average pass\textasciicircum{}k over a standard prompt-based tool-calling approach, with the largest gains under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.

AI.tldr: LedgerAgent improves tool-calling agents in customer-service domains by maintaining a separate ledger for task states and using it for state-dependent policy enforcement, outperforming standard prompt-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Standard tool-calling agents do not explicitly represent task states; they rely on implicit state reconstruction from prompts, leading to failures from stale/missing information and policy violations due to state-dependent constraints.
AI.method: LedgerAgent maintains observed task states in a separate ledger, renders these states into the prompt, and uses the ledger to check state-dependent policy constraints before executing environment-changing tool calls, blocking violations.
AI.result: Across four customer-service domains and mixed open/closed-weight models, LedgerAgent improves average pass^k over standard prompt-based tool-calling, with largest gains under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.
AI.conclusion: Explicit state management via a ledger reduces failures from implicit state handling and improves policy adherence in tool-calling agents for customer service.
