title: How Do Instructions Shape Speech? Cross-Attention Attribution for Style-Captioned Text-to-Speech
summary: Style-captioned text-to-speech systems use natural language to control voice characteristics, but how individual words influence acoustic output remains unclear. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failure modes and improving controllability in expressive TTS. We propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models, adapting the DAAM framework to the speech domain for the first time, and apply it to CapSpeech-TTS. Our method extracts per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps. We analyze 3,600 (style caption, text transcript) combinations comprising 120 style captions conditioning the generation of 30 text transcripts each, revealing how caption tokens shape waveforms. Results show: (1) style tokens have lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning; (2) style attention correlates with F0 and energy; (3) style conditioning peaks in early steps and deep layers; (4) attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, co-occurring with the style importance peak, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical stage. This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models

AI.tldr: First application of DAAM-style cross-attention attribution to speech diffusion models (CapSpeech-TTS), analyzing how 120 style captions influence acoustic output across 3,600 combinations. Reveals style tokens have lower temporal variance, correlate with prosodic features (F0/energy), peak in early/layer-deep stages, and exhibit maximal network selectivity at layer 17.
AI.motivation: Style-captioned TTS lacks interpretability—how individual words control voice characteristics is unknown, which hinders diagnosing failures and improving controllability in expressive TTS.
AI.method: Adapted DAAM framework to speech diffusion models; computed per-token cross-attention heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps for CapSpeech-TTS using 120 style captions × 30 text transcripts = 3,600 combinations.
AI.result: (1) Style tokens show lower temporal variance than content/function tokens. (2) Style attention correlates with F0 and energy. (3) Style conditioning peaks in early ODE steps and deep layers. (4) Attention entropy is minimized at layer 17, coinciding with style importance peak.
AI.conclusion: First study interpreting how natural language shapes cross-attention in speech diffusion models, providing insights into style controllability mechanisms.

title: Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift
summary: Calibration aligns a model's predictive uncertainty with the frequencies of its empirical outcomes and is important for understanding and trusting reported probabilities. Recent work shows that enforcing calibration at the level of individual predictors can improve ensemble accuracy and calibration, with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models showing strong empirical improvements in particular; however, the conditions under which calibration helps MoE are not well understood. In this work, we study how MoE models behave under distribution shift, focusing on how routing mechanisms interact with expert-level calibration. We show that expert calibration is sufficient to ensure calibration of the overall model under a broad class of distribution shifts in hard-routed models, but is insufficient for calibrating soft-routed models. To address this, we propose an adversarial reweighting that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift, and we demonstrate that it improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult subsets of the data, across model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how calibration interacts with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models under distribution shift, showing expert calibration is sufficient for hard-routed but not soft-routed models, and proposes adversarial reweighting to improve the accuracy-calibration tradeoff.
AI.motivation: To understand the conditions under which calibration helps mixture-of-experts models, particularly under distribution shift where routing mechanisms interact with expert-level calibration.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze expert calibration sufficiency for hard-routed vs. soft-routed MoE models under distribution shift, and propose an adversarial reweighting method that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift.
AI.result: Expert calibration is sufficient for overall model calibration under broad distribution shifts in hard-routed models but insufficient for soft-routed models. The proposed adversarial reweighting improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff across model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: The work provides theoretical understanding of calibration in MoE models under distribution shift and offers a practical method (adversarial reweighting) that effectively improves both accuracy and calibration, particularly on difficult data subsets.

title: Human Universal Grasping
summary: Humans can grasp objects effortlessly, whereas multi-fingered robots are far from this level of generality. We argue that the most natural source of robot grasping data is from humans, who pick up thousands of objects every day. We present HUG, a flow-matching model that generates diverse human grasps for any user-specified object in a single RGB-D image captured from a stereo camera. Using smart glasses, we first collect 1M-HUGs, an egocentric dataset of human grasps spanning 1M frames (27.8 hrs) and 6,707 object instances across 41 buildings. Next, to model the distribution of natural human grasps, our novel flow-matching model fuses RGB and depth observations to output a grasp parameterized by wrist translation, wrist rotation, and MANO hand pose. Predicted grasps can be retargeted to various robot hands, enabling zero-shot grasping in everyday scenes. To standardize evaluation, we build a new simulated benchmark, HUG-Bench, of 90 unseen objects from five geometric categories and various sizes, with metric-scale 3D meshes. We evaluate HUG in the real world on the 30-object test set of HUG-Bench across multiple stereo cameras, robot embodiments, and household environments. HUG outperforms the state-of-the-art grasping baselines by +23% and +34% on our challenging object set. Code, data, benchmark, checkpoints, and an interactive demo are released on our website: https://grasping.io/

AI.tldr: HUG is a flow-matching model that generates diverse human grasps from a single RGB-D image, trained on a large-scale egocentric dataset (1M-HUGs) collected via smart glasses, enabling zero-shot grasping for robot hands with state-of-the-art performance (+23-34% over baselines).
AI.motivation: Multi-fingered robots cannot grasp objects with the same generality as humans. The authors argue that human grasping data is the most natural source for teaching robots to grasp, motivating the need for a large-scale egocentric human grasp dataset and a model that learns from it.
AI.method: A flow-matching model that fuses RGB and depth observations from a single stereo camera image to output wrist translation, wrist rotation, and MANO hand pose. The model is trained on 1M-HUGs, a 1M-frame egocentric dataset collected via smart glasses across 41 buildings with 6,707 object instances. Predicted grasps are retargeted to various robot hands.
AI.result: HUG outperforms state-of-the-art grasping baselines by +23% and +34% on the HUG-Bench object set, demonstrated in real-world experiments across multiple stereo cameras, robot embodiments, and household environments.
AI.conclusion: The HUG model, trained on large-scale egocentric human grasp data, enables zero-shot robot grasping in everyday scenes and significantly outperforms prior methods, suggesting that human grasp data is a highly effective source for robot grasping.
